questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Explain and calculate liquidity trading risk via cost of liquidation and liquidity-adjusted VaR (LVaR).
questions.reading: Hull, Risk Management and Financial Institutions, Ch. 24: Liquidity Risk
questions.question: A junior analyst at a European asset manager is assessing the market liquidity of a corporate bond that trades infrequently. The bond is quoted bid EUR 89.00, offer EUR 96.00. Which of the following is closest to the proportional bid-offer spread of the bond?
questions.solution:
Hull defines two spread measures. The dollar bid-offer spread is the raw price difference; the proportional bid-offer spread divides that difference by the mid-market price, where the mid-market price is halfway between the bid and the offer.

$$p = \text{Offer price} - \text{Bid price}$$
$$s = \frac{\text{Offer price} - \text{Bid price}}{\text{Mid-market price}}$$

**Step 1. Dollar spread:** $p = 96.00 - 89.00 = \text{EUR } 7.00$.

**Step 2. Mid-market price:** $(96.00 + 89.00) \div 2 = \text{EUR } 92.50$. This is the price Hull treats as the fair price of the asset.

**Step 3. Proportional spread:**
$$s = 7.00 \div 92.50 = 0.075676, \text{ or about } 7.57\%$$

Interpretation: a round trip in this bond costs roughly 7.6% of its fair value. Hull notes that proportional spreads range from about 0.05% for very liquid instruments to 5% or even 10% for illiquid ones, so 7.6% places this bond firmly at the illiquid end.

a.reason: 0.0378 is exactly half of the correct spread. It is what you get by applying the one-half unwind factor ($s\alpha/2$) when the question asked for the spread itself, not for the cost of liquidation.

c.reason: 0.1538 = 7.00 ÷ 45.50. This divides by half the mid-market price instead of the mid-market price, doubling the answer.

d.reason: 7.0000 is the dollar bid-offer spread p, not the proportional spread s. The question asked for the proportional measure.

trap.explanation: Three distinct failure modes are on offer. Option A is the intermediate-result trap: the one-half factor belongs to the unwind cost formula, not the spread definition. Option C is a denominator error: the divisor is the full mid-market price, not half of it. Option D is a units error: dollar spread reported where a proportion was asked. Under time pressure the safest habit is to write the mid down explicitly before dividing.

questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a dealer bank is presenting to a group of newly hired analysts on how quoted bid and offer prices behave as trade size changes. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: In the market for large trades between sophisticated financial institutions, the bid price tends to fall and the offer price tends to rise as the size of the trade increases, because hedging the exposure created by the trade becomes more difficult.
A market maker's quote is firm for any size, so the proportional bid-offer spread of an instrument is independent of the quantity transacted.
In the retail market, a customer requesting a larger foreign exchange transaction will generally receive a worse quote, mirroring the pattern observed in the wholesale market.
Where no market maker quotes an instrument, there is no bid-offer spread, so the cost of unwinding a position in that instrument is zero.

questions.solution:
Hull identifies four determinants of the price at which an asset can actually be sold: (1) the mid-market price or estimate of value, (2) how much is to be sold, (3) how quickly it is to be sold, (4) the economic environment.

For instruments with a market maker, the quoted bid and offer are firm only up to the market maker's size limit. Beyond that limit the bid schedule slopes down and the offer schedule slopes up, because the market maker knows that hedging the exposure created by a larger trade is harder. This is the pattern in Figure 1.1 of the reading.

Two refinements matter for the exam. First, the retail market sometimes shows the opposite pattern: an individual doing a larger foreign exchange transaction or a larger deposit at a bank branch is likely to get a better quote. Second, where there is no market maker, there is still an implicit bid-offer spread, because the price quoted by a counterparty or interdealer broker depends on which side of the trade you want.

Practical consequence: because $s$ increases with position size, holding many small positions rather than a few large ones reduces liquidity trading risk, and position-size limits are therefore a liquidity risk control, not only a market risk control.

a.reason: This is the wholesale pattern in Figure 1.1, with the hedging-difficulty rationale the reading gives for it.

b.reason: The quote is firm only up to a stated size. Beyond that the spread widens. The word 'any' converts a conditional truth into an absolute claim.

c.reason: Polarity reversal. The reading states that retail bid-offer spreads sometimes show the opposite pattern to the wholesale market: the larger the retail transaction, the better the quote.

d.reason: Where there is no market maker there is still an implicit bid-offer spread, so the unwind cost is not zero. This is an absolute claim of the kind that is almost always wrong on this exam.

trap.explanation: Option C is the one that catches prepared candidates, because it states a true mechanism (spreads widen with size) and simply attaches it to the wrong market. Whenever a statement pairs a direction with a venue, check the venue. Options B and D are eliminable on the absolute-claim heuristic alone ('any size', 'no bid-offer spread', 'zero').

questions.loText: Explain and calculate liquidity trading risk via cost of liquidation and liquidity-adjusted VaR (LVaR).
questions.reading: Hull, Risk Management and Financial Institutions, Ch. 24: Liquidity Risk
questions.question: A risk consultant is preparing a note for a bank's board on the lessons of the 2007 credit crisis for market liquidity. Which of the following best characterises the relationship between transparency and liquidity described in the reading?

options.text: Assets whose nature is not well understood are unlikely to trade in a liquid market for long, and when they trade again prices are likely to be low and bid-offer spreads high.
Complex structured products can sustain a liquid market indefinitely provided that credit ratings are available, because ratings substitute adequately for an understanding of the instrument.
During the crisis, credit default swaps became illiquid while ABS CDO tranches continued to trade actively, showing that standardisation does not protect liquidity.
The sale by Merrill Lynch of ABS CDO tranches at 22 cents on the dollar demonstrated that transparency had been restored to the securitisation market.

questions.solution:
The reading is explicit: the market can get carried away trading complex products that are not transparent, but when it comes to its senses liquidity for those products soon disappears, and when they trade again prices are low and bid-offer spreads are high.

The mechanism is informational. Portfolios of subprime mortgages were securitised, re-securitised, and re-re-securitised. Some ABS CDOs contained non-mortgage assets and tranches of other ABS CDOs. After August 2007 participants realised they knew very little about the risks in instruments they had bought, and belatedly recognised that they had been using credit ratings as a substitute for understanding. Institutions could not mark the positions to market because they had neither the models nor solid information on the underlying portfolios.

The contrast case matters. Well-defined credit derivatives such as plain credit default swaps continued to trade actively throughout the crisis. Complexity and opacity, not the derivative form itself, destroyed liquidity.

The Merrill Lynch transaction (USD 30.6 billion of previously AAA-rated ABS CDO tranches sold to Lone Star Funds at 22 cents on the dollar in July 2008) is cited as evidence of how low prices go when an opaque market reopens, not as evidence of restored transparency.

a.reason: This is the reading's stated conclusion, including both the price and the spread consequence.

b.reason: Reverses the lesson. The reading identifies reliance on ratings as a substitute for understanding as part of the problem, not as a remedy.

c.reason: Sibling swap. The two instrument classes are transposed: CDS continued to trade actively; the ABS CDOs became illiquid.

d.reason: Misattribution. The 22-cent sale illustrates the depth of the price discount in a reopened opaque market, not a return of transparency.

trap.explanation: Option C is the dangerous one. A candidate who remembers that 'one of them kept trading and one of them did not' but not which is which has a fifty per cent chance of getting it wrong. Fix the direction: simple and standardised survived, complex and re-securitised did not.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Explain and calculate liquidity trading risk via cost of liquidation and liquidity-adjusted VaR (LVaR).
questions.reading: Hull, Risk Management and Financial Institutions, Ch. 24: Liquidity Risk
questions.question:
An investor holds two equity positions:

| Position | Mid-market value | Proportional bid-offer spread |
|---|---|---|
| Company A | Short GBP 10,000 | 0.030 |
| Company B | Long GBP 17,000 | 0.040 |

Assuming normal market conditions, which of the following is closest to the cost of unwinding the two-position portfolio?

options.text: GBP 340
GBP 455
GBP 490
GBP 980

questions.solution:
Liquidating a position costs half the spread applied to the mid-market value of the position, because trades are executed at the bid or the offer rather than at the mid. Summing over positions:

$$\text{Cost of liquidation (normal market)} = \sum_i \left( s_i \times \alpha_i \right) \div 2$$

where $s_i$ is the proportional bid-offer spread of instrument $i$ and $\alpha_i$ is the dollar (mid-market) value of the position in instrument $i$.

**Step 1.** Company A (short GBP 10,000). Unwinding a short means buying back, which is done at the offer. The direction of the position does not change the cost, only the side of the spread paid, so $\alpha_A = 10{,}000$ in absolute value:
$$0.030 \times 10{,}000 \div 2 = \text{GBP } 150$$

**Step 2.** Company B (long GBP 17,000). Unwinding a long means selling at the bid:
$$0.040 \times 17{,}000 \div 2 = \text{GBP } 340$$

**Step 3. Total cost of liquidation:**
$$150 + 340 = \text{GBP } 490$$

Interpretation: GBP 490 is what it costs, in normal market conditions, to convert this book to cash at prevailing spreads. Note that the two legs add rather than net. Hull makes the point explicitly: diversification reduces market risk but does not necessarily reduce liquidity trading risk.

a.reason: GBP 340 is the Company B leg alone. It results from treating the short position as costless to unwind, or from netting the short against the long and pricing only the residual.

b.reason: GBP 455 = (0.040 × 10,000 + 0.030 × 17,000) ÷ 2. The two spreads have been assigned to the wrong positions.

d.reason: GBP 980 = 0.030 × 10,000 + 0.040 × 17,000. The one-half factor has been omitted from both legs.

trap.explanation: Option A is the conceptual trap and the one worth rehearsing: candidates instinctively net a short against a long, as they would for market risk. Liquidity trading risk does not net; both legs must be traded and both pay half a spread. Option D is the mechanical trap, the omitted one-half, which recurs in every question built on this formula.

questions.loText: Explain and calculate liquidity trading risk via cost of liquidation and liquidity-adjusted VaR (LVaR).
questions.reading: Hull, Risk Management and Financial Institutions, Ch. 24: Liquidity Risk
questions.question: Cathleen Wilson is the liquidity manager for CPR Bank. The bank holds 50 million shares of one company and 20 million ounces of a commodity. The shares are quoted bid USD 80.40, offer USD 80.80. The commodity is quoted bid USD 30.60; Wilson cannot recall the commodity's offer price. She does know that the mid-market value of the commodity position is USD 614 million and that the cost of liquidating the whole book in a normal market is USD 12.0 million. Which of the following is closest to the offer price of the commodity?
questions.solution:
Start from the formula and solve for the unknown leg.

$$\text{Cost of liquidation} = (s_{\text{shares}} \times \alpha_{\text{shares}}) \div 2 + (s_{\text{comm}} \times \alpha_{\text{comm}}) \div 2$$

**Step 1. Shares.** Mid-market price = $(80.40 + 80.80) \div 2 = \text{USD } 80.60$, so the mid-market value of the position is $80.60 \times 50 \text{ million} = \text{USD } 4{,}030 \text{ million}$. The proportional spread is $0.40 \div 80.60 = 0.0049628$.
$$\text{Shares leg} = 0.0049628 \times 4{,}030 \div 2 = \text{USD } 10.00 \text{ million}$$

**Step 2.** The commodity leg must therefore account for the remainder:
$$12.00 - 10.00 = \text{USD } 2.00 \text{ million} = (s_{\text{comm}} \times 614) \div 2$$
$$s_{\text{comm}} = 4.00 \div 614 = 0.0065147$$

**Step 3. Recover the offer price.** The commodity position is 20 million ounces with a mid-market value of USD 614 million, so the mid-market price is $614 \div 20 = \text{USD } 30.70$. Let $w$ be the offer price. By definition of the proportional spread:
$$(w - 30.60) \div 30.70 = 0.0065147$$
$$w = 30.60 + (0.0065147 \times 30.70) = 30.60 + 0.20 = \text{USD } 30.80$$

Check: bid 30.60 and offer 30.80 give a mid of 30.70, consistent with the stated position value of USD 614 million over 20 million ounces. The internal consistency check is the fastest way to confirm the answer under exam conditions.

a.reason: USD 30.70 is the commodity's mid-market price, not its offer. It also arises from omitting the one-half factor on the commodity leg (setting $s \times 614 = 2.00$), which halves the required spread.

c.reason: USD 30.90 results from adding the half-spread to the mid-market price rather than to the bid. The offer sits half a spread above the mid, not a full spread.

d.reason: USD 31.80 results from attributing the entire USD 12.0 million cost to the commodity leg, ignoring the USD 10.0 million contributed by the share position.

trap.explanation: Option A is the intermediate-result trap in its purest form: the mid-market price is a legitimate quantity computed on the way to the answer, and it sits in the option list waiting to be selected. Option D is the excess-data trap in reverse, discarding a leg that was given rather than an input that was redundant. Always write down what each intermediate number is before you look at the options.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Explain and calculate liquidity trading risk via cost of liquidation and liquidity-adjusted VaR (LVaR).
questions.reading: Hull, Risk Management and Financial Institutions, Ch. 24: Liquidity Risk
questions.question:
A bank holds a position in shares with a mid-market value of AUD 1,400 million and a position in a commodity with a mid-market value of AUD 840 million. The following data are available:

| | Mean | Standard deviation |
|---|---|---|
| Bid-offer spread, shares | AUD 1.0 million | AUD 1.1 million |
| Bid-offer spread, commodity | AUD 0.1 million | AUD 0.1 million |
| Proportional bid-offer spread, shares | 0.0340 | 0.0180 |
| Proportional bid-offer spread, commodity | 0.0044 | 0.0044 |

Assuming the spreads are normally distributed, which of the following is closest to the cost of liquidation in a stressed market at a 95% confidence level?

options.text: AUD 25.65 million
AUD 44.53 million
AUD 49.42 million
AUD 98.83 million

questions.solution:
The stressed-market measure replaces the point estimate of the spread with a high percentile of its distribution:

$$\text{Cost of liquidation (stressed market)} = \sum_i (\mu_i + \lambda \sigma_i) \times \alpha_i \div 2$$

where $\mu_i$ and $\sigma_i$ are the mean and standard deviation of the proportional bid-offer spread of instrument $i$, $\alpha_i$ is the mid-market value of the position, and $\lambda$ sets the confidence level. At 95% with normally distributed spreads, $\lambda = 1.645$.

**Step 1.** Identify which inputs are needed. The formula takes proportional spreads because it is multiplied by the dollar value of the position. The two dollar-spread rows are redundant here and should be ignored.

**Step 2. Shares leg:**
$$1{,}400 \times (0.0340 + 1.645 \times 0.0180) \div 2 = 700 \times 0.063610 = \text{AUD } 44.53 \text{ million}$$

**Step 3. Commodity leg.** Because the mean equals the standard deviation, the bracket simplifies to $0.0044 \times (1 + 1.645) = 0.0044 \times 2.645$:
$$840 \times (0.0044 + 1.645 \times 0.0044) \div 2 = 420 \times 0.011638 = \text{AUD } 4.89 \text{ million}$$

**Step 4. Total:**
$$44.53 + 4.89 = \text{AUD } 49.42 \text{ million}$$

Interpretation: in a stressed market this book costs about AUD 49.4 million to liquidate, against AUD 25.6 million in normal conditions, roughly double. Note the built-in conservatism: the stressed-market formula assumes the spreads on all instruments are perfectly correlated. Hull defends this, on the ground that when liquidity tightens spreads widen across the board.

a.reason: AUD 25.65 million is the normal-market cost of liquidation, which uses the mean spreads only and drops the $\lambda\sigma$ stress term entirely.

b.reason: AUD 44.53 million is the shares leg alone. The commodity position has been omitted.

d.reason: AUD 98.83 million omits the one-half factor on both legs, doubling the answer.

trap.explanation: The dollar-spread rows are deliberate excess data, a signature GARP move. A candidate who reaches for AUD 1.0 million and AUD 1.1 million because they appear first in the table will produce a nonsensical figure and lose two minutes. Option A is the scope trap (right formula family, wrong market condition) and it is the one most likely to look plausible if you misread 'stressed' as a scene-setting adjective rather than a formula selector.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Explain and calculate liquidity trading risk via cost of liquidation and liquidity-adjusted VaR (LVaR).
questions.reading: Hull, Risk Management and Financial Institutions, Ch. 24: Liquidity Risk
questions.question: JCT Bank holds a position in shares of company X and a separate position in commodity Y. The bank holds 1 million units of each. The mid-market value of the share position is USD 72,000,000 and the mid-market value of the commodity position is USD 47,000,000. The mean and standard deviation of the dollar bid-offer spread are USD 1.30 and USD 1.03 for the shares, and USD 1.32 and USD 0.88 for the commodity. Assuming spreads are approximately normally distributed, which of the following is closest to the cost of liquidation in a stressed market at a 99% confidence level?

options.text: USD 1.31 million
USD 2.88 million
USD 3.53 million
USD 7.06 million

questions.solution:
The formula requires proportional spreads:

$$\text{Cost of liquidation (stressed market)} = \sum_i (\mu_i + \lambda \sigma_i) \times \alpha_i \div 2, \quad \lambda = 2.326 \text{ at } 99\%$$

**Long route.** Convert dollar spreads to proportional spreads by dividing by the unit price. With 1 million units, the unit price of the shares is $72{,}000{,}000 \div 1{,}000{,}000 = \text{USD } 72$ and the unit price of the commodity is USD 47.

Shares: $\mu = 1.30 \div 72 = 0.018056$; $\sigma = 1.03 \div 72 = 0.014306$

Commodity: $\mu = 1.32 \div 47 = 0.028085$; $\sigma = 0.88 \div 47 = 0.018723$

$$\text{Shares leg} = 72{,}000{,}000 \times (0.018056 + 2.326 \times 0.014306) \div 2 = \text{USD } 1{,}847{,}894$$
$$\text{Commodity leg} = 47{,}000{,}000 \times (0.028085 + 2.326 \times 0.018723) \div 2 = \text{USD } 1{,}683{,}439$$
$$\text{Total} = \text{USD } 3{,}531{,}333, \text{ or about USD } 3.53 \text{ million}$$

**Shortcut.** The division by the unit price and the multiplication by the position value cancel, leaving the number of units. This lets you work directly in dollars per unit:

$$\text{Cost} = \sum_i (\mu_i^\$ + \lambda \sigma_i^\$) \times N_i \div 2 = 1{,}000{,}000 \times [(1.30 + 2.326 \times 1.03) + (1.32 + 2.326 \times 0.88)] \div 2 = \text{USD } 3.53 \text{ million}$$

Finding the shortcut saves roughly ninety seconds and removes four opportunities for a rounding slip. Small differences against published answers (for example USD 3,531,536) come from rounding the proportional spreads to four decimals before multiplying.

a.reason: USD 1.31 million = 1,000,000 × (1.30 + 1.32) ÷ 2. This is the normal-market cost using mean spreads only, dropping the $\lambda\sigma$ term.

b.reason: USD 2.88 million uses $\lambda = 1.645$, the 95% deviate, instead of $\lambda = 2.326$ for 99%.

c.reason: USD 3.53 million.

d.reason: USD 7.06 million is exactly twice the correct figure, from omitting the one-half factor.

trap.explanation: The primary trap is the unit twin: the stem hands you dollar spreads where the formula expects proportional spreads, and multiplying USD 1.30 by USD 72,000,000 produces an absurd number that a rushed candidate may still round toward an option. Option B is the confidence-level twin, 1.645 for 2.326, which is the single most common numerical slip in this chapter. Write the deviate down before you start.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Explain and calculate liquidity trading risk via cost of liquidation and liquidity-adjusted VaR (LVaR).
questions.reading: Hull, Risk Management and Financial Institutions, Ch. 24: Liquidity Risk
questions.question: A portfolio holds 100,000 shares of a stock, a single position worth SGD 3.0 million. The stock is quoted bid SGD 29.00, offer SGD 31.00. The stock's daily volatility is 1.43%. Assume arithmetic returns are normally distributed and the expected daily return rounds to zero, so that absolute and relative VaR coincide. Assume a constant bid-offer spread. Which of the following is closest to the position's one-day 99% liquidity-adjusted value at risk (LVaR)?
questions.solution:
Hull's first definition of LVaR adds the normal-market cost of liquidation to conventional VaR:

$$\text{Liquidity-adjusted VaR} = \text{VaR} + \sum_i (s_i \times \alpha_i) \div 2$$

The logic is that VaR measures the worst-case mark-to-market move assuming you could trade at the mid, while the cost of liquidation measures what you give up at the spread assuming prices do not move. The two are separate sources of loss and are simply added.

**Step 1. Market VaR at 99% (deviate 2.326):**
$$\text{VaR} = 2.326 \times 0.0143 \times 3{,}000{,}000 = \text{SGD } 99{,}785$$
This is the worst one-day mark-to-market loss not expected to be exceeded 99% of the time.

**Step 2. Liquidity cost.** Mid-market price = $(31.00 + 29.00) \div 2 = \text{SGD } 30.00$, so the proportional spread is $2.00 \div 30.00 = 0.06667$:
$$LC = 0.06667 \times 3{,}000{,}000 \div 2 = \text{SGD } 100{,}000$$
This is what unwinding costs at prevailing spreads even if the price never moves.

**Step 3. Add:**
$$LVaR = 99{,}785 + 100{,}000 = \text{SGD } 199{,}785, \text{ or about SGD } 200{,}000$$

Interpretation: adding the liquidity adjustment roughly doubles the risk number for this position. That ratio is the point of the exercise. For a wide-spread instrument the liquidity component can dominate the price component, which is invisible to a conventional VaR framework.

a.reason: SGD 100,000 is either component taken alone: the liquidity cost is exactly SGD 100,000 and the market VaR of SGD 99,785 also rounds to SGD 100,000. Either way it is an intermediate result, not the LVaR.

b.reason: SGD 170,000 uses the 95% deviate of 1.645 instead of the 99% deviate of 2.326: $1.645 \times 0.0143 \times 3{,}000{,}000 = \text{SGD } 70{,}571$, plus SGD 100,000.

d.reason: SGD 300,000 omits the one-half factor in the liquidity cost, giving SGD 200,000 of liquidity cost plus SGD 99,785 of VaR.

trap.explanation: Option A is unusually nasty because two different mistakes converge on it: stopping after the VaR, or stopping after the liquidity cost. When a question gives you a spread and a volatility, both must appear in the final answer. If your answer uses only one of them, you have answered a different question.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Explain and calculate liquidity trading risk via cost of liquidation and liquidity-adjusted VaR (LVaR).
questions.reading: Hull, Risk Management and Financial Institutions, Ch. 24: Liquidity Risk
questions.question: A position worth CNY 2.0 million consists of 50,000 shares. The stock is quoted bid CNY 39.00, offer CNY 41.00. The standard deviation of the proportional bid-offer spread is 2.0%. The stock's daily volatility is 2.00%. Assume arithmetic returns are normally distributed and the expected daily return rounds to zero. The risk manager wants the liquidity component measured under stressed conditions, that is, using a volatile rather than a constant spread. Using a normal deviate of 1.65, which of the following is closest to the position's one-day 95% liquidity-adjusted value at risk?
questions.solution:
Hull's second definition of LVaR uses the stressed-market formula for the liquidity leg:

$$\text{Liquidity-adjusted VaR} = \text{VaR} + \sum_i (\mu_i + \lambda \sigma_i) \times \alpha_i \div 2$$

**Step 1. Market VaR at 95%:**
$$\text{VaR} = 1.65 \times 0.0200 \times 2{,}000{,}000 = \text{CNY } 66{,}000$$

**Step 2.** Mean proportional spread. Mid-market price = $(41.00 + 39.00) \div 2 = \text{CNY } 40.00$, so $\mu = 2.00 \div 40.00 = 0.050$. The standard deviation of the proportional spread is given as $\sigma = 0.020$.

**Step 3. Stressed liquidity cost.** Note that the same deviate of 1.65 is applied to the spread distribution:
$$LC = (0.050 + 1.65 \times 0.020) \div 2 \times 2{,}000{,}000 = (0.050 + 0.033) \div 2 \times 2{,}000{,}000 = 0.04150 \times 2{,}000{,}000 = \text{CNY } 83{,}000$$

**Step 4. Add:**
$$LVaR = 66{,}000 + 83{,}000 = \text{CNY } 149{,}000$$

Interpretation: allowing the spread to be volatile raises the liquidity component from CNY 50,000 (the constant-spread figure) to CNY 83,000, an increase of two thirds. Note that the liquidity component now exceeds the market VaR component. Using the exact deviate 1.645 gives CNY 148,691, which still rounds to CNY 149,000.

a.reason: CNY 83,000 is the stressed liquidity cost alone. The market VaR has been omitted.

b.reason: CNY 116,000 = 66,000 + 50,000. This uses the constant-spread liquidity cost (0.050 ÷ 2 × 2,000,000) and so ignores the stated spread volatility, answering the normal-market question instead of the stressed one.

d.reason: CNY 232,000 = 66,000 + 166,000. The one-half factor has been omitted from the liquidity cost.

trap.explanation: Option B is the scope trap and the one to rehearse: the stem gives a spread volatility of 2.0%, and if you do not use it you have silently downgraded a stressed-market question to a normal-market one. Treat any stated spread standard deviation as an instruction about which formula to use. Option A is the familiar intermediate-result trap.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Explain and calculate liquidity trading risk via cost of liquidation and liquidity-adjusted VaR (LVaR).
questions.reading: Hull, Risk Management and Financial Institutions, Ch. 24: Liquidity Risk
questions.question: A position worth BRL 1.0 million consists of 50,000 shares of an asset quoted bid BRL 19.00, offer BRL 21.00. The asset has an expected return of 14.0% per annum and an annual volatility of 26.0%. The risk manager measures lognormal VaR over a one-year horizon, that is, geometric returns are assumed to be normally distributed. Assuming a constant spread and a 95% confidence level, which of the following is closest to the one-year liquidity-adjusted VaR?
questions.solution:
The liquidity adjustment is added to whatever VaR the institution computes. The VaR method changes the first term only.

$$\text{Lognormal VaR} = V \times [1 - \exp(\mu - \sigma z)]$$

**Step 1. Lognormal VaR at 95% (z = 1.645):**
$$\mu - \sigma z = 0.140 - (0.260 \times 1.645) = 0.140 - 0.42770 = -0.28770$$
$$\exp(-0.28770) = 0.75001$$
$$\text{VaR} = 1{,}000{,}000 \times (1 - 0.75001) = \text{BRL } 249{,}986$$

Interpretation of this intermediate: over one year, the position is 95% likely to retain at least 75% of its value, so the worst-case mark-to-market loss is about BRL 250,000. Because the lognormal form bounds the loss at 100% of value, it produces a smaller figure than the normal approximation at long horizons.

**Step 2. Liquidity cost.** Mid-market price = $(21.00 + 19.00) \div 2 = \text{BRL } 20.00$, so $s = 2.00 \div 20.00 = 0.100$:
$$LC = 0.100 \times 1{,}000{,}000 \div 2 = \text{BRL } 50{,}000$$

**Step 3. Add:**
$$LVaR = 249{,}986 + 50{,}000 = \text{BRL } 299{,}986, \text{ or about BRL } 300{,}000$$

a.reason: BRL 250,000 is the lognormal VaR alone, with the liquidity adjustment omitted. This is the intermediate-result trap.

c.reason: BRL 350,000 = 250,000 + 100,000. The one-half factor has been dropped from the liquidity cost.

d.reason: BRL 478,000 = (1.645 × 0.260 × 1,000,000) + 50,000. This uses relative normal VaR of BRL 427,700 instead of lognormal VaR, ignoring both the drift term and the lognormal transformation.

trap.explanation: Option D is the method twin and it is the substantive test here: over a one-year horizon the difference between normal and lognormal VaR is large (BRL 427,700 against BRL 249,986), so the phrase 'geometric returns are normally distributed' is doing real work in the stem and must be read. Option A punishes anyone who computes the harder leg and then forgets the easy one.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Explain and calculate liquidity trading risk via cost of liquidation and liquidity-adjusted VaR (LVaR).
questions.reading: Hull, Risk Management and Financial Institutions, Ch. 24: Liquidity Risk
questions.question: A trader must unwind a large position in an illiquid asset over $n$ trading days. The dollar bid-offer spread is an increasing function of the quantity traded in a single day, and daily mid-market price changes are normally distributed. The trader wishes to minimise value at risk after trading costs. Which of the following statements about the resulting optimal schedule is most accurate?

options.text: The position should be liquidated in equal daily tranches of V divided by n, because equal tranches minimise the average bid-offer spread paid over the unwind.
More than V divided by n should be traded on the first day, and as the confidence level used in the objective is reduced the daily amounts become more even.
Less than V divided by n should be traded on the first day, because the bid-offer spread rises with daily volume and front-loading therefore maximises total spread cost.
Raising the confidence level from 95% to 99% makes the daily amounts more even, because the trader becomes more concerned with expected cost than with the variability of cost.

questions.solution:
The trader faces a genuine trade-off. Unwinding quickly means large daily volumes and therefore wide bid-offer spreads, but little exposure to adverse mid-market moves. Unwinding slowly means narrower spreads but more days of price risk on the residual position.

Formally, with $q_i$ the units traded on day $i$ and $x_i$ the residual position at the end of day $i$, the trader minimises
$$\sum_i p(q_i) q_i \div 2 + \lambda \sigma \sqrt{\sum_i x_i^2} \quad \text{subject to} \quad \sum_i q_i = V$$

The first term is the cumulative half-spread cost; the second is the VaR of the residual position over the unwind, with $\lambda$ the confidence multiple.

The reading's conclusion is unambiguous: when a position is to be closed out over $n$ days, more than one $n$th of the position should be traded on the first day, because the longer any part of the position is held the greater the risk of adverse market moves.

The comparative static is equally testable. In Hull's Example 1.3, unwinding 100 million units over five days:

| Confidence level | Units traded on days 1 to 5 (millions) |
|---|---|
| 95% | 48.9, 30.0, 14.1, 5.1, 1.9 |
| 90% | 45.0, 29.1, 15.6, 7.0, 3.3 |
| 75% | 36.1, 26.2, 17.7, 11.6, 8.4 |
| 50% | 20.0 each day |

As the confidence level falls, $\lambda$ falls, the price-risk term matters less, and the schedule flattens. In the limit at 50% confidence the trader cares only about expected cost, and the schedule becomes exactly even at $V \div n$.

a.reason: Equal tranches are optimal only in the limiting case where the trader is indifferent to the variability of cost, that is at a 50% confidence level. Equal tranches do minimise spread cost, but the objective is not spread cost alone.

b.reason: Both halves match the reading: front-load day one, and the schedule flattens as the confidence level is reduced.

c.reason: Polarity reversal. The statement correctly identifies that spread cost rises with daily volume but ignores the price-risk term, which is what pushes trading forward rather than back.

d.reason: Polarity reversal on the comparative static. A higher confidence level increases $\lambda$, which weights price risk more heavily and makes the schedule more front-loaded, not more even. It also inverts the interpretation of $\lambda$: a high $\lambda$ means the trader cares more about variability, not less.

trap.explanation: Options C and D are both defensible-sounding because each states one true mechanism and then draws the wrong conclusion by ignoring the other term in the objective. The discipline is to hold both terms in view: spread cost pushes toward slow, price risk pushes toward fast, and price risk wins on day one.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Explain and calculate liquidity trading risk via cost of liquidation and liquidity-adjusted VaR (LVaR).
questions.reading: Hull, Risk Management and Financial Institutions, Ch. 24: Liquidity Risk
questions.question: A quantitative analyst is comparing measures of market liquidity beyond the bid-offer spread. Which of the following statements about the Amihud illiquidity measure is most accurate?

options.text: It is the average over the period of daily dollar volume divided by the absolute value of the daily return, and a higher value indicates lower liquidity.
It is the average over the period of the absolute value of the daily return divided by daily dollar volume, and a higher value indicates lower liquidity; expected returns rise as liquidity falls.

It is the average over the period of the absolute value of the daily return divided by daily dollar volume, and a higher value indicates lower liquidity; expected returns fall as liquidity falls, because investors pay a premium for hard-to-access assets.
It measures the number of trades executed per day, and is preferred to the bid-offer spread because illiquid assets characteristically exhibit high trade counts.

questions.solution:
The reading lists several measures of market liquidity beyond the spread: the volume of trading per day, the price impact of a trade of a given size, and a proxy for price impact proposed by Amihud that is easier to compute.

$$\text{Amihud illiquidity} = \text{average over the period of} \left( \frac{|\text{daily return}|}{\text{daily dollar volume}} \right)$$

Read the ratio as price impact per unit of volume. If a small amount of trading moves the price a lot, the numerator is large relative to the denominator and the ratio is high, indicating an illiquid asset. A liquid asset absorbs large volume with little price movement, giving a low ratio.

The economic finding attached to the measure is the one GARP is most likely to corrupt: Amihud shows that an asset's expected return increases as its liquidity decreases. Investors do get compensated for illiquidity. This illiquidity premium is the bridge to the Investment Management readings on illiquid assets.

On trading volume: an asset that is highly illiquid often shows zero trading volume on a given day, so low volume signals low liquidity, not high.

a.reason: The ratio is inverted. Placing volume in the numerator makes the measure a liquidity measure, in which case a higher value would indicate greater liquidity, contradicting the second half of the statement.

b.reason: Correct construction, correct direction, and the correct sign on the illiquidity premium.

c.reason: The construction and direction are right but the premium is reversed. Expected returns rise, not fall, as liquidity falls; investors demand compensation for illiquidity rather than paying up for it.

d.reason: Misdescribes the measure and reverses the volume relationship. Illiquid assets characteristically show low or zero daily volume.

trap.explanation: Option A is a numerator and denominator flip that is internally inconsistent, so it can be eliminated by checking the stated direction against the stated ratio. Option C is the real discriminator: it is correct in every respect except the sign of the illiquidity premium. Anchor the direction with the intuition that an investor locking money into something hard to sell demands to be paid for it.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Evaluate Basel III liquidity risk ratios and BIS principles for sound liquidity risk management.
questions.reading: Hull, Risk Management and Financial Institutions, Ch. 24: Liquidity Risk
questions.question: A regulatory affairs analyst is documenting the acute stress scenario embedded in the 30-day period used to calculate the liquidity coverage ratio (LCR). One component of that scenario is a credit downgrade of three notches, for example from AA+ to A+. Which of the following most accurately states the remaining components?

options.text: A partial loss of wholesale funding, a complete loss of retail deposits, reduced haircuts on secured funding, and drawdowns on lines of credit.
A partial loss of deposits, a complete loss of wholesale funding, increased haircuts on secured funding, and drawdowns on lines of credit.
A complete loss of deposits, a partial loss of wholesale funding, increased haircuts on secured funding, and cancellation of undrawn lines of credit.
A partial loss of deposits, a complete loss of wholesale funding, reduced haircuts on secured funding, and drawdowns on lines of credit.

questions.solution:
The LCR requirement is:

$$\text{High-quality liquid assets} \div \text{Net cash outflows in a 30-day period} \geq 100\%$$

The 30-day period is a scenario of acute stress with five stated components:

| # | Component | Direction to memorise |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | A downgrade of three notches (for example AA+ to A+) | Three notches, not one |
| 2 | A partial loss of deposits | Partial, because deposits are comparatively sticky |
| 3 | A complete loss of wholesale funding | Complete, because wholesale funding is the volatile leg |
| 4 | Increased haircuts on secured funding | Increased, since stress reduces the cash raised per unit of collateral |
| 5 | Drawdowns on lines of credit | Customers draw on committed facilities, raising outflows |

The internal logic is worth holding onto, because it makes the pairings recoverable rather than memorised. Retail depositors are slow and dispersed, so their flight is partial. Wholesale funders are professional and concentrated, so their flight is total. Stress always makes collateral worth less, so haircuts rise. And borrowers hoard cash when credit tightens, so undrawn lines get drawn.

Implementation note: the LCR was phased in between 2015 and 2019, from a required 60% in 2015 to 100% in 2019.

a.reason: Two defects. The 'partial' and 'complete' labels are transposed between wholesale funding and deposits, and haircuts are said to fall rather than rise.

b.reason: All four remaining components stated with the correct qualifiers and directions.

c.reason: The partial and complete labels are transposed, and lines of credit are said to be cancelled rather than drawn. Cancellation would reduce the bank's outflows, which is the wrong direction for a stress scenario.

d.reason: Correct on the deposit and wholesale pairing but reverses the haircut direction. Reduced haircuts would imply more liquidity, not less, and cannot belong in a stress scenario.

trap.explanation: Option D is the discriminating distractor: three of its four components are right and it fails on a single word, which is exactly the depth at which this exam operates. Use the consistency test as a safety net, since every component of a stress scenario must worsen liquidity. Any option containing 'reduced haircuts' or 'cancelled lines of credit' can be struck without recalling the list at all.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Evaluate Basel III liquidity risk ratios and BIS principles for sound liquidity risk management.
questions.reading: Hull, Risk Management and Financial Institutions, Ch. 24: Liquidity Risk
questions.question: An analyst is comparing the two Basel III liquidity requirements. Which of the following correctly identifies the ratio whose numerator includes the bank's regulatory capital, and gives the correct reason?

options.text: The liquidity coverage ratio, because regulatory capital is a component of high-quality liquid assets.
The liquidity coverage ratio, because capital is available to absorb net cash outflows over the 30-day stress window.
The net stable funding ratio, because required stable funding includes the capital needed to support the asset base.
The net stable funding ratio, because available stable funding is computed by applying available stable funding factors to each category of funding, including capital.

questions.solution:
The two ratios answer different questions and are built from different sides of the balance sheet.

| | LCR | NSFR |
|---|---|---|
| Formula | HQLA ÷ net cash outflows over 30 days | Available stable funding ÷ required stable funding |
| Horizon | 30 days | 1 year |
| Numerator is about | Assets: the stock of liquid assets held | Liabilities and capital: the stability of the funding base |
| Denominator is about | Stressed outflows | Assets and off-balance-sheet items requiring funding |
| Where capital sits | Not in the numerator | In the numerator, at a 100% ASF factor |
| Threshold | ≥ 100% | ≥ 100% |
| Implementation | Phased 2015 to 2019 | 1 January 2018 |

The NSFR numerator is built by multiplying each category of funding, meaning capital, wholesale deposits, retail deposits and so on, by an available stable funding factor reflecting its stability. Capital is the most stable funding a bank has and therefore attracts the highest factor. The denominator applies a required stable funding factor to each asset and off-balance-sheet item, reflecting how permanently that item must be funded.

a.reason: Regulatory capital is not an asset and is not part of HQLA. The LCR numerator is a stock of unencumbered liquid assets.

b.reason: Confuses capital adequacy with liquidity. Capital absorbs losses; it does not by itself provide cash to meet outflows.

c.reason: Right ratio, wrong side. Capital sits in available stable funding, the numerator, not in required stable funding, the denominator.

d.reason: Capital is a funding category weighted by an ASF factor in the NSFR numerator.

trap.explanation: Option C is the numerator and denominator flip and it is the sharp end of this item, because a candidate who knows the answer is the NSFR still has a coin flip left. Anchor it with the structural rule: the NSFR numerator is the right-hand side of the balance sheet (how the bank is funded) and the denominator is the left-hand side (what needs funding). Capital is a funding source, so it goes on top.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Evaluate Basel III liquidity risk ratios and BIS principles for sound liquidity risk management.
questions.reading: Hull, Risk Management and Financial Institutions, Ch. 24: Liquidity Risk
questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a regional bank is presenting to a group of newly hired analysts on how the net stable funding ratio is constructed. She stresses that the ratio's meaning lies in the factors applied to each category rather than in the arithmetic. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: A one-year retail term deposit receives a lower available stable funding factor than short-term wholesale funding obtained from another financial institution, because retail depositors are more numerous and therefore harder to monitor.

Cash and central bank reserves receive a required stable funding factor at the low end of the scale while long-dated performing loans receive a factor at the high end, because the latter must be funded on a durable basis.
Regulatory capital is assigned a required stable funding factor of 100%, reflecting the permanence of the funding it supplies to the balance sheet.

The available stable funding factor applied to a liability rises as its remaining maturity shortens, since short-dated funding can be rolled over more frequently and is therefore continuously renewed.

questions.solution:
The reading defines the ratio structurally rather than arithmetically:

$$\text{NSFR} = \text{amount of stable funding} \div \text{required amount of stable funding} \geq 100\%$$

The numerator is calculated by multiplying each category of funding (capital, wholesale deposits, retail deposits and so on) by an available stable funding factor, reflecting their stability. The denominator is calculated from the assets and off-balance-sheet items requiring funding, each multiplied by a required stable funding factor to reflect the permanence of the funding.

Two directional rules follow, and both are what the question tests.

| Side | Factor rises when | Illustration |
|---|---|---|
| Available stable funding (numerator, funding side) | The funding is more stable: longer dated, more granular, less likely to run | Capital sits at the top; retail deposits next; short-dated funding from other financial institutions at the bottom |
| Required stable funding (denominator, asset side) | The asset must be funded more durably: longer dated, less liquid, less readily monetised | Cash and central bank reserves at the bottom; long-dated performing loans and other illiquid assets at the top |

The economic logic is symmetrical. Anything that cannot be turned into cash quickly needs permanent funding behind it, so it attracts a high RSF factor. Anything that will not run needs no replacement, so it attracts a high ASF factor. A bank fails the NSFR when it funds high-RSF assets with low-ASF liabilities, which is the structural version of borrowing short and lending long.

Note also where capital sits. Capital is a category of funding, so it belongs in the numerator with the highest ASF factor. It does not appear in the denominator at all.

a.reason: Polarity flip. Retail term deposits are among the most stable funding a bank has and attract a higher ASF factor than short-dated wholesale funding from another financial institution, which is the least stable category. The stated reason is also spurious.

b.reason: Cash requires almost no durable funding behind it, so its RSF factor is at the bottom of the scale; long-dated performing loans must be funded for their whole life, so their factor is near the top.

c.reason: Numerator and denominator flip. Capital is a funding source and belongs in available stable funding, the numerator. The reading lists capital first among the categories multiplied by an ASF factor.

d.reason: Polarity flip. The ASF factor falls as remaining maturity shortens. Frequent rollover is a vulnerability, not a source of stability, since each rollover is a point at which funding can be withdrawn.

trap.explanation: Options A and D are the same polarity flip applied to the funding side twice, and D dresses it in a plausible-sounding rationale about continuous renewal, which is exactly the argument a bank in trouble would have made in August 2007. Option C is the numerator and denominator flip that also appears in the structural comparison question: capital is funding, so it goes on top. Anchor both sides with a single sentence, that stable funding sits in the numerator and assets needing funding sit in the denominator.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Evaluate Basel III liquidity risk ratios and BIS principles for sound liquidity risk management.
questions.reading: Hull, Risk Management and Financial Institutions, Ch. 24: Liquidity Risk
questions.question: An internal auditor is reviewing a bank's liquidity risk management framework against the BIS Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management and Supervision, and recommending improvements to conform with the guidance. Which of the following statements is most consistent with those principles?

options.text: The board of directors should develop the liquidity risk management strategy, policies and practices, and senior management should review and approve them at least annually.

Liquidity costs, benefits and risks should be incorporated into internal pricing, performance measurement and new product approval for all significant business activities, both on and off balance sheet.
Supervisors should assess a bank's liquidity risk management framework but should not intervene in its liquidity position, which remains the sole responsibility of the bank.
A bank should maintain a cushion of high-quality liquid assets, which may be encumbered provided they are held at the parent entity.

questions.solution:
Following the liquidity crisis of 2007, bank regulators issued a revised set of 17 principles. Thirteen are addressed to banks and four (numbers 14 to 17) to supervisors. The exam tests the allocation of roles at least as often as the content.

| Principle | Substance |
|---|---|
| 1 | The bank is responsible for sound liquidity risk management; supervisors assess and act promptly where the bank is deficient. |
| 2 | Articulate a liquidity risk tolerance appropriate to the business strategy and systemic role. |
| 3 | Senior management develops strategy, policies and practices; the board reviews and approves them at least annually. |
| 4 | Incorporate liquidity costs, benefits and risks into internal pricing, performance measurement and new product approval for all significant activities, on and off balance sheet. |
| 7 | Establish a funding strategy providing effective diversification in sources and tenor of funding. |
| 9 | Actively manage collateral, differentiating encumbered from unencumbered assets. |
| 11 | Maintain a formal contingency funding plan with clear invocation and escalation procedures, regularly tested. |
| 12 | Maintain a cushion of unencumbered high-quality liquid assets with no legal, regulatory or operational impediment to their use. |
| 13 | Publicly disclose information enabling market participants to judge the bank's liquidity position. |
| 16 | Supervisors should intervene to require effective and timely remedial action. |

Principle 4 is the one candidates most often underrate. Its purpose is to align the incentives of individual business lines with the liquidity risk their activities create for the bank as a whole. If a desk can write a facility without being charged for the liquidity it consumes, it will write too many.

a.reason: Role reversal. Senior management develops the strategy, policies and practices; the board reviews and approves them at least annually. The two actors have been swapped.

b.reason: This is Principle 4, including the explicit extension to off-balance-sheet activities.

c.reason: Principle 16 states that supervisors should intervene to require effective and timely remedial action. The statement understates the supervisory role.

d.reason: Principle 12 requires the cushion to be unencumbered, with no legal, regulatory or operational impediment to its use. Encumbered assets are precisely what cannot be mobilised in a stress.

trap.explanation: Governance questions on this exam are almost always decided by who does what, not by what is done. Option A states an entirely sensible-sounding division of labour and fails on the direction of a single reporting line. Build the habit of reading governance options actor-first: identify the subject of the sentence before you evaluate the verb. Option D fails on one word, 'encumbered' for 'unencumbered', which reverses the meaning of the entire principle.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Evaluate Basel III liquidity risk ratios and BIS principles for sound liquidity risk management.
questions.reading: Hull, Risk Management and Financial Institutions, Ch. 24: Liquidity Risk
questions.question: An internal auditor is assessing a bank's liquidity framework against the BIS Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management and Supervision, and is preparing a memorandum for the risk committee. Which of the following statements is correct to include?

options.text: The contingency funding plan is the responsibility of the bank's supervisor, who sets out the strategies for addressing liquidity shortfalls in emergency situations and tests them regularly.

A bank should conduct stress tests on a regular basis for a variety of short-term and protracted, institution-specific and market-wide scenarios, and should use the outcomes to adjust its liquidity risk management strategies, policies and positions.

Supervisors should communicate with other supervisors and public authorities within national borders only, since cross-border information sharing is properly the responsibility of the banks themselves.

A bank's funding strategy should concentrate on a small number of proven funding sources, since diversification across tenors dilutes relationships with funds providers and reduces fund-raising capacity.

questions.solution:
The seventeen principles split cleanly: numbers 1 to 13 address banks and numbers 14 to 17 address supervisors. Governance questions on this material are decided by who does what at least as often as by what is done.

| Principle | Actor | Substance |
|---|---|---|
| 7 | Bank | Establish a funding strategy providing effective diversification in the sources and tenor of funding; maintain an ongoing presence in chosen funding markets and strong relationships with funds providers; regularly gauge capacity to raise funds from each source |
| 10 | Bank | Conduct stress tests regularly across short-term and protracted, institution-specific and market-wide scenarios, individually and in combination; use the outcomes to adjust strategies, policies and positions and to develop contingency plans |
| 11 | Bank | Maintain a formal contingency funding plan with clear invocation and escalation procedures, regularly tested and updated |
| 13 | Bank | Publicly disclose information on a regular basis enabling market participants to judge the soundness of its framework and position |
| 14, 15 | Supervisor | Perform regular comprehensive assessments; supplement them with internal reports, prudential reports and market information |
| 16 | Supervisor | Intervene to require effective and timely remedial action |
| 17 | Supervisor | Communicate with other supervisors and public authorities such as central banks, both within and across national borders, with information sharing intensifying in times of stress |

Option B restates Principle 10 accurately, including the four-way scenario requirement (short term and protracted, institution-specific and market-wide) and the feedback loop into strategy, which is the part most often dropped from summaries.

a.reason: Role misassignment. Principle 11 places the contingency funding plan squarely with the bank, including the obligation to test and update it. Supervisors assess the framework; they do not author the plan.

b.reason: This is Principle 10, stated with both the scenario range and the requirement to feed outcomes back into strategy, policies and positions.

c.reason: Scope error. Principle 17 requires supervisors to communicate both within and across national borders, and the obligation sits with supervisors rather than with banks.

d.reason: Polarity flip. Principle 7 requires effective diversification in both the sources and the tenor of funding, alongside strong relationships with funds providers. Concentration is the vulnerability the principle exists to prevent, as Northern Rock demonstrated.

trap.explanation: Option A is a role misassignment and is the highest-frequency trap on governance material, because the statement is otherwise a faithful description of a contingency funding plan and only the actor is wrong. Read the subject of the sentence before evaluating the verb. Option C is a scope error on a single qualifier, 'within national borders only', which reverses the cross-border cooperation the principle exists to require. Option D is a polarity flip dressed as a relationship-management argument.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.
questions.reading: Hull, Risk Management and Financial Institutions, Ch. 24: Liquidity Risk
questions.question: A senior regulator is preparing remarks on the systemic consequences of harmonised prudential rules. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: A liquidity black hole arises when a price decline attracts contrarian buyers, so that prices revert quickly to fundamental value and the market clears.

A uniform regulatory environment can contribute to liquidity black holes, because banks holding similar positions respond identically when volatilities and correlations rise, all seeking to reduce exposure at the same time.
Life insurance companies and pension funds should be subject to the same market risk capital rules as banks, so that no type of institution gains a competitive advantage.
The Basel Committee addressed procyclicality in credit risk capital by requiring probability of default estimates to reflect current point-in-time conditions.

questions.solution:
A liquidity black hole, also called a crowded exit, is a situation in which liquidity dries up in a market because everyone wants to sell and no one wants to buy, or the reverse. The distinguishing feature is that a price decline causes more participants to want to sell, driving prices well below where they eventually settle. In a well-functioning market a price decline instead attracts buyers and a new equilibrium is established.

The regulatory channel works as follows:

volatilities and correlations rise → market risk VaR rises → market risk capital requirements rise → banks cut exposures → similar positions, similar trades, one-sided market

Harmonised rules are a laudable goal, since before Basel I banks competed under unevenly enforced capital regimes. But uniformity has a cost: all banks respond in the same way to the same external event, which is the opposite of the diversity a liquid market requires.

Two related points the reading makes explicitly. First, credit risk capital under the Basel II internal-ratings-based models is procyclical, since default probabilities are high at the trough and low at the peak. The Basel Committee addressed this by asserting that the probability of default should be an average through the economic or credit cycle, not a point-in-time estimate. Second, life insurers and pension funds should not be regulated like banks: they have longer horizons, should not be penalised for holding illiquid assets, and should not be forced to adjust portfolios when volatilities and correlations rise, since those parameters are mean reverting.

a.reason: This describes a well-functioning market, in which negative feedback traders restore the price. A black hole is defined by the absence of that stabilising response.

b.reason: This is the reading's stated mechanism linking uniform regulation to black holes.

c.reason: The reading poses this exact question and answers no. Longer-horizon institutions should not be penalised for holding illiquid assets or forced to rebalance when volatilities spike.

d.reason: Polarity flip. The Basel Committee's remedy was through-the-cycle average probability of default, precisely to avoid the point-in-time estimate that generates procyclicality.

trap.explanation: Option C is engineered around the level-playing-field intuition, which is genuinely appealing and which the reading raises before rejecting. Option D is a single-word polarity flip on a technical remedy, and it is the type most likely to survive a quick read. Anchor it by asking what problem the fix was meant to solve: if the problem is that capital moves with the cycle, the fix cannot be an input that moves with the cycle.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.
questions.reading: Hull, Risk Management and Financial Institutions, Ch. 24: Liquidity Risk
questions.question: Peter's start-up has built an exchange platform for trading derivatives on certain cryptocurrencies. He knows that participants prefer continuous liquidity and will avoid a market that lacks it. He is drafting a brochure promoting the platform's liquidity characteristics. Which of the following features would most appropriately be promoted, that is, which contributes to a stable market with respect to liquidity?

options.text: Widespread use of stop-loss rules by participants on the platform.
A high concentration of trend-following and breakout strategies among participants.
Heavy use of programmes that synthetically create put options on participants' portfolios.
A substantial presence of negative feedback traders, who buy when prices fall and sell when prices rise.

questions.solution:
The reading divides traders into two types and is precise about the direction of each:

| | Negative feedback traders | Positive feedback traders |
|---|---|---|
| Behaviour | Buy when prices fall, sell when prices rise | Sell when prices fall, buy when prices rise |
| Effect on price | Creates demand when the price is too low and supply when it is too high, restoring a reasonable level | Reinforces the move, driving prices further from equilibrium |
| Effect on liquidity | Market is liquid, with a good balance of buyers and sellers | Market becomes one-sided, unstable and illiquid |

In liquid markets negative feedback traders dominate. A market Peter would want to advertise is one where a price dislocation attracts capital rather than repelling it.

The other three options are all mechanisms the reading names as sources of positive feedback trading, so a brochure boasting of them would be advertising the platform's fragility.

a.reason: Stop-loss rules are named as a permanent source of positive feedback trading: an automatic sell is triggered when a price falls below a threshold, reinforcing the decline.

b.reason: Trend trading and breakout trading are the first named cause of positive feedback trading: buy as the price trends up, sell as it trends down.

c.reason: Synthetically creating put options requires selling after a price decline and buying after a price increase. This is the portfolio insurance mechanism behind the crash of October 1987.

d.reason: Negative feedback traders buy low and sell high, supplying liquidity where it is scarce and stabilising the price.

trap.explanation: The stem's qualifier does the work: it asks what would be promoted, meaning what is good for liquidity. A candidate who skims and treats this as a list-the-causes question will pick one of A, B or C, all of which are correct answers to the question that was not asked. The naming convention is also counterintuitive and worth fixing in memory: negative feedback is the good kind.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.
questions.reading: Hull, Risk Management and Financial Institutions, Ch. 24: Liquidity Risk
questions.question: A dealer bank is reviewing which of its activities could reduce market liquidity under stress. Each of the following is identified in the reading as a cause of positive feedback trading EXCEPT:

options.text: Stop-loss rules that trigger automatic sales once a price falls below a set level.
Margin calls on highly leveraged positions following a large adverse move in market variables.
Dynamically hedging a long position in a call option.
Predatory trading ahead of a large liquidation that other participants have anticipated.

questions.solution:
The reading names seven sources of positive feedback trading:

| # | Cause | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Trend trading and breakout trading | Buy on an uptrend, sell on a downtrend |
| 2 | Stop-loss rules | Automatic sale once a threshold is breached; always present in the market |
| 3 | Dynamic hedging of a short option position | Buy after a rise, sell after a decline |
| 4 | Creating options synthetically | Equivalent to hedging a short option; the portfolio insurance behind October 1987 |
| 5 | Margins | Margin calls force leveraged traders to close out, reinforcing the move; exchanges then raise margin requirements, worsening it |
| 6 | Predatory trading | Traders short ahead of a known forced seller, reinforcing the decline |
| 7 | LTCM | Leveraged relative-value positions unwound into the 1998 flight to quality, widening the spreads further |

The exception is option C, and the reason is worth stating precisely. Hedging a short option position, whether a call or a put, requires buying after a price rise and selling after a price decline, which is positive feedback. Hedging a long position in a call or a put requires the opposite, selling after a price rise and buying after a price decline, which is negative feedback and should not interfere with market liquidity.

Short option, dynamically hedged → positive feedback | Long option, dynamically hedged → negative feedback

The historical illustration is the sale by banks of a large volume of options on long-term interest rates to British insurance companies. As the banks hedged those short positions, the behaviour of long-term UK interest rates was dramatically affected.

a.reason: Stop-loss rules are cause 2 and are described as a source of positive feedback trading that is always present in the market. Not the exception.

b.reason: Margins are cause 5. Margin calls force leveraged traders to close out, reinforcing the original move. Not the exception.

c.reason: Hedging a long option position requires selling after a rise and buying after a decline, which is negative feedback trading. This is the exception.

d.reason: Predatory trading is cause 6, and is also the reason large positions must usually be unwound slowly. Not the exception.

trap.explanation: This item turns on a single word, 'long' where the cause requires 'short'. Candidates who have memorised 'dynamic hedging causes positive feedback' without the qualifier will read straight past it. Anchor the direction with the option seller's problem: a short option position has negative gamma, so the hedger is always chasing the market, buying high and selling low. The buyer of an option has positive gamma and trades against the market. The negative-qualifier construction compounds the risk, since the exception here is the only statement that is not a cause.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.
questions.reading: Hull, Risk Management and Financial Institutions, Ch. 24: Liquidity Risk
questions.question: A macroprudential analyst is describing the leveraging and deleveraging cycle to a risk committee. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: In a deleveraging cycle, forced asset sales depress prices, which raises investors' measured leverage and forces further sales.
In a deleveraging cycle, forced asset sales depress prices, which lowers investors' measured leverage, so the cycle is self-correcting.
In a leveraging cycle, rising asset prices raise investors' measured leverage, which obliges them to sell assets to restore their target ratios.
Hedge funds are largely insulated from the cycle, because prime brokers set leverage limits contractually in advance and cannot vary them during a stress.

questions.solution:
The two cycles run in opposite directions and each is self-reinforcing.

| | Leveraging | Deleveraging |
|---|---|---|
| Credit conditions | Banks are awash with liquidity, so credit is easily available and credit spreads fall | Banks become less liquid, so they are reluctant to lend and credit spreads rise |
| Demand and prices | Demand for financial and non-financial assets rises, so asset prices rise | Demand falls, so asset prices fall |
| Collateral | Collateral values rise, so borrowing capacity rises | Collateral values fall, so banks cut lines of credit |
| Measured leverage | Investors' measured leverage falls, so they can lever up again | Investors' measured leverage rises, so further sales are required |

The direction of leverage is the point most often corrupted. Leverage is a ratio of debt to equity or of assets to equity. When asset prices fall, equity absorbs the loss first, so the denominator shrinks faster than the numerator and measured leverage rises. That is what forces the next round of selling, and why the cycle does not self-correct.

Hedge funds are singled out as particularly exposed. A fund able to borrow twenty times equity before 2007 might receive a call from its prime broker in the second half of that year requiring leverage of five times. It can only comply by selling. Prices fall as it and other funds sell, its equity declines, and further sales become necessary.

a.reason: Falling prices erode equity faster than debt, raising measured leverage and forcing further sales. This is the mechanism in Figure 1.3 of the reading.

b.reason: Polarity flip on the leverage effect, with a conclusion that reverses the chapter's thesis. If deleveraging were self-correcting there would be no liquidity black hole to explain.

c.reason: Polarity flip on the leveraging cycle. Rising asset prices lower measured leverage, which permits further borrowing and further purchases.

d.reason: The reading states the opposite. Prime brokers cut permitted leverage sharply during the crisis, and hedge funds are described as particularly affected by the cycle.

trap.explanation: Options B and C are the same polarity error applied to the two halves of the cycle, which means a candidate who has the direction backwards will find one of them and feel confirmed. Fix it with a single numerical anchor: assets 100, equity 10, leverage 10 times. Lose 5 of asset value and equity is 5 against assets of 95, so leverage is 19 times. Falling prices raise leverage. Everything else in the cycle follows from that.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Discuss how asset-liability management strategies can help a bank hedge against interest rate risk.
questions.reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
questions.question: A newly appointed treasurer is being briefed on the evolution of asset-liability management at depository institutions. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Under an asset management strategy, the key control lever is price, meaning the interest rate and other terms offered on deposits and borrowings, used to achieve the desired volume, mix and cost of funds.

Under a liability management strategy, the amount and kinds of deposits the institution holds are treated as largely determined by its customers, so the only real decision area is the allocation of incoming funds.
Under a funds management strategy, control over assets must be coordinated with control over liabilities so that the two are internally consistent and do not pull against each other.
The asset-liability committee reports to the head of the risk function and its principal responsibility is approving individual credit exposures above a stated threshold.

questions.solution:
The reading traces three strategies in historical order.

| Strategy | What is taken as given | Key decision lever |
|---|---|---|
| Asset management | Liabilities and equity. The public determines the relative amounts of deposits and other funds available. | Allocation of incoming funds: who receives the scarce loans available and on what terms. |
| Liability management | Nothing on the funding side. The goal is to gain control over funds sources comparable to the control long exercised over assets. | Price: the interest rate and other terms offered on deposits and borrowings. |
| Funds management | Neither side. This is the approach that dominates today. | Coordinated control of the volume, mix and return or cost of both assets and liabilities. |

Funds management rests on three stated objectives: exercise as much control as possible over the volume, mix and return or cost of both sides of the balance sheet; coordinate the two so they are internally consistent and do not pull against each other; and develop policies that recognise that revenues and costs arise from both sides.

On the asset-liability committee (ALCO): it is usually composed of key officers representing different departments, meets regularly, and conveys the firm's financial condition and remedial suggestions to the board of directors. It lays out the funding plan, the quality of loans to be taken on, and limits to off-balance-sheet exposure, and it estimates the firm's risk exposure to its net interest margin and net worth ratios.

a.reason: Sibling swap. Price as the control lever over funding is the defining feature of liability management, not asset management.

b.reason: Sibling swap in the other direction. Treating deposits as customer-determined and confining management to fund allocation is the asset management view.

c.reason: This is the second of the three stated objectives of funds management.

d.reason: Role misassignment. The ALCO reports the firm's financial condition to the board, and its remit is interest rate risk and other risk exposures, funding plans and risk limits, not individual credit approvals.

trap.explanation: Options A and B are the same swap run in opposite directions, which is the cleanest possible construction for a definitions question and means a candidate who has the two labels the wrong way round will find a distractor that confirms it. Fix the mnemonic: asset management came first and took funding for granted; liability management arrived when deregulation let banks bid for funds on price.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Discuss how asset-liability management strategies can help a bank hedge against interest rate risk.
questions.reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
questions.question: A risk analyst is describing the two principal forms of interest rate risk faced by a lending institution. Which of the following is most accurate?

options.text: Price risk arises when market interest rates fall, causing the market values of most bonds and fixed-rate loans to decline, so that sales in a falling rate period realise capital losses.
Reinvestment risk arises when market interest rates rise, forcing the institution to place incoming funds in lower-yielding earning assets and reducing expected future income.

Price risk arises when market interest rates rise and the institution must accept capital losses if it sells fixed-rate instruments; reinvestment risk arises when rates fall and incoming funds must be placed at lower yields.

Because a financial intermediary is usually on both the supply and the demand side of the loanable funds market at the same time, it can set the level of rates on its own loans and deposits and so neutralise both forms of risk.

questions.solution:
The two risks sit on opposite sides of the rate move, which is exactly why they are so easy to transpose under exam pressure.

| | Price risk | Reinvestment risk |
|---|---|---|
| Triggered when rates | Rise | Fall |
| Mechanism | Market values of most bonds and fixed-rate loans fall | Incoming funds must be placed in lower-yielding earning assets |
| Where the damage shows up | Capital losses if the instruments are sold | Lower expected future income |

The underlying reason both risks are unavoidable is that managers cannot control either the level of or the trend in market rates. Whether a firm is supplying credit (granting loans) or demanding it (taking deposits, issuing non-deposit IOUs), it is only one participant among many thousands. As the reading puts it, most financial managers must be price takers, not price makers, and must accept interest rate levels as given and plan accordingly.

A large part of asset-liability management consists precisely of finding ways to deal with these two forms of risk, and the two main tools in this chapter map onto the two consequences: interest-sensitive gap management protects the net interest margin (the income effect), while duration gap management protects net worth (the value effect).

a.reason: Polarity flip. Price risk arises when rates rise, since that is when fixed-rate instrument values fall.

b.reason: Polarity flip, and internally inconsistent: if rates rise, incoming funds are placed at higher, not lower, yields.

c.reason: Both risks are attached to the correct direction of rate movement and to the correct consequence.

d.reason: An absolute claim that contradicts the price-taker point. Being on both sides of the market does not confer pricing power; each institution, however large, is one participant among thousands.

trap.explanation: This is a pure direction test, and options A and B are the same transposition presented twice so that a candidate with the pair reversed can find confirmation either way. The anchor worth memorising: price risk hurts the value of what you already hold, and values fall when rates rise; reinvestment risk hurts what you will buy next, and next year's yields are worse when rates fall.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Discuss how asset-liability management strategies can help a bank hedge against interest rate risk.
questions.reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
questions.question: A bank's chief economist is explaining to the asset-liability committee why consistently accurate interest rate forecasting is virtually impossible. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: Market interest rates are set by the interactions of thousands of credit suppliers and demanders, and any particular rate is composed of a real risk-free rate plus several risk premiums, any of which can shift.
A sufficiently large institution can influence the level of market interest rates through the scale of its own lending and deposit-taking, so forecasting is materially more tractable for large banks.
Under the Fisher effect the nominal interest rate equals the real rate minus the expected rate of inflation, so nominal rates are relatively stable even when inflation expectations move.
Nominal interest rates cannot fall below zero, which places a firm lower bound on the forecasting problem.

questions.solution:
Two separate obstacles are identified in the reading, and the correct answer states both.
