First, the level is not controllable. Rates are determined by the interaction of thousands of suppliers and demanders of loanable funds, which makes consistently accurate forecasting virtually impossible for any single participant.

Second, the structure is layered. Any particular rate is built from multiple components:

$$\text{Nominal market rate} = \text{risk-free real rate} + \text{risk premiums (default or credit, inflation, term or maturity, liquidity, call, and so on)}$$

Not only does the real risk-free rate move with the demand and supply of loanable funds, but market perceptions of each risk premium also change over time, which is why market rates move up and down, often erratically. A forecaster must therefore get several moving parts right at once.

Two related points that appear as distractors. The Fisher effect states that the nominal rate equals the real rate plus expected inflation, not minus it. And nominal rates are not floored at zero: the reading cites negative rates during the Great Depression, briefly in the repurchase agreement market in the autumn of 2003, and briefly in the Treasury bill market in 2008.

a.reason: Both obstacles are stated correctly: the market-determined level and the multi-component structure of any individual rate.

b.reason: Contradicts the price-taker point. Each institution, no matter how large, is only one supplier and one demander in an international market containing many thousands of participants.

c.reason: Polarity flip on the Fisher effect. Nominal equals real plus expected inflation, which is precisely why nominal rates move when inflation expectations move.

d.reason: Factually wrong. Nominal rates can and have gone negative, as the reading notes for the 1930s, the 2003 repurchase agreement market and the 2008 Treasury bill market.

trap.explanation: Option C is the sharp one: it invokes a real relationship and inverts a single operator. The Fisher effect appears across several FRM readings and the sign is the only thing ever tested on it. Option D exploits a widely held but incorrect intuition; treat 'cannot' and 'never' in a rates context as a signal to look harder, not as a safe generalisation.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Discuss how asset-liability management strategies can help a bank hedge against interest rate risk.
questions.reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
questions.question: A bank's asset-liability committee is discussing how the shape of the yield curve affects profitability. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Most lending institutions run a negative maturity gap, because their security holdings and loans mature sooner than the deposits and borrowings that fund them.
Most lending institutions run a positive maturity gap, so an upward-sloping yield curve tends to support a positive net interest margin, while a flat or negatively sloped curve compresses it.
A negatively sloped yield curve is generally associated with rising interest rates and with expansion in the economy.
Short-term interest rates typically move over a narrower range than long-term rates, so the spread between short and long maturities is approximately constant over the cycle.

questions.solution:
Two facts combine to produce the answer.

**Fact one: the typical maturity gap is positive.** Lending institutions hold security portfolios and loans with longer maturities than their sources of funds. That is the positive maturity gap, the excess of average asset maturity over average liability maturity.

**Fact two: an upward-sloping curve pays for that gap.** If long-term rates exceed short-term rates, revenues from longer-term assets outstrip expenses from shorter-term liabilities, normally producing a positive net interest margin. A flat or negatively sloped curve generates a small or even negative margin, putting downward pressure on the earnings of firms that borrow short and lend long.

| Curve shape | Definition | Conventional signal | Effect on a positive maturity gap |
|---|---|---|---|
| Upward sloping | Long rates above short rates | Rising rates and economic expansion | Supports the net interest margin |
| Horizontal | Long and short rates about equal | Rates may be stable for a time | Compresses the margin |
| Downward sloping | Short rates above long rates | Rates may begin falling; possible recession ahead | Compresses or reverses the margin |

A further point that appears as a distractor: short-term rates tend to rise and fall faster and over a wider range than long-term rates, so the short-to-long spread is emphatically not constant. In recessions short rates tend to fall relative to long rates and the spread widens; a period of prosperity usually begins with a wide gap that then narrows and sometimes turns negative.

a.reason: Polarity flip. Lending institutions typically hold assets with longer maturities than their liabilities, which is a positive maturity gap.

b.reason: Positive maturity gap plus an upward-sloping curve produces a positive net interest margin; a flat or inverted curve compresses it.

c.reason: Reverses the signal. An upward-sloping curve is associated with rising rates and expansion; a negatively sloped curve suggests falling rates and a possible recession.

d.reason: Polarity flip. Short-term rates move over a wider range than long-term rates, and relative changes in the two clearly vary over time.

trap.explanation: Three of the four options are single-direction reversals, which is how this material is almost always tested. The one to guard hardest is option A, because 'banks borrow short and lend long' is a phrase most candidates can recite while still fumbling which side of the maturity gap that makes positive. Assets long, liabilities short, gap positive.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe interest-sensitive gap management and apply this strategy to maximize a bank's net interest margin.
questions.reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
questions.question:
A senior manager at ABC Bank is explaining the bank's use of the net interest margin to the rest of the management team. The following figures are available:

| Item | Amount |
|---|---|
| Cash and cash equivalents | USD 93,000,000 |
| Interest income from loans and investments | USD 143,000,000 |
| Shareholders' equity | USD 300,000,000 |
| Interest expense on deposits and borrowed funds | USD 128,000,000 |
| Total earning assets | USD 950,000,000 |

Which of the following is closest to the bank's net interest margin?
questions.solution:
$$\text{NIM} = \frac{\text{interest income from loans and investments} - \text{interest expense on deposits and borrowed funds}}{\text{total earning assets}}$$

**Step 1. Net interest income:**
$$143{,}000{,}000 - 128{,}000{,}000 = \text{USD } 15{,}000{,}000$$

**Step 2. Divide by total earning assets, which is given directly:**
$$15{,}000{,}000 \div 950{,}000{,}000 = 0.015789, \text{ or } 1.58\%$$

Cash and cash equivalents and shareholders' equity are not inputs. Cash is not an earning asset and equity is a funding source, not an asset at all.

Interpretation: a 1.58% margin is thin, and the reading stresses that this is not the bank's profit from borrowing and lending, because non-interest expenses such as salaries, taxes and overheads have not yet been deducted. Once they are, there is very little margin for error against interest rate risk, which is the whole motivation for the hedging techniques in the rest of the chapter. The industry average cited in the reading is around 3.5%, so this bank sits well below it.

a.reason: 1.44% = 15,000,000 ÷ (950,000,000 + 93,000,000). Cash has been added to the denominator, but cash is a non-earning asset and total earning assets was already given.

c.reason: 5.00% = 15,000,000 ÷ 300,000,000. Shareholders' equity has been used as the denominator, which produces a return-on-equity style ratio, not a margin.

d.reason: 15.05% = 143,000,000 ÷ 950,000,000. Interest expense has not been subtracted, so this is a gross asset yield rather than a net margin.

trap.explanation: Two of the five table rows are planted and both have a distractor built on them. Option D is the more dangerous of the pair because omitting the expense line is an omission rather than an insertion, and omissions are harder to notice on review. A fast sanity check: bank net interest margins live in the 1% to 4% range, so any answer above roughly 5% is almost certainly a gross yield or a wrong denominator.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe interest-sensitive gap management and apply this strategy to maximize a bank's net interest margin.
questions.reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
questions.question: Davidson Bank reported a net interest margin of 2.45% in its most recent financial statements, with total interest revenues of USD 100 million and total interest expenses of USD 64 million. Which of the following is closest to the volume of earning assets the bank must hold?

options.text: USD 14.69 million
USD 1,469.39 million
USD 2,612.24 million
USD 4,081.63 million

questions.solution:
$$\text{NIM} = \frac{\text{net interest income}}{\text{total earning assets}}$$

**Step 1. Net interest income:**
$$100 - 64 = \text{USD } 36 \text{ million}$$
This is the numerator. It is net, so both the revenue and the expense line must be used.

**Step 2. Rearrange and solve:**
$$\text{Total earning assets} = \text{net interest income} \div \text{NIM} = 36 \div 0.0245 = \text{USD } 1{,}469.39 \text{ million}$$

Sanity check: $36 \div 1{,}469.39 = 0.0245$. The bank holds roughly USD 1.47 billion of earning assets to generate USD 36 million of net interest income.

A useful extension the reading poses in its own end-of-chapter problems: if interest revenues and costs both rise by one proportion while earning assets rise by a different proportion, the margin moves in the direction of whichever grew faster. The identity is worth holding in a form you can rearrange in any direction, since GARP will ask for any one of the three quantities given the other two.

a.reason: USD 14.69 million = 36 ÷ 2.45, treating the margin as the plain number 2.45 rather than the decimal 0.0245. A decimal-place error of two orders of magnitude.

c.reason: USD 2,612.24 million = 64 ÷ 0.0245, using interest expense as the numerator.

d.reason: USD 4,081.63 million = 100 ÷ 0.0245, using gross interest revenue as the numerator instead of net interest income.

trap.explanation: Option D is the principal trap and is the same error as option D in the previous question, seen from the other side: forgetting that the margin's numerator is net. Because the question is posed in reverse, the mistake now inflates the answer by a factor of roughly 2.8 rather than deflating it, which makes it harder to catch by eye. Option A is a pure decimal slip and is worth one deliberate check whenever a percentage appears in a denominator.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe interest-sensitive gap management and apply this strategy to maximize a bank's net interest margin.
questions.reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
questions.question: A bank earns an average yield of 5% on its rate-sensitive assets and 10% on its fixed (non-rate-sensitive) assets. It pays an average cost of 4% on its rate-sensitive liabilities and 6% on its fixed (non-rate-sensitive) liabilities. During the coming week the bank holds USD 542 million of rate-sensitive assets and USD 156 million of rate-sensitive liabilities, and total assets are USD 1,212 million. Assume equity is zero and that these annualised rates remain steady. Which of the following is closest to the bank's annualised net interest income?

options.text: USD 18.10 million
USD 20.86 million
USD 24.50 million
USD 87.86 million

questions.solution:
$$\text{Net interest income} = [y_{RS} \times RSA + y_F \times FA] - [c_{RS} \times RSL + c_F \times FL]$$

where $y$ is an average yield, $c$ an average cost, $RSA$ and $RSL$ are rate-sensitive assets and liabilities, and $FA$ and $FL$ are the fixed-rate remainders.

**Step 1. Split the balance sheet.** With equity of zero, total liabilities equal total assets of USD 1,212 million:
$$\text{Fixed assets} = 1{,}212 - 542 = \text{USD } 670 \text{ million}$$
$$\text{Fixed liabilities} = 1{,}212 - 156 = \text{USD } 1{,}056 \text{ million}$$

**Step 2. Total interest income:**
$$0.05 \times 542 + 0.10 \times 670 = 27.10 + 67.00 = \text{USD } 94.10 \text{ million}$$

**Step 3. Total interest cost:**
$$0.04 \times 156 + 0.06 \times 1{,}056 = 6.24 + 63.36 = \text{USD } 69.60 \text{ million}$$

**Step 4. Net interest income:**
$$94.10 - 69.60 = \text{USD } 24.50 \text{ million}$$

Interpretation: note how lopsided the composition is. Only 45% of assets reprice this week but just 13% of liabilities do, so the bank is heavily asset sensitive in the short window and the bulk of its funding cost is locked in. The decomposition matters because a rate move changes only the first term in each bracket, which is exactly what the interest-sensitive gap measures.

a.reason: USD 18.10 million transposes the two asset yields, applying 10% to rate-sensitive assets and 5% to fixed assets: 54.20 + 33.50 − 69.60.

b.reason: USD 20.86 million = 27.10 − 6.24, using only the rate-sensitive legs and ignoring the fixed-rate assets and liabilities entirely.

d.reason: USD 87.86 million = 94.10 − 6.24, omitting the fixed-rate liability cost of USD 63.36 million. The largest single term in the calculation has been dropped.

trap.explanation: Option B is the conceptual trap: candidates primed by gap analysis focus on the rate-sensitive buckets and forget that net interest income is a whole-balance-sheet quantity, not a gap quantity. Option D is the arithmetic trap and is worth guarding against with a structural check, since fixed liabilities are the largest block on the balance sheet at USD 1,056 million and any answer that omits their cost will be conspicuously too large.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe interest-sensitive gap management and apply this strategy to maximize a bank's net interest margin.
questions.reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
questions.question: A treasury analyst is classifying balance sheet items for the coming month's interest-sensitivity report. Each of the following is correctly classified as interest-sensitive (repriceable) EXCEPT:

options.text: Federal funds purchased and repurchase agreement borrowings.
Adjustable-rate residential mortgages held in the loan book.
Cash held in the vault and reserve deposits at the central bank.
Money market deposit accounts whose rates are adjusted frequently.

questions.solution:
An item is repriceable, or interest-sensitive, if it matures, comes up for renewal, or has its rate reset within the planning period. The reading tabulates the two sides explicitly.

| | Repriceable (interest-sensitive) | Non-repriceable |
|---|---|---|
| Assets | Short-term government and private securities about to mature; short-term loans about to mature; variable-rate loans and securities | Vault cash and deposits at the central bank (legal reserves); long-term fixed-rate loans; long-term fixed-rate securities; buildings and equipment |
| Liabilities | Money market borrowings such as federal funds and repurchase agreements; short-term savings accounts; money market deposits with frequently adjusted rates | Demand deposits paying no interest or a fixed rate; long-term savings and retirement accounts; equity capital |

Vault cash and central bank reserves are the clearest non-repriceable assets. They are perfectly liquid, but liquidity is not the test. The test is whether the item's yield resets with market rates, and reserves either earn nothing or earn an administered rate that is not part of the repricing schedule. An item can be highly liquid and still be rate-insensitive.

The reading also flags a practical difficulty worth remembering for the limitations objective: the point at which some items reprice is not easy to identify. Checkable deposits and passbook savings accounts may have their rates adjusted up or down at any time, and the choice of planning period is itself arbitrary, so items can fall between the cracks.

a.reason: Federal funds and repurchase agreement borrowings are money market liabilities whose rates are often adjusted several times a day. They are the most rate-sensitive liabilities a bank has. Not the exception.

b.reason: Adjustable-rate mortgages are named in the reading as a familiar example of a repriceable asset. Not the exception.

c.reason: Vault cash and central bank reserve deposits are listed as non-repriceable assets. Their yield does not move with market rates within the planning period. This is the exception.

d.reason: Money market deposits are listed as repriceable liabilities, since their yields are adjustable frequently. Not the exception.

trap.explanation: The trap is conflating liquidity with rate sensitivity. Vault cash is the most liquid asset on the balance sheet, which makes it feel like it must be the most sensitive to anything. Ask the repricing question instead: within the planning window, does this item's interest rate reset? For cash the answer is no, so it belongs in the fixed bucket alongside long-dated fixed-rate loans.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe interest-sensitive gap management and apply this strategy to maximize a bank's net interest margin.
questions.reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
questions.question: Acme Bank reports interest-sensitive assets (ISA) of USD 490.0 million and interest-sensitive liabilities (ISL) of USD 610.0 million for the coming month. Following the worked example in the reading, the relative interest-sensitive gap is computed as the dollar interest-sensitive gap scaled by interest-sensitive assets. Respectively, what are the bank's relative interest-sensitive gap, its interest sensitivity ratio (ISR), and the effect of rising interest rates on its net interest margin?

options.text: Relative IS GAP of −0.245; ISR of 1.245; rising rates will raise the NIM.
Relative IS GAP of −0.245; ISR of 0.803; rising rates will lower the NIM.
Relative IS GAP of −0.197; ISR of 0.803; rising rates will lower the NIM.
Relative IS GAP of +0.245; ISR of 1.245; rising rates will raise the NIM.

questions.solution:
**Step 1. Dollar interest-sensitive gap:**
$$\text{Dollar IS GAP} = ISA - ISL = 490.0 - 610.0 = -\text{USD } 120.0 \text{ million}$$
A negative dollar gap means the bank is liability sensitive: more liabilities than assets will reprice this month.

**Step 2. Relative interest-sensitive gap, scaling by the stated size measure:**
$$\text{Relative IS GAP} = -120.0 \div 490.0 = -0.245$$

**Step 3. Interest sensitivity ratio:**
$$ISR = ISA \div ISL = 490.0 \div 610.0 = 0.803$$

**Step 4. Direction.** The three measures must agree, and they do:

| | Asset sensitive | Liability sensitive |
|---|---|---|
| Dollar IS GAP | Positive | Negative |
| Relative IS GAP | Positive | Negative |
| ISR | Greater than 1 | Less than 1 |
| Rates rise | NIM increases | NIM decreases |
| Rates fall | NIM decreases | NIM increases |

Because this bank is liability sensitive, a rise in rates lifts the cost of repricing liabilities by more than it lifts revenue from repricing assets, and the net interest margin falls. Management has, consciously or not, positioned the bank for falling rates over this horizon.

Definitional caution. The reading states the relative IS GAP as the dollar gap divided by the size of the institution, 'measured, for example, by total assets', but its own worked example divides −USD 50 million by USD 150 million, which is the interest-sensitive asset figure rather than total assets. Published question banks split on this point. The sign and the interpretation are unaffected either way; only the magnitude changes. If an exam item does not state the denominator, resolve it from whichever figure is supplied.

a.reason: The relative gap is right but the ISR is inverted (610 ÷ 490 = 1.245) and the direction has been read off that inverted ratio. An ISR above 1 would indicate asset sensitivity, which contradicts the negative gap in the same option.

b.reason: −120 ÷ 490 = −0.245; 490 ÷ 610 = 0.803; liability sensitive, so rising rates lower the NIM.

c.reason: −0.197 = −120 ÷ 610, scaling the gap by interest-sensitive liabilities rather than by the stated size measure. The ISR and the direction are right, so only one element is defective.

d.reason: The gap sign has been flipped and the ISR inverted, producing an internally consistent but entirely reversed picture of an asset-sensitive bank.

trap.explanation: The ISR inversion in options A and D is the classic error, and it is worth noting that option A is internally contradictory: it pairs a negative relative gap with an ISR above one, which cannot both be true. Use the consistency table as a free check. If your three measures do not all point the same way, one of them is wrong before you even consider the direction of the margin.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe interest-sensitive gap management and apply this strategy to maximize a bank's net interest margin.
questions.reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
questions.question: National Bank reports a cumulative interest-sensitive gap for the coming year of +USD 128 million. Market interest rates are expected to fall by one and a half percentage points. Which of the following is closest to the expected change in the bank's net interest income?

options.text: A decrease of USD 1.92 million
An increase of USD 1.92 million
A decrease of USD 19.20 million
No change, because a positive cumulative gap insulates net interest income from rate movements.

questions.solution:
$$\Delta \text{NII} = \text{overall change in interest rate (in percentage points)} \times \text{size of the cumulative gap (in dollars)}$$

**Step 1.** Express the rate change as a decimal. A fall of one and a half percentage points is $-0.015$.

**Step 2. Multiply:**
$$\Delta \text{NII} = (-0.015) \times (+128) = -\text{USD } 1.92 \text{ million}$$

Interpretation and direction check. The bank is asset sensitive over the year, with USD 128 million more assets than liabilities due to reprice. Falling rates therefore cut interest revenue by more than they cut interest cost, and net interest income drops by USD 1.92 million. The general rule the reading states:

| Cumulative gap | Rates rise | Rates fall |
|---|---|---|
| Positive | Net interest income gains | Net interest income falls |
| Negative | Net interest income falls | Net interest income gains |

The cumulative gap, rather than any single period's gap, is what matters over a planning horizon. The reading's illustrative table shows an institution with a positive gap in the next 24 hours but a negative cumulative gap over seven days, so a forecast of rising rates over the week would be bad news despite the favourable one-day position. If management expects the adverse move, it can shift assets and liabilities to reduce the cumulative gap or hedge with futures.

b.reason: The magnitude is right but the sign is reversed. This treats a fall in rates as favourable to a positive gap, which is the rule for a negative gap.

c.reason: USD 19.20 million applies a rate change of 15 percentage points rather than 1.5, a decimal slip of one order of magnitude.

d.reason: Confuses a positive gap with a zero gap. Only a gap of zero leaves the net interest margin protected regardless of which way rates go, and even then only approximately, since asset and liability rates are not perfectly correlated.

trap.explanation: Option B is the pure sign trap and it catches candidates who memorise 'positive gap is good' without attaching it to a rate direction. Option D is the more instructive error: it is the confusion between having a gap that is positive and having no gap at all. Only the zero gap immunises, and the reading is careful to add that even a zero gap does not eliminate all interest rate risk, because loan rates lag money market rates in practice.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe interest-sensitive gap management and apply this strategy to maximize a bank's net interest margin.
questions.reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
questions.question: Kestrel Bank is currently asset sensitive, with a positive interest-sensitive gap over the coming quarter. Management has become firmly convinced that market interest rates will fall over that horizon and wishes to protect net interest income. Which of the following actions is most appropriate?

options.text: Increase interest-sensitive assets and reduce interest-sensitive liabilities, widening the positive gap so as to capture the anticipated move.
Extend asset maturities or shorten liability maturities, which reduces the volume of interest-sensitive assets relative to interest-sensitive liabilities.
Shorten asset maturities or lengthen liability maturities, which is the standard corrective for a bank in this position.
Take no action, since a defensive gap strategy requires the gap to be held at its existing positive level irrespective of the rate forecast.

questions.solution:
**Step 1. Identify the exposure.** A positive gap means interest-sensitive assets exceed interest-sensitive liabilities. The risk attached to that position is losses if interest rates fall, because revenue from repricing assets will drop by more than the cost of repricing liabilities. That is precisely the scenario management now expects.

**Step 2. Apply the remedy.** The reading tabulates three possible responses to a positive gap:

| Position | The risk | Possible management responses |
|---|---|---|
| Positive gap (ISA above ISL, asset sensitive) | Losses if rates fall, because the NIM is reduced | 1. Do nothing, if rates may rise or be stable. 2. Extend asset maturities or shorten liability maturities. 3. Increase interest-sensitive liabilities or reduce interest-sensitive assets. |
| Negative gap (ISA below ISL, liability sensitive) | Losses if rates rise, because the NIM is reduced | 1. Do nothing, if rates may fall or be stable. 2. Shorten asset maturities or lengthen liability maturities. 3. Decrease interest-sensitive liabilities or increase interest-sensitive assets. |

Extending asset maturities pushes assets out of the repricing window, shrinking ISA; shortening liability maturities pulls liabilities into it, raising ISL. Both move the gap toward zero.

**Step 3. Distinguish the two postures.** Under aggressive gap management the firm deliberately shades the gap toward its rate forecast: expecting falling rates, it would let interest-sensitive liabilities climb above interest-sensitive assets, so that liability costs drop by more than revenues and the margin grows. Under defensive gap management it simply sets the gap as close to zero as possible to reduce the volatility of net interest income. The stem says management wishes to protect net interest income, which is the defensive objective.

The reading's own warning is worth carrying into the exam: consistently correct rate forecasting is impossible, and most financial managers have learned to rely on hedging against rather than forecasting rate changes, because rates that move the wrong way magnify losses under an aggressive strategy.

a.reason: This is the aggressive response to a forecast of rising rates. Widening a positive gap into a fall in rates maximises the loss rather than avoiding it.

b.reason: Extending asset maturities or shortening liability maturities is listed as the second response to a positive gap, and it closes the exposure the forecast implies.

c.reason: Sibling swap. Shortening assets and lengthening liabilities is the corrective for a negative gap, and applied here it would widen the positive gap.

d.reason: Misstates the defensive strategy, which is to set the gap as close to zero as possible, not to freeze it wherever it happens to be. 'Do nothing' is a listed response only when rates may move favourably or remain stable, which is not the case here.

trap.explanation: Options B and C are the two remedy lists presented side by side, so a candidate who has memorised the pairs but not which pair goes with which sign has a coin flip. The reliable route is to reason from the mechanism rather than recall the table: extending assets removes them from the repricing bucket, which is what an asset-sensitive bank facing falling rates wants. Option D is a scope error on the word 'defensive'.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe interest-sensitive gap management and apply this strategy to maximize a bank's net interest margin.
questions.reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
questions.question:
A bank's rate-sensitive positions and the interest rate sensitivity weights estimated for each are shown below (all amounts in USD millions):

| Item | Balance | Sensitivity weight |
|---|---|---|
| Federal funds loans | 60 | 1.00 |
| Government securities and other investments | 40 | 1.30 |
| Loans and leases | 150 | 1.50 |
| Interest-bearing deposits | 180 | 0.86 |
| Other money market borrowings | 90 | 0.91 |

Which of the following gives the bank's weighted interest-sensitive gap and the predicted change in net interest income if the federal funds rate rises by two percentage points?

options.text: A gap of −USD 20.0 million and a decrease of USD 0.40 million.
A gap of +USD 67.0 million and an increase of USD 1.34 million.
A gap of +USD 100.3 million and a decrease of USD 2.01 million.
A gap of +USD 100.3 million and an increase of USD 2.01 million.

questions.solution:
The conventional gap assumes every rate-sensitive item reprices one for one with market rates. In practice rates attached to different assets and liabilities change by different amounts and at different speeds, a phenomenon the reading calls basis risk. The weighted gap refigures the balance sheet to reflect this.

**Step 1.** The unweighted position, for reference:
$$\text{Unweighted ISA} = 60 + 40 + 150 = \text{USD } 250 \text{ million}$$
$$\text{Unweighted ISL} = 180 + 90 = \text{USD } 270 \text{ million}$$
$$\text{Unweighted IS GAP} = 250 - 270 = -\text{USD } 20.0 \text{ million (liability sensitive)}$$

**Step 2.** Refigure each side using its sensitivity weight. Federal funds loans track market rates one for one, so their weight is 1.00 and they serve as the benchmark. Investments are somewhat more rate-volatile at 1.30, and loans and leases the most volatile at 1.50. On the funding side, deposit and money market rates move less than one for one.
$$\text{Weighted ISA} = 60(1.00) + 40(1.30) + 150(1.50) = 60.0 + 52.0 + 225.0 = \text{USD } 337.0 \text{ million}$$
$$\text{Weighted ISL} = 180(0.86) + 90(0.91) = 154.8 + 81.9 = \text{USD } 236.7 \text{ million}$$
$$\text{Weighted IS GAP} = 337.0 - 236.7 = +\text{USD } 100.3 \text{ million (asset sensitive)}$$

**Step 3.** Predict the effect of a two percentage point rise in the benchmark rate:
$$\Delta \text{NII} = +0.02 \times (+100.3) = +\text{USD } 2.01 \text{ million}$$

The economic point is that the gap has changed sign. On the conventional balance sheet this bank appears liability sensitive and would be forecast to lose USD 0.40 million on a two point rise. On the refigured balance sheet it is asset sensitive and gains USD 2.01 million. Management's response to a forecast of rising rates would be entirely different under the two readings. As the reading puts it, when it comes to assessing interest rate risk, things are not always as they appear.

a.reason: This is the unweighted position and the prediction it implies. It is the answer the question is designed to show is misleading.

b.reason: +USD 67.0 million = 337.0 − 270.0, applying the sensitivity weights to the asset side only and leaving liabilities at their book values. Weighting must be applied consistently to both sides.

c.reason: The gap is right but the sign of the income effect is reversed. A positive gap gains from rising rates.

d.reason: Weighted gap of +USD 100.3 million; +0.02 × 100.3 = +USD 2.01 million.

trap.explanation: Option A rewards the candidate who computes the gap the familiar way and stops. Option B is the half-applied weighting, which is easy to commit when the asset weights are visually grouped at the top of a table and the liability weights sit below a mental dividing line. The structural warning worth carrying forward: asset weights here all exceed 1.00 while liability weights are below 1.00, so the weighting must push the gap in the positive direction. If your weighted gap moves the other way, you have applied the weights to the wrong side.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe duration gap management and apply this strategy to protect a bank's net worth.
questions.reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
questions.question: A bank holds a three-year loan with a face value of USD 1,000 that pays an annual coupon of 8%. The loan's current yield to maturity is also 8%, so it is priced at par. Which of the following is closest to the loan's duration?

options.text: 2.24 years
2.58 years
2.78 years
3.00 years

questions.solution:
Duration is a value- and time-weighted measure of maturity. It measures the average time needed to recover the funds committed to an investment.

$$D = \sum_t \left[ \frac{CF_t \times t}{(1 + YTM)^t} \right] \div \text{current market price}$$

where $CF_t$ is the cash flow in period $t$ and the denominator is the instrument's price, which is itself the sum of the present values of the cash flows.

**Step 1.** Lay out the cash flows and discount them at 8%.

| Period $t$ | Cash flow | PV at 8% | PV × t |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 80.00 | 74.07 | 74.07 |
| 2 | 80.00 | 68.59 | 137.17 |
| 3 | 1,080.00 | 857.34 | 2,572.02 |
| Total | 1,240.00 | 1,000.00 | 2,783.26 |

The present value column sums to USD 1,000, confirming that the loan is priced at par, as it must be when the coupon equals the yield.

**Step 2. Divide:**
$$D = 2{,}783.26 \div 1{,}000.00 = 2.78 \text{ years}$$

Interpretation. The loan runs for three calendar years but its duration is 2.78 years, because some cash is returned before maturity. This illustrates the general rule the reading states in the limitations section: for any instrument that pays out gradually over time, duration is always less than calendar maturity. Only for zero-coupon securities, single-payment loans and Treasury bills are the two equal. The more frequently an instrument pays interest or principal, the shorter its duration.

a.reason: 2.24 years = 2,783.26 ÷ 1,240.00, dividing the time-weighted present values by the sum of the nominal cash flows instead of by the price. The denominator of the duration formula is the present value sum.

b.reason: 2.58 years = 2.78 ÷ 1.08. This is modified duration, which is the measure used to convert directly into a percentage price change. The question asked for duration itself.

d.reason: 3.00 years equates duration with calendar maturity, which holds only for zero-coupon and single-payment instruments.

trap.explanation: Option D is the conceptual trap and it is the one the reading singles out: candidates want duration to equal maturity because that would make matching assets and liabilities easy, which is precisely why finding matched durations is described as a frustrating task. Option B is the sibling swap between duration and modified duration, and it is worth noting that Rose and Hudgins do not divide by (1 + y) in the duration definition; they apply that factor separately in the price-change formula.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe duration gap management and apply this strategy to protect a bank's net worth.
questions.reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
questions.question: A savings institution holds a bond with a duration of 6.5 years and a current market price of USD 980. Market interest rates on comparable bonds are currently 6.00% and are forecast to rise to 6.75%. Which of the following is closest to the resulting percentage change in the bond's market price?

options.text: A decrease of 41.39%
A decrease of 4.88%
A decrease of 4.60%
An increase of 4.60%

questions.solution:
The risk-management value of duration is that it measures the sensitivity of an instrument's market value to a change in interest rates:

$$\Delta P \div P = -D \times \left[ \frac{\Delta i}{1 + i} \right]$$

where $\Delta P \div P$ is the percentage change in market price, $D$ is duration, $\Delta i$ is the change in the interest rate, and $i$ is the initial rate. The negative sign records that prices and rates move in opposite directions.

**Step 1.** Identify the change in rates, not their level:
$$\Delta i = 0.0675 - 0.0600 = 0.0075, \text{ or } 75 \text{ basis points}$$

**Step 2.** Form the relative rate change, discounting at the initial rate:
$$\Delta i \div (1 + i) = 0.0075 \div 1.06 = 0.0070755$$

**Step 3.** Multiply by duration:
$$\Delta P \div P = -6.5 \times 0.0070755 = -0.04599, \text{ or } -4.60\%$$

In money terms the position loses about $0.0460 \times \text{USD } 980 = \text{USD } 45.07$.

The relationship the formula encodes is that interest rate risk is directly proportional to duration. An instrument with a duration of 2 is twice as volatile in price terms as one with a duration of 1, holding the rate move constant. That proportionality is what makes duration usable as a hedging control variable, and it is the basis for the duration gap framework that follows.

a.reason: −41.39% = −6.5 × 0.0675 ÷ 1.06, using the new level of rates in place of the change in rates. The formula takes $\Delta i$, not $i$.

b.reason: −4.88% = −6.5 × 0.0075, omitting the division by (1 + i). This is the modified-duration form applied to a duration figure, and it overstates the price move.

d.reason: The magnitude is right but the sign is reversed. Rising rates lower the market price of a fixed-rate instrument.

trap.explanation: Option A is the level-for-change substitution and produces an answer an order of magnitude too large, which should be caught on inspection: a 75 basis point move cannot destroy 41% of a medium-duration bond. Option B is the subtler and more common error, since dividing by (1 + i) is easy to skip and the resulting figure is plausible. Keep the distinction clean: duration times the relative rate change, where relative means divided by one plus the starting rate.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe duration gap management and apply this strategy to protect a bank's net worth.
questions.reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
questions.question: Thomas Peters, the chief risk officer at ABC Bank, is assessing the sensitivity of the bank's net worth to a 200 basis point change in interest rates using duration analysis. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: A prepayable mortgage loan carries a longer duration than an otherwise comparable non-prepayable loan, and is therefore more vulnerable to a change in the market's average interest rate.

The market values of assets and liabilities are more sensitive to a change in interest rates when the coupon is lower, when the duration is higher, or when the overall level of interest rates is lower.
The percentage change in the value of an asset or liability is directly proportional to its duration and is independent of the size of the relative change in interest rates.
Paying a USD 50 million cash dividend out of the bank's cash balances leaves the average duration of its asset portfolio unchanged.

questions.solution:
Three separate determinants of price sensitivity are being tested, and the correct option states all three with the right direction.

| Determinant | Direction | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Coupon | Lower coupon means greater sensitivity | Less cash is returned early, so weight shifts toward the distant principal payment and duration lengthens |
| Duration | Higher duration means greater sensitivity | Price sensitivity is directly proportional to duration |
| Level of rates | Lower rate level means greater sensitivity | The convexity effect: price movement for a given rate change is greater at low rates than at high rates |

On prepayment: a prepayable mortgage typically has a shorter duration than a comparable non-prepayable investment, because the borrower's option to repay early pulls cash flows forward. A shorter duration means less vulnerability to a change in the average level of rates, though it introduces a distinct problem of its own, since prepayments distort expected cash flows and make duration harder to estimate in the first place.

On the dividend: cash has a duration of zero. Paying a dividend out of cash removes a zero-duration asset from the portfolio, which mechanically raises the value-weighted average duration of the assets that remain, as well as shrinking the balance sheet.

a.reason: Polarity flip. A prepayable mortgage has a shorter duration than a comparable non-prepayable loan, and is therefore less sensitive to a change in the average level of rates.

b.reason: All three determinants are stated with the correct direction.

c.reason: The first half is right and the second half is wrong. The percentage price change is proportional to duration and to the relative change in interest rates, as the formula makes explicit.

d.reason: Cash carries zero duration, so removing it raises the value-weighted average duration of the remaining asset portfolio. The bank's overall asset level also falls.

trap.explanation: Option D is the sleeper. It sounds like a question about liquidity or capital and is actually a question about weighting: any transaction that changes the mix of a portfolio changes its value-weighted duration, and paying out the lowest-duration asset raises the average of what remains. Option C is a partial truth with a fatal second clause, which is the standard four-statement audit construction.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe duration gap management and apply this strategy to protect a bank's net worth.
questions.reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
questions.question: A portfolio manager is documenting the role of convexity in the bank's duration-based interest rate risk framework. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Convexity decreases as the duration of an asset increases, which is why long-dated instruments can be hedged adequately using duration alone.

Holding maturity and yield constant, convexity falls as the promised coupon rate rises, and an asset's price movement for a given rate change tends to be greater at low interest rates than at high interest rates.
Holding maturity and yield constant, convexity rises as the promised coupon rate rises, and price risk is greater when interest rates are high than when they are low.
Convexity can be disregarded in duration gap management, because the duration gap model already assumes a nonlinear relationship between asset prices and interest rates.

questions.solution:
Convexity refers to the presence of a nonlinear relationship between changes in an asset's price and changes in market interest rates. It is a number designed to help managers measure and control market risk, and an asset bearing both low duration and low convexity normally displays relatively small market risk.

| Property | Direction |
|---|---|
| Convexity and duration or maturity | Convexity increases with duration |
| Convexity and coupon rate (maturity and yield held constant) | Convexity falls as the coupon rate rises |
| Price movement and the level of rates | Price movement for a given rate change is greater at low rates; price risk is greater when rates are low |
| Convexity and price volatility | Lower convexity, meaning lower curvature, means lower price volatility |

The reading's illustration of the rate-level effect: if the yield on a 30-year bond falls from 6.5% to 6.0%, the price rises by roughly 8 points per USD 1,000 of face value. If instead the yield falls from 10.0% to 9.5%, the same half-point move raises the price by only slightly more than 4 points. Identical rate change, roughly double the price response at the lower rate level.

Why this matters for the duration gap framework: duration gap models assume a linear relationship between market values and interest rates, which is not strictly true. That assumption is acceptable for small, roughly parallel yield curve shifts. For a large move of one or two percentage points, the linear approximation gives a distorted reading of the interest rate risk the manager actually faces, and convexity is the term that captures what duration alone misses.

a.reason: Polarity flip, with a conclusion that follows from it. Convexity increases with duration, so long-dated instruments are exactly the ones for which duration alone is least adequate.

b.reason: Both statements match the reading: convexity falls as the coupon rises, and price movement is greater at low rate levels.

c.reason: Both halves are reversed. Convexity falls rather than rises with the coupon rate, and price risk is greater at low rather than high rate levels.

d.reason: Reverses the model's assumption. Duration gap analysis assumes a linear relationship, which is precisely why convexity has to be considered separately for large rate movements.

trap.explanation: Option D is the one to watch, because it correctly identifies convexity as being about nonlinearity and then attributes that nonlinearity to the wrong model. Duration is the linear approximation; convexity is the correction to it. Options B and C are the same pair of directions stated twice, so a candidate who has either one backwards will find a confirming option. Anchor the coupon result with the duration link: a higher coupon shortens duration, and shorter duration means lower convexity.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe duration gap management and apply this strategy to protect a bank's net worth.
questions.reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
questions.question:
Green House National Bank reports the following portfolio (all amounts in USD millions):

| Asset | Amount | Duration (years) | Liability | Amount | Duration (years) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Investment-grade bonds | 80 | 7.50 | Deposits | 376 | 2.30 |
| Commercial loans | 423 | 4.23 | Non-deposit borrowings | 25 | 0.12 |
| Consumer loans | 145 | 3.20 | | | |
| Total assets | 648 | | Total liabilities | 401 | |

Respectively, what are the dollar-weighted duration of the bank's liability portfolio, the dollar-weighted duration of its asset portfolio, and its leverage-adjusted duration gap?

options.text: 2.16 years, 4.40 years, 0.56 years
2.16 years, 4.40 years, 2.24 years
2.16 years, 4.40 years, 3.06 years
4.40 years, 2.16 years, 3.06 years

questions.solution:
**Step 1.** Dollar-weighted duration of the asset portfolio. Each component duration is weighted by its share of total market value:
$$D_A = 7.50(80 \div 648) + 4.23(423 \div 648) + 3.20(145 \div 648) = 0.926 + 2.761 + 0.716 = 4.40 \text{ years}$$

**Step 2.** Dollar-weighted duration of the liability portfolio:
$$D_L = 2.30(376 \div 401) + 0.12(25 \div 401) = 2.157 + 0.007 = 2.16 \text{ years}$$

**Step 3.** Leverage-adjusted duration gap. The dollar volume of assets exceeds that of liabilities, otherwise the bank would be insolvent, so the liability duration must be scaled by the ratio of total liabilities to total assets:
$$\text{Leverage-adjusted duration gap} = D_A - D_L \times (\text{total liabilities} \div \text{total assets})$$
$$= 4.40 - 2.16 \times (401 \div 648) = 4.40 - 2.16 \times 0.6188 = 4.40 - 1.34 = +3.06 \text{ years}$$

Interpretation. A large positive leverage-adjusted duration gap means the bank's net worth is highly exposed to rising rates: asset values will fall by considerably more than liability values. Commercial loans dominate the asset duration, contributing 2.76 of the 4.40 years, so any hedging programme would start there. Note also how little the non-deposit borrowings matter: at USD 25 million and 0.12 years they contribute under a hundredth of a year to the liability duration.

a.reason: The two durations are right but the gap of 0.56 years applies the leverage ratio to the asset duration instead of the liability duration: 4.40 × 0.6188 − 2.16.

b.reason: The two durations are right but 2.24 years is the raw duration gap, 4.40 − 2.16, with the leverage adjustment omitted altogether.

d.reason: All three figures are correct but the first two are reported in the wrong order. The question asked for the liability duration first.

trap.explanation: Option D is the order trap and it is entirely avoidable: the stem asks for the liability portfolio first and the asset portfolio second, which is the reverse of the order in which most candidates will naturally compute them. Underline the sequence in the stem before you start. Option B is the omitted leverage adjustment, the single most common error in this calculation, and option A applies the adjustment to the wrong side, which is what happens when the formula is recalled as a shape rather than as a statement about which side is larger.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe duration gap management and apply this strategy to protect a bank's net worth.
questions.reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
questions.question: Millennial National Bank has an average asset duration of 2.53 years and an average liability duration of 0.65 years. Total assets are USD 367 million and total liabilities are USD 219 million. Interest rates were originally 5.0% and then rise to 8.5%. Respectively, what are the bank's leverage-adjusted duration gap and the estimated change in its net worth?

options.text: +1.88 years and a decrease of USD 26.21 million
+2.14 years and a decrease of USD 26.21 million
+2.14 years and a decrease of USD 27.52 million
+2.14 years and a decrease of USD 30.95 million

questions.solution:
**Step 1. Leverage-adjusted duration gap:**
$$= D_A - D_L \times (L \div A) = 2.53 - 0.65 \times (219 \div 367) = 2.53 - 0.65 \times 0.5967 = 2.53 - 0.388 = +2.14 \text{ years}$$

A positive gap tells us immediately that net worth will fall when rates rise, before any arithmetic is done. That is a useful direction check on the second half of the answer.

**Step 2. Change in the value of net worth:**
$$\Delta NW = [-D_A \times \Delta r \div (1 + r) \times A] - [-D_L \times \Delta r \div (1 + r) \times L]$$

where $r$ is the original rate of 5.0% and $\Delta r$ is $+0.035$.
$$\Delta r \div (1 + r) = 0.035 \div 1.05 = 0.033333$$

Asset leg:
$$-2.53 \times 0.033333 \times 367 = -\text{USD } 30.95 \text{ million}$$

Liability leg (which is subtracted, so it enters as a gain):
$$-[-0.65 \times 0.033333 \times 219] = +\text{USD } 4.75 \text{ million}$$

**Step 3. Combine:**
$$\Delta NW = -30.95 + 4.75 = -\text{USD } 26.21 \text{ million}$$

Interpretation. The 3.5 percentage point rise destroys USD 26.21 million of net worth. Against a starting net worth of $367 - 219 = \text{USD } 148$ million, that is a loss of nearly 18% of the owners' investment from a single parallel rate move, which is why duration gap management exists alongside interest-sensitive gap management.

A useful shortcut: since both legs share the factor $\Delta r \div (1 + r)$, the calculation collapses to $-[D_A A - D_L L] \times \Delta r \div (1 + r) = -[928.51 - 142.35] \times 0.033333 = -\text{USD } 26.21 \text{ million}$.

a.reason: The change in net worth is right but 1.88 years is the raw duration gap, 2.53 − 0.65, with no leverage adjustment.

b.reason: +2.14 years and −USD 26.21 million.

c.reason: USD 27.52 million uses $\Delta r = 0.035$ directly without dividing by (1 + r), which overstates the loss by about 5%.

d.reason: USD 30.95 million is the asset leg alone. The offsetting fall in the value of liabilities has been omitted.

trap.explanation: Option D is the intermediate-result trap and it is the largest of the four figures, which makes it attractive to anyone who expects a big number from a 350 basis point move. Option C is the omitted (1 + r) discounting, worth noting because the error is small in percentage terms and therefore survives a rough sanity check. Option A tests only the first half of the question, so a candidate who computes the net worth change first and then reaches for the nearest matching option will be caught by the gap figure.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe duration gap management and apply this strategy to protect a bank's net worth.
questions.reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
questions.question:
ABC Bank is stress testing a 300 basis point rise in interest rates from a current level of 3.0%. Its balance sheet and the durations of its individual positions are as follows (amounts in USD millions):

| Assets | Amount | Duration | Liabilities and equity | Amount | Duration |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cash | 75 | 0.0 | Interest-bearing marketable deposits | 300 | 0.5 |
| Federal funds loans | 130 | 1.0 | Other borrowings | 270 | 3.0 |
| Government securities and mortgages | 160 | 4.0 | Total liabilities | 570 | |
| Loans and leases | 240 | 2.0 | Shareholders' equity | 35 | |
| Total assets | 605 | | Total | 605 | |

Which of the following best describes the effect of the stress scenario on the bank's net worth?

options.text: A decrease of USD 8.45 million
A decrease of USD 8.70 million
A decrease of USD 36.41 million
An increase of USD 8.45 million

questions.solution:
**Long route.** Compute the two portfolio durations first.
$$D_A = [75(0) + 130(1) + 160(4) + 240(2)] \div 605 = 1{,}250 \div 605 = 2.0661 \text{ years}$$
$$D_L = [300(0.5) + 270(3)] \div 570 = 960 \div 570 = 1.6842 \text{ years}$$

Then apply the change-in-net-worth formula with $r = 0.03$ and $\Delta r = +0.03$:
$$\Delta NW = -2.0661 \times (0.03 \div 1.03) \times 605 + 1.6842 \times (0.03 \div 1.03) \times 570 = -36.41 + 27.96 = -\text{USD } 8.45 \text{ million}$$

**Shortcut.** Notice that $D_A$ is computed as 1,250 divided by 605, and is then multiplied by 605 again. The division and multiplication cancel. The same happens on the liability side. The formula therefore reduces to the difference of the two dollar-duration sums:
$$\Delta NW = -[\Sigma(D \times A) - \Sigma(D \times L)] \times \Delta r \div (1 + r) = -[1{,}250 - 960] \times (0.03 \div 1.03) = -290 \times 0.029126 = -\text{USD } 8.45 \text{ million}$$

Finding the shortcut removes two divisions and their rounding error, and takes roughly forty seconds instead of two minutes. Under exam conditions that is the difference between finishing the quantitative questions and running out of time on the qualitative ones.

Interpretation. The loss of USD 8.45 million must be set against shareholders' equity of USD 35 million: a single 300 basis point move erases roughly a quarter of the bank's book equity. Note that cash contributes nothing to the asset duration, so its USD 75 million balance is doing no work in this calculation at all.

b.reason: USD 8.70 million = 290 × 0.03, using the raw rate change without dividing by (1 + r).

c.reason: USD 36.41 million is the asset leg alone, omitting the offsetting decline in the value of liabilities.

d.reason: The magnitude is right but the sign is reversed. With a positive leverage-adjusted duration gap, rising rates reduce net worth.

trap.explanation: Option C is the intermediate-result trap in its most tempting form, since the asset leg is the harder half of the calculation and a candidate who has done that work may stop. Guard against it structurally: any answer that ignores one side of the balance sheet cannot be a net worth change. Option B is the omitted discounting, which here costs only about 3% and so will not announce itself as wrong.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe duration gap management and apply this strategy to protect a bank's net worth.
questions.reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
questions.question: ABC Bank has an average asset duration of four years and an average liability duration of three years. Total assets are USD 180 million and total liabilities are USD 150 million. Interest rates initially stood at 9% and then rise suddenly to 13%. Which of the following is closest to the bank's net worth after the increase in interest rates?

options.text: USD 3.59 million
USD 9.91 million
USD 20.09 million
USD 46.51 million

questions.solution:
**Step 1. Original net worth from the balance sheet identity:**
$$NW = A - L = 180 - 150 = \text{USD } 30 \text{ million}$$

**Step 2. Change in net worth.** With $r = 0.09$ and $\Delta r = +0.04$:
$$\Delta r \div (1 + r) = 0.04 \div 1.09 = 0.036697$$

Asset leg:
$$-4 \times 0.036697 \times 180 = -\text{USD } 26.42 \text{ million}$$

Liability leg, which is subtracted and so enters as a gain:
$$-[-3 \times 0.036697 \times 150] = +\text{USD } 16.51 \text{ million}$$

$$\Delta NW = -26.42 + 16.51 = -\text{USD } 9.91 \text{ million}$$

**Step 3. New level of net worth:**
$$NW_{new} = 30.00 - 9.91 = \text{USD } 20.09 \text{ million}$$

Direction check. The leverage-adjusted duration gap is $4 - 3 \times (150 \div 180) = 4 - 2.5 = +1.5$ years. A positive gap plus rising rates means falling net worth, which is what the arithmetic produced. The bank remains solvent, with net worth down by about a third.

a.reason: USD 3.59 million = 30.00 − 26.42, subtracting only the asset-side loss and ignoring the offsetting fall in the value of liabilities.

b.reason: USD 9.91 million is the magnitude of the change in net worth, not the resulting level. This is the answer to the question that was not asked.

d.reason: USD 46.51 million = 30.00 + 16.51, adding the liability-side gain while omitting the larger asset-side loss.

trap.explanation: Option B is the whole point of the item. The duration formula returns a change, and almost every question in this chapter asks for exactly that, so the habit is deeply grooved by the time a question asks for a level instead. Read the final noun in the stem. Options A and D are the two one-legged calculations, and note that they sit either side of the correct answer, so magnitude alone will not rescue you.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe duration gap management and apply this strategy to protect a bank's net worth.
questions.reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
questions.question: A financial firm wishes to be fully hedged against interest rate fluctuations using duration gap analysis. Total assets exceed total liabilities. Which of the following describes the condition for a full hedge?

options.text: The dollar-weighted duration of assets equals the dollar-weighted duration of liabilities, with no further adjustment.
The leverage-adjusted duration gap is zero, which given that liabilities are smaller than assets requires the average liability duration to exceed the average asset duration.
The leverage-adjusted duration gap is zero, which given that liabilities are smaller than assets requires the average asset duration to exceed the average liability duration.
The interest sensitivity ratio equals one, since equal repricing volumes on the two sides also equalise the durations.

questions.solution:
**Step 1. State the condition.** A full hedge of net worth requires:
$$D_A - D_L \times (L \div A) = 0$$

**Step 2. Solve for the required liability duration:**
$$D_L = D_A \times (A \div L)$$

**Step 3. Read the implication.** Because a solvent institution has $A$ greater than $L$, the ratio $A \div L$ exceeds one, so the required liability duration must be greater than the asset duration. As the reading puts it, the value of liabilities must change by slightly more than the value of assets to eliminate the firm's overall interest rate risk exposure. The smaller base of liabilities has to work harder per dollar.

The reading's own worked case makes this concrete. A bank with $D_A$ of 3.047 years, assets of USD 300 million and liabilities of USD 275 million needs an average liability duration of:
$$D_L = 3.047 \times (300 \div 275) = 3.324 \text{ years}$$

At that liability duration a two percentage point rise in rates produces −USD 16.93 million on the asset side and +USD 16.93 million on the liability side, netting to exactly zero. The firm is immunised: net worth does not move whichever way rates go.

Note what this rules out. Simply matching $D_A$ to $D_L$ leaves a positive leverage-adjusted gap, since $D_A - D_L(L \div A)$ is positive whenever $A$ exceeds $L$, so a bank that has 'matched durations' in the naive sense is still exposed to rising rates.

a.reason: Matching the two durations without the leverage adjustment leaves a positive leverage-adjusted gap and therefore leaves net worth exposed to rising rates. This is the incomplete condition.

b.reason: A zero leverage-adjusted gap requires $D_L = D_A(A \div L)$, and since $A$ exceeds $L$ this makes the liability duration the longer of the two.

c.reason: The condition is stated correctly but the implication is reversed. Solving the zero-gap equation puts the larger duration on the liability side, not the asset side.

d.reason: Sibling swap between the two tools. The interest sensitivity ratio belongs to interest-sensitive gap management, which protects the net interest margin; it says nothing about durations and does not protect net worth.

trap.explanation: Option C is the trap that separates candidates who have memorised the formula from those who have solved it. The intuition that assets are 'the long side' of a bank balance sheet is correct about maturities and wrong about the immunising duration, because the leverage adjustment inverts the comparison. Option A is the naive matching condition, which is what most people mean when they say durations are matched. Option D is the tool confusion: net interest margin against net worth.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe duration gap management and apply this strategy to protect a bank's net worth.
questions.reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
questions.question: Harrier Bank has a dollar-weighted average asset duration of 3.60 years, total assets of USD 840 million and total liabilities of USD 760 million. Which of the following is closest to the average liability duration the bank must achieve in order to immunise the market value of its net worth against a parallel shift in interest rates?

options.text: 2.95 years
3.26 years
3.60 years
3.98 years

questions.solution:
Set the leverage-adjusted duration gap to zero and solve:
$$0 = D_A - D_L \times (L \div A)$$
$$D_L = D_A \times (A \div L)$$

**Step 1.** Form the leverage ratio. Note the direction: assets over liabilities, which is greater than one.
$$A \div L = 840 \div 760 = 1.10526$$

**Step 2. Multiply:**
$$D_L = 3.60 \times 1.10526 = 3.979, \text{ or about } 3.98 \text{ years}$$

Verification. Substitute back into the gap formula:
$$3.60 - 3.979 \times (760 \div 840) = 3.60 - 3.60 = 0$$

Interpretation. The bank must lengthen its funding by about 0.38 years beyond its asset duration. The economic reason is that only USD 760 million of liabilities must absorb the value change of USD 840 million of assets, so each liability dollar has to be more rate-sensitive than each asset dollar. Equity of USD 80 million is the wedge that makes the two sides unequal.

In practice the reading is candid that achieving this is difficult: finding assets and liabilities of the required duration that also fit the institution's portfolio is described as a frustrating task, and duration itself drifts as instruments approach maturity and as rates move, so the position needs continual rebalancing.

a.reason: 2.95 years = 3.60 × (760 ÷ 840)², applying the leverage ratio in the wrong direction twice.

b.reason: 3.26 years = 3.60 × (760 ÷ 840), applying $L \div A$ instead of $A \div L$. This inverts the required adjustment and would leave the bank exposed to rising rates.

c.reason: 3.60 years simply sets the liability duration equal to the asset duration, omitting the leverage adjustment entirely.

trap.explanation: Option B is the ratio inversion and it is the trap with the highest hit rate, because the leverage-adjusted gap formula contains $L \div A$ and the eye reaches for the ratio it has just seen rather than the one the rearranged equation requires. The one-second guard: the answer must be larger than the asset duration, so any option at or below 3.60 years can be struck without computing anything. Option C is the naive matching answer.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe duration gap management and apply this strategy to protect a bank's net worth.
questions.reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
questions.question: A risk committee is reviewing how the sign of the leverage-adjusted duration gap governs the response of net worth to interest rate movements. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: With a negative leverage-adjusted duration gap, a rise in interest rates will increase the market value of net worth, because liability values decrease faster than asset values.
With a negative leverage-adjusted duration gap, a fall in interest rates will increase the market value of net worth, because asset values rise by more than liability values.
With a positive leverage-adjusted duration gap, a rise in interest rates will increase the market value of net worth, because asset values fall by less than liability values.
A management team that firmly expects interest rates to rise should increase the average duration of assets and reduce the average duration of liabilities.

questions.solution:
The mechanism is that the leverage-adjusted gap determines which side of the balance sheet revalues more for a given parallel rate move.

| Leverage-adjusted duration gap | If rates rise | If rates fall |
|---|---|---|
| Positive ($D_A$ above $D_L \times L/A$) | Net worth decreases | Net worth increases |
| Negative ($D_A$ below $D_L \times L/A$) | Net worth increases | Net worth decreases |
| Zero | No change | No change |

With a negative gap, a parallel change in rates generates a larger change in liability values than in asset values. When rates rise, liability values fall faster than asset values, so the difference between them, which is net worth, increases. When rates fall, liabilities gain more value than assets and net worth declines.

With a positive gap the reverse holds: asset values move more, so a rise in rates pushes asset values down further than liability values and net worth falls.

The aggressive management implications follow directly, and they are the reverse of what intuition suggests:

| Rate expectation | Action | Gap moves toward |
|---|---|---|
| Rates will rise | Reduce $D_A$ and increase $D_L$ | Negative |
| Rates will fall | Increase $D_A$ and reduce $D_L$ | Positive |

In each case net worth increases if the forecast proves correct. The reading is careful to note that this is a bet, and that more conservative managers prefer immunisation at a zero gap despite its being the seemingly less ambitious strategy.

a.reason: A negative gap means liability values move more, so a rate rise cuts liabilities faster than assets and net worth increases.

b.reason: Polarity flip. With a negative gap, falling rates raise liability values by more than asset values, so net worth decreases.

c.reason: Polarity flip. With a positive gap, asset values move more, so a rate rise pushes assets down further than liabilities and net worth decreases.

d.reason: Reverses the aggressive strategy. Expecting rates to rise, management should reduce asset duration and increase liability duration, moving toward a negative gap, so that a rate rise raises net worth.

trap.explanation: Three of the four options are single-direction reversals of the same table, which is how this material is always tested. Rather than memorising six rows, derive them from one sentence: the gap tells you which side of the balance sheet moves more, and net worth is assets minus liabilities. Positive gap means assets move more; rates up means values down; assets falling further means net worth falls. Every other row follows by symmetry.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Discuss the limitations of interest-sensitive gap management and duration gap management.
questions.reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
questions.question: A risk manager is documenting the shortcomings of the bank's interest-sensitive gap framework for its model validation file. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: A zero interest-sensitive gap fully immunises the net interest margin, because equal repricing volumes on the two sides guarantee that interest revenue and interest cost move together.

Interest rates paid on liabilities, which are mostly short term, tend to move faster than interest rates earned on assets, many of which are long term, so the technique's implicit assumption of parallel repricing is imperfect.
The technique overstates a bank's exposure to rate movements because it captures the effect of those movements on both net income and the market value of shareholders' equity.
The repricing dates of checkable deposits and passbook savings accounts are fixed by contract, so the arbitrary choice of planning period is the technique's only material source of imprecision.

questions.solution:
The reading lists several problems with interest-sensitive gap management, and option B states the first of them directly.

| Limitation | Consequence |
|---|---|
| Interest rates paid on liabilities, mostly short term, tend to move faster than rates earned on assets, many of which are long term | The gap treats the two sides as repricing in step when in practice the liability side moves first |
| Rates attached to assets and liabilities do not move at the same speed as rates in the open market | Basis risk, which motivates the weighted interest-sensitive gap |
| The point at which some items reprice is not easy to identify; checkable deposits and passbook savings may be repriced at any time | Classification into the repriceable bucket is partly a matter of judgement |
| The choice of planning period is arbitrary, and items may fall just short of the horizon | A gap measured over 30 days and one measured over 90 days can point in opposite directions |
| The technique analyses the effect of rate changes on net income and neglects the effect on the market value of shareholders' equity | This is the specific gap that duration gap management was developed to close |
| A zero gap does not eliminate all interest rate risk | Loan rates lag money market rates, so revenue and cost do not move together even when repricing volumes match |

The last row is worth stating separately because it is the one candidates most often get backwards. Setting the gap to zero is the defensive strategy, but it is a reduction in the volatility of net interest income rather than an elimination of interest rate risk. The imperfect correlation between asset and liability rates survives the matching of volumes.

a.reason: Absolute-claim trap. A zero gap reduces but does not eliminate interest rate risk, because interest rates attached to assets and liabilities are not perfectly correlated: loan rates tend to lag money market rates even when repricing volumes are matched.

b.reason: This is the first stated limitation, and it is why the framework's implicit assumption that both sides reprice together is imperfect.

c.reason: Scope error with a polarity flip attached. The technique captures the effect on net income only and neglects the effect on the market value of equity. It therefore understates the full exposure rather than overstating it.

d.reason: Factually reversed and then compounded by an absolute claim. The repricing point of checkable deposits and passbook savings is precisely what the reading identifies as difficult to pin down, since their rates can be adjusted up or down at any time, and the arbitrary planning period is one limitation among several rather than the only one.

trap.explanation: Option A is an absolute-claim trap and the most instructive miss in this objective, because 'zero gap equals immunisation' is a shortcut that works well enough for the calculation questions and fails on the limitations question. Option C is a scope error whose direction word ('overstates') reverses the actual criticism; the technique's problem is that it sees too little, not too much. Option D uses 'only', which on this exam is nearly always a signal to reject.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Discuss the limitations of interest-sensitive gap management and duration gap management.
questions.reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
questions.question: A risk manager is documenting the drawbacks of duration gap management for the bank's model validation file. Each of the following is a limitation of duration gap management EXCEPT:

options.text: Finding assets and liabilities of the same duration that also fit the institution's portfolio is often a frustrating task.
Duration itself shifts as market rates move and as instruments approach maturity, so a matched position requires continual and costly rebalancing.
The technique analyses the effect of rate changes on the institution's net income while neglecting their effect on the market value of shareholders' equity.
The model assumes a linear relationship between market values and interest rates, so its accuracy declines for large rate changes unless convexity is taken into account.

questions.solution:
The exception is option C, and the reason is that this is the limitation of the other tool. The reading is explicit that interest-sensitive gap management does not consider the impact of changing interest rates on the stockholders' position as represented by net worth, and that this shortcoming is exactly what motivated the development of duration gap management. Duration gap analysis exists to protect net worth, so it cannot be criticised for ignoring it.

| Limitations of interest-sensitive gap management | Limitations of duration gap management |
|---|---|
| Ignores the effect of rate changes on the market value of equity | Assets and liabilities of matching duration are hard to find and fit into the portfolio |
| Liability rates, being mostly short term, move faster than asset rates | Duration is always below calendar maturity except for zero-coupon and single-payment instruments |
| Rates on assets and liabilities do not move at the same speed as open market rates (basis risk) | Cash flows on checkable and passbook accounts are not well defined, so their duration is hard to compute |
| The repricing point of some items, such as checkable deposits, is hard to identify | Prepayments and defaults distort expected cash flows |
| The choice of planning period is arbitrary and items fall between the cracks | The model assumes a linear price and rate relationship; accuracy falls for large or non-parallel rate moves |
| Even a zero gap does not eliminate risk, since asset and liability rates are imperfectly correlated | Immunisation is dynamic: durations drift, so the position needs continual and costly rebalancing |

The reading closes on a note of qualified confidence: recent research suggests duration balancing remains effective even under moderate violations of its assumptions, and the concept remains a valuable managerial tool because it addresses the value of the firm to its shareholders.

a.reason: This is a stated limitation of duration gap management, and the reading notes it would be far easier if maturity equalled duration, which it does not. Not the exception.

b.reason: Duration drift is a stated limitation. Immunisation is a dynamic problem, since durations change as instruments near maturity and as rates move. Not the exception.

c.reason: This is the limitation of interest-sensitive gap management, and it is the specific gap that duration gap management was developed to close. This is the exception.

d.reason: The linearity assumption and the resulting need to consider convexity for large rate moves is a stated limitation of duration gap analysis. Not the exception.

trap.explanation: This is a negative-qualifier question in which every option is a genuine limitation of something, so plausibility screening is useless. The discriminator is ownership: which tool does each criticism belong to? Hold the two tools apart by their objective, since interest-sensitive gap protects the net interest margin (an income measure) and duration gap protects net worth (a value measure). Any criticism about neglecting value belongs to the income tool, and vice versa.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Discuss the limitations of interest-sensitive gap management and duration gap management.
questions.reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
questions.question: A model validation team is explaining to the risk committee why duration gap estimates of the change in net worth degrade under certain conditions. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Because the duration gap model assumes a linear relationship between market values and interest rates, its accuracy declines as the size of the rate change grows, and for a positively convex position the model understates the gain from a rate fall and overstates the loss from a rate rise.

Because the duration gap model assumes a linear relationship between market values and interest rates, its accuracy declines as the size of the rate change grows, and for a positively convex position the model overstates the gain from a rate fall and understates the loss from a rate rise.
The model's accuracy is unaffected by the size of the rate change but deteriorates when the yield curve shifts in parallel, since duration is defined only for non-parallel movements in rates.
Duration remains constant as instruments approach maturity, so a matched position established today requires no rebalancing for as long as the level of interest rates is unchanged.

questions.solution:
The duration relationship is a first-order approximation:
$$\Delta P \div P = -D \times [\Delta i \div (1 + i)]$$
