It describes a straight line. The reading states plainly that duration gap models assume a linear relationship between the market values of assets and liabilities and interest rates, which is not strictly true, and that for a large rate change of one or two percentage points the linear approximation gives a distorted reading of the exposure.

**Why the error has a direction.** The true price and rate relationship is convex, not straight. The reading's own illustration: a fall in the yield on a 30-year bond from 6.5% to 6.0% raises the price by roughly 8 points per USD 1,000 of face value, while an identical half-point fall from 10.0% to 9.5% raises it by only slightly more than 4 points. The curve is steeper at low rates and flatter at high rates.

For a position with positive convexity, the true price curve lies above the straight line tangent to it, on both sides of the current rate. That single geometric fact fixes both directions of the error:

| Rate move | True price change | Duration-based estimate | Nature of the error |
|---|---|---|---|
| Rates fall | Price rises by more than the line predicts | Below the truth | The model understates the gain |
| Rates rise | Price falls by less than the line predicts | Below the truth | The model overstates the loss |

The error is therefore conservative for a positively convex position, and it grows with the square of the rate change, which is why the reading confines the technique to small and roughly parallel shifts.

Two further conditions worth holding alongside it. First, the model assumes the yield curve shifts in parallel; non-parallel shifts, in which short and long rates move by different amounts, degrade it further. Second, duration is dynamic: it changes as rates change and as instruments approach maturity, so immunisation is a continual and costly rebalancing exercise rather than a one-off trade.

a.reason: Positive convexity puts the true price curve above the duration tangent on both sides, so the linear estimate is too low in each direction: it understates the gain and overstates the loss.

b.reason: Polarity flip. The direction of the convexity error is reversed. If the model overstated the gain and understated the loss, the true curve would lie below the tangent, which is negative convexity.

c.reason: Two reversals in one statement. Accuracy does decline with the size of the rate change, and duration assumes parallel shifts, so non-parallel movements are what degrade it rather than parallel ones.

d.reason: Factually reversed. Duration changes as instruments approach maturity as well as when rates move, which is exactly why the reading describes immunisation as a dynamic problem requiring continual and costly portfolio restructuring.

trap.explanation: Option B is a clean polarity flip on the direction of the convexity error and cannot be eliminated without knowing which side of the tangent the true curve sits on. Fix it with the geometry rather than a rule: positive convexity means the curve bows upward away from the straight line, so the line is too low in both directions, which makes gains larger and losses smaller than duration alone predicts. Option D is the duration-drift reversal and is attractive because it offers the convenient conclusion that a hedge, once set, stays set.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Discuss the limitations of interest-sensitive gap management and duration gap management.
questions.reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
questions.question: A consultant is reviewing a bank's asset-liability management documentation. Each of the following statements in the documentation is true EXCEPT:

options.text: A bank whose total assets exceed its total liabilities must by construction have a positive leverage-adjusted duration gap.
A limitation of duration gap management is that it is often difficult to find assets and liabilities of matching duration that also fit the institution's portfolio.

For an instrument that pays out gradually over time, duration is always less than calendar maturity, and the two are equal only for instruments such as zero-coupon securities, single-payment loans and Treasury bills.
Under duration gap analysis the institution is fully hedged when its leverage-adjusted duration gap is zero.

questions.solution:
Option A is the false statement. Solvency is a statement about the amounts on the two sides of the balance sheet; the duration gap is a statement about their timing. The two are independent.

Solvency: $A > L$   |   Leverage-adjusted duration gap: $D_A - D_L \times (L \div A)$

A solvent bank can hold any sign of gap it chooses. Consider a solvent institution with assets of USD 200 million, liabilities of USD 150 million, an asset duration of 2.0 years and a liability duration of 4.0 years:
$$\text{Gap} = 2.0 - 4.0 \times (150 \div 200) = 2.0 - 3.0 = -1.0 \text{ year}$$

Solvent, and negative. The reading's own Fannie Mae case makes the same point from the real world: the institution reported a negative duration gap of about 14 months at the close of 2002, with liabilities lengthening and assets shortening, and it was manifestly not insolvent. Fannie targets a gap between negative and positive six months and reported figures within one month of zero by September 2007.

The only thing solvency does guarantee is that the leverage ratio $L \div A$ is less than one, which is why the leverage adjustment shrinks the liability duration term. That makes a positive gap somewhat more likely for a typical bank, since the adjustment works in that direction, but it guarantees nothing. A bank with sufficiently long-dated funding will show a negative gap regardless of how well capitalised it is.

a.reason: False, and so this is the exception. Solvency concerns the relative amounts of assets and liabilities; the duration gap concerns their relative timing. A solvent institution can have a positive, negative or zero leverage-adjusted duration gap.

b.reason: True, and stated as the first limitation of duration gap management in the reading. Not the exception.

c.reason: True. Duration is always less than calendar maturity for instruments paying out over time, and equals maturity only for zero-coupon securities, single-payment loans and Treasury bills. Not the exception.

d.reason: True. A zero leverage-adjusted duration gap is the immunisation condition for the market value of net worth. Not the exception.

trap.explanation: Option A is compelling because the leverage adjustment does contain the term $L \div A$, which is less than one precisely when the bank is solvent, so solvency and a positive gap feel connected. They are not: the adjustment shrinks one term of the gap but says nothing about the durations themselves, and those can take any values. Whenever a statement links a balance sheet size fact to a timing conclusion, treat it as suspect until you can construct a counterexample, which here takes about ten seconds.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Evaluate Basel III liquidity risk ratios and BIS principles for sound liquidity risk management.
questions.reading: Hull, Risk Management and Financial Institutions, Ch. 24: Liquidity Risk
questions.question:
The following data are extracted from ABC Bank's balance sheet:

| Description | 2018 | 2019 |
|---|---|---|
| High-quality liquid assets | 2,100 | 1,458 |
| Average monthly withdrawals | 1,200 | 2,458 |
| Expected 30-day net cash outflows in a stressed scenario | 1,600 | 1,700 |

Which of the following is closest to the bank's liquidity coverage ratio for 2018 and 2019 respectively?
questions.solution:
$$\text{LCR} = \text{High-quality liquid assets} \div \text{Net cash outflows in a 30-day period} \geq 100\%$$

**Step 1.** Select the denominator. The LCR denominator is net cash outflows over 30 days under the stress scenario, not average or business-as-usual withdrawals. The 'average monthly withdrawals' row is therefore redundant data and is discarded.

**Step 2. 2018:**
$$2{,}100 \div 1{,}600 = 1.3125, \text{ or } 131\%$$

**Step 3. 2019:**
$$1{,}458 \div 1{,}700 = 0.8576, \text{ or } 86\%$$

Interpretation. In 2018 the bank held 31% more HQLA than it needed to survive the 30-day stress scenario and was compliant. In 2019 the ratio fell below 100%, meaning the stock of unencumbered high-quality liquid assets would be exhausted before the end of the 30-day window. That is a breach requiring remedial action, and it is the substantive point of the question: the movement matters as much as the level. Note the deterioration came from both directions at once, with HQLA falling 31% while stressed outflows rose.

a.reason: 75% and 35% add the average monthly withdrawals to the stressed outflows in the denominator, double-counting the outflow.

b.reason: 76% and 117% invert the ratio, dividing outflows by HQLA. The tell is that the direction of travel reverses, showing improvement where there was deterioration.

d.reason: 175% and 59% use average monthly withdrawals as the denominator instead of stressed net outflows.

trap.explanation: The average-withdrawals row is planted excess data, and option D is built directly from taking the bait. Option B is the inversion trap; guard against it with a sanity check, since a healthy bank should show an LCR above 100% and the ratio should fall when HQLA falls. If your two answers move in the opposite direction to the underlying data, you have inverted the ratio.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Evaluate Basel III liquidity risk ratios and BIS principles for sound liquidity risk management.
questions.reading: Hull, Risk Management and Financial Institutions, Ch. 24: Liquidity Risk
questions.question:
A treasury analyst is computing the net stable funding ratio for a commercial bank from the following data (all figures in JPY billions):

| Funding category | Amount | ASF factor | Asset category | Amount | RSF factor |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Tier 1 and Tier 2 capital | 8,000 | 100% | Cash and central bank reserves | 5,000 | 0% |
| Stable retail deposits | 20,000 | 95% | Level 1 HQLA | 10,000 | 5% |
| Less stable retail deposits | 10,000 | 90% | Performing residential mortgages, 1 year or more | 30,000 | 65% |
| Financial institution funding, under 6 months | 25,000 | 0% | Performing corporate loans, 1 year or more | 20,000 | 85% |
| Other wholesale funding, 6 months to under 1 year | 12,000 | 50% | Other assets | 6,000 | 100% |

Which of the following is closest to the bank's NSFR, and what should the analyst conclude?

options.text: 79.1%, and the bank is below the regulatory minimum.
97.7%, and the bank is below the regulatory minimum.
102.4%, and the bank meets the regulatory minimum.
105.6%, and the bank meets the regulatory minimum.

questions.solution:
$$\text{NSFR} = \text{Available stable funding} \div \text{Required stable funding} \geq 100\%$$

**Step 1. Available stable funding.** Multiply each funding category by its ASF factor:
$$8{,}000(1.00) + 20{,}000(0.95) + 10{,}000(0.90) + 25{,}000(0.00) + 12{,}000(0.50)$$
$$= 8{,}000 + 19{,}000 + 9{,}000 + 0 + 6{,}000 = \text{JPY } 42{,}000 \text{ billion}$$

Note the two ends of the scale. Capital receives a 100% factor because it never runs. Short-dated funding from other financial institutions receives 0% because it is the first money out of the door in a stress, which is the regulatory codification of the Northern Rock lesson.

**Step 2. Required stable funding.** Multiply each asset by its RSF factor:
$$5{,}000(0.00) + 10{,}000(0.05) + 30{,}000(0.65) + 20{,}000(0.85) + 6{,}000(1.00)$$
$$= 0 + 500 + 19{,}500 + 17{,}000 + 6{,}000 = \text{JPY } 43{,}000 \text{ billion}$$

**Step 3:**
$$\text{NSFR} = 42{,}000 \div 43{,}000 = 0.977, \text{ or } 97.7\%$$

Conclusion: the ratio is below the 100% minimum, so the bank is not compliant. It is funding roughly JPY 1,000 billion of long-dated assets with funding that does not qualify as stable. Remediation would mean lengthening funding (moving money out of the 0% financial institution bucket), raising capital, or shortening the asset side.

a.reason: 79.1% = 34,000 ÷ 43,000, which omits the JPY 8,000 billion of capital from available stable funding. The conclusion happens to be right for the wrong reason.

b.reason: 42,000 ÷ 43,000 = 97.7%, which is below the 100% minimum.

c.reason: 102.4% = 43,000 ÷ 42,000, the ratio inverted. Both the number and the compliance conclusion are wrong.

d.reason: 105.6% = 75,000 ÷ 71,000, using the raw unweighted amounts and ignoring every ASF and RSF factor.

trap.explanation: Option A rewards a candidate who forgets that capital is a funding source, and it is doubly dangerous because it reaches the correct compliance conclusion, so a candidate checking only the verdict will not notice the error. Option C inverts the ratio and flips the verdict with it; the quick guard is that a ratio near 100% must be read carefully in the right direction. Option D is the unweighted trap, which is the one to watch if you are short on time and tempted to skip the factors.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Evaluate Basel III liquidity risk ratios and BIS principles for sound liquidity risk management.
questions.reading: Hull, Risk Management and Financial Institutions, Ch. 24: Liquidity Risk
questions.question:
A supervisor is reviewing the Basel III liquidity position of two banks in the same jurisdiction (all amounts in EUR millions):

| Item | Bank A | Bank B |
|---|---|---|
| High-quality liquid assets | 1,800 | 1,200 |
| Net cash outflows over a 30-day stress period | 1,500 | 1,400 |
| Available stable funding | 9,000 | 10,200 |
| Required stable funding | 9,500 | 9,800 |

Which of the following best characterises the two banks' compliance with the Basel III liquidity requirements?

options.text: Bank A breaches the liquidity coverage ratio while Bank B breaches the net stable funding ratio.
Bank A meets the liquidity coverage ratio but breaches the net stable funding ratio, while Bank B breaches the liquidity coverage ratio but meets the net stable funding ratio.
Both banks satisfy both requirements, since every ratio computed exceeds the 80% supervisory floor.
Bank B is the sounder of the two, because its surplus on the net stable funding ratio offsets its shortfall on the liquidity coverage ratio.

questions.solution:
The two ratios answer different questions over different horizons, so each must be computed and judged on its own.

$$\text{LCR} = \text{high-quality liquid assets} \div \text{net cash outflows over 30 days} \geq 100\%$$
$$\text{NSFR} = \text{available stable funding} \div \text{required stable funding} \geq 100\%$$

**Step 1. Bank A:**
$$\text{LCR} = 1{,}800 \div 1{,}500 = 1.200, \text{ or } 120.0\% \text{ (compliant)}$$
$$\text{NSFR} = 9{,}000 \div 9{,}500 = 0.947, \text{ or } 94.7\% \text{ (breach)}$$

**Step 2. Bank B:**
$$\text{LCR} = 1{,}200 \div 1{,}400 = 0.857, \text{ or } 85.7\% \text{ (breach)}$$
$$\text{NSFR} = 10{,}200 \div 9{,}800 = 1.041, \text{ or } 104.1\% \text{ (compliant)}$$

| | LCR | Verdict | NSFR | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bank A | 120.0% | Meets | 94.7% | Breaches |
| Bank B | 85.7% | Breaches | 104.1% | Meets |

**Step 3.** Interpret the pattern, which is the substance of the evaluation. The two banks fail in opposite directions and would require opposite remedies.

Bank A holds ample liquid assets for a 30-day shock but funds its longer-dated asset base with funding the framework does not treat as stable. It survives an acute run and struggles over a year. Its remedy is to lengthen funding or raise capital, both of which lift available stable funding.

Bank B has a durable one-year funding profile but too small a buffer of unencumbered liquid assets to survive the acute 30-day stress scenario. Its remedy is to build the HQLA stock. Restoring compliance requires $\text{EUR } 1{,}400 - \text{EUR } 1{,}200 = \text{EUR } 200$ million of additional HQLA, assuming outflows are unchanged.

Neither ratio offsets the other. They are separate minimum requirements: the LCR governs the acute 30-day horizon and the NSFR the structural one-year horizon, and a surplus on one does not cure a deficit on the other.

a.reason: The two banks have been transposed. Bank A breaches the NSFR, not the LCR, and Bank B breaches the LCR, not the NSFR.

b.reason: Bank A: LCR 120.0% compliant, NSFR 94.7% breach. Bank B: LCR 85.7% breach, NSFR 104.1% compliant.

c.reason: The minimum for both ratios is 100%, not 80%. The 60% figure that appears in the reading is the LCR's phase-in requirement for 2015, rising to 100% by 2019, and it has no application to a current assessment.

d.reason: Treats the two ratios as a single netted requirement. They are separate minima covering different horizons, so an NSFR surplus does not cure an LCR shortfall. It also draws a soundness conclusion from a comparison the framework does not support.

trap.explanation: Option D is the substantive trap and the one that tests evaluation rather than arithmetic: a candidate can compute all four ratios correctly and still fail by treating them as offsetting. Option C exploits the phase-in schedule, which is the only place an 80% or 60% figure appears anywhere near these ratios. Option A is the transposition, and it is worth noting that it can be eliminated on structure alone, since a bank with 120% on one ratio cannot be the one breaching it.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Evaluate Basel III liquidity risk ratios and BIS principles for sound liquidity risk management.
questions.reading: Hull, Risk Management and Financial Institutions, Ch. 24: Liquidity Risk
questions.question: A bank supervisor in Country X is explaining reserve requirements to a group of trainees. Country X imposes a 25% reserve requirement on transaction deposits. A customer places CNY 200 million of new funds into the banking system. Ignoring cash leakage and voluntary excess reserves, which of the following is closest to the increase in the total money supply beyond the initial deposit?

options.text: CNY 50 million
CNY 150 million
CNY 600 million
CNY 800 million

questions.solution:
Reserve requirements oblige banks to hold a set percentage of deposits as vault cash or on deposit with the central bank. The requirement applies only to transaction deposits, that is, chequing accounts. Beyond the liquidity floor it creates, the requirement also determines how much credit the banking system can create from a given injection of deposits.

Trace the cascade with $r = 25\%$:
$$200 \times 0.75 = 150 \text{ lent, redeposited}; \quad 150 \times 0.75 = 112.5 \text{ lent}; \quad 112.5 \times 0.75 = 84.375 \text{ lent; and so on}$$

This is a geometric series with first term $D(1 - r)$ and ratio $(1 - r)$:
$$\text{Increase beyond the initial deposit} = D \times (1 - r) \div r = 200 \times 0.75 \div 0.25 = 200 \times 3 = \text{CNY } 600 \text{ million}$$

Cross-check against the reading's own worked figures. With $r = 10\%$ and a deposit of 100, the series $90 + 81 + 72.9 + \ldots$ sums to 900, which equals $100 \times 0.9 \div 0.1$. With $r = 20\%$, $80 + 64 + 51.2 + \ldots$ sums to $400 = 100 \times 0.8 \div 0.2$. The formula reproduces both.

Two scope facts that are separately testable. First, the requirement applies only to transaction deposits, not to all deposits. Second, most countries do not use the reserve requirement as a monetary policy tool; some, such as Canada and the United Kingdom, have no compulsory requirement at all, while China is the noted exception that changes it frequently.

a.reason: CNY 50 million = 200 × 0.25, the reserve held against the initial deposit. This is a component of the calculation, not the answer.

b.reason: CNY 150 million = 200 × 0.75, the first round of lending only. The cascade has been truncated after one step.

d.reason: CNY 800 million = 200 ÷ 0.25, the simple deposit multiplier 1 ÷ r. This gives total deposits in the system including the original CNY 200 million, not the increase beyond it.

trap.explanation: Option D is the intended trap and the more dangerous one, because 1 ÷ r is the formula most candidates have memorised. The stem's word 'beyond' is the qualifier that decides between CNY 800 million and CNY 600 million. Read what the question wants counted before you pick a multiplier.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Discuss how asset-liability management strategies can help a bank hedge against interest rate risk.
questions.reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
questions.question: A government bond can be purchased today for USD 750. It pays USD 150 per year in interest for four years, at the end of which it is redeemed for USD 1,000. Which of the following is closest to the bond's yield to maturity?
questions.solution:
The yield to maturity is the discount rate that equalises the current market value of a security with the expected stream of future income it will generate:

$$750 = \frac{150}{(1+y)} + \frac{150}{(1+y)^2} + \frac{150}{(1+y)^3} + \frac{150}{(1+y)^4} + \frac{1{,}000}{(1+y)^4}$$

There is no closed-form solution, so solve by trial and interpolation.

**Step 1. Try $y = 25\%$:**
$$120.00 + 96.00 + 76.80 + 61.44 + 409.60 = \text{USD } 763.84$$
Too high, so the yield must exceed 25%.

**Step 2. Try $y = 26\%$:**
$$119.05 + 94.48 + 74.99 + 59.51 + 396.75 = \text{USD } 744.78$$
Too low, so the yield lies between 25% and 26%.

**Step 3. Linear interpolation:**
$$y = 0.25 + \left[ \frac{763.84 - 750.00}{763.84 - 744.78} \right] \times 0.01 = 0.25 + 0.00726 = 25.73\%$$

Interpretation: the bond is priced at a deep discount to its redemption value, so the investor earns not only the USD 150 annual coupon but also a USD 250 capital gain at maturity. That gain is why the yield to maturity greatly exceeds both the 15% coupon rate on face value and the 20% current yield on price.

a.reason: 15.00% = 150 ÷ 1,000, the coupon rate expressed against face value. It ignores both the discounted purchase price and the capital gain at redemption.

b.reason: 20.00% = 150 ÷ 750, the current yield. It captures the discounted purchase price but still ignores the USD 250 redemption gain.

c.reason: 25.73%, from interpolation between 25% and 26%.

d.reason: 28.33% = [(150 × 4) + (1,000 − 750)] ÷ 4 ÷ 750, a simple undiscounted average annual return. It counts the capital gain but applies no time value, so it overstates the yield.

trap.explanation: The three wrong options form a ladder of increasingly complete but still incorrect measures: coupon rate, then current yield, then undiscounted total return. Each is a real financial measure with its own name, which is what makes them plausible. The discriminator is whether the measure both discounts and includes the redemption amount; only the yield to maturity does both.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Discuss how asset-liability management strategies can help a bank hedge against interest rate risk.
questions.reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
questions.question:
John Doe is a treasury analyst at ABC Bank. He has been asked to quote the bank discount rate on a money market security with the following characteristics:

| Input | Value |
|---|---|
| Purchase price | USD 95 |
| Required rate of return | 12% |
| Face value | USD 100 |
| Yield to maturity | 8% |
| Days to maturity | 85 |

Which of the following is closest to the bank discount rate?
questions.solution:
$$DR = \left[ \frac{100 - \text{purchase price}}{100} \right] \times \left[ \frac{360}{\text{days to maturity}} \right]$$

**Step 1.** Identify the inputs the formula actually needs: purchase price and days to maturity. The required rate of return and the stated yield to maturity are not inputs to the discount rate and are discarded.

**Step 2. Discount from face value:**
$$(100 - 95) \div 100 = 0.0500$$

**Step 3. Annualise on a 360-day basis:**
$$360 \div 85 = 4.2353$$
$$DR = 0.0500 \times 4.2353 = 0.21176, \text{ or } 21.18\%$$

Two conventions define this measure and both are examinable. It uses the face value as the base rather than the purchase price, and it uses a 360-day year. The reading is explicit that using face value is a simplification that makes calculation easier but is theoretically incorrect: the purchase price is a much better base for computing an instrument's true rate of return. The discount rate also ignores compounding.

a.reason: 8.00% is the yield to maturity read straight off the table. It is a genuine property of the security but not the measure requested.

c.reason: 21.47% uses a 365-day year in place of the 360-day year: 0.0500 × (365 ÷ 85). The 365-day convention belongs to the yield-to-maturity-equivalent measure, not the discount rate.

d.reason: 22.29% uses the purchase price as the base instead of the face value: (100 − 95) ÷ 95 × (360 ÷ 85). This mixes the equivalent-yield base with the discount rate's day count.

trap.explanation: Options C and D isolate the two conventions one at a time, so a candidate who has the discount rate and the equivalent yield partly conflated will land on one of them. Write the two conventions down before computing: discount rate means face value and 360 days; equivalent yield means purchase price and 365 days. Option A is the excess-data trap, and note that a table listing a required return, a yield to maturity and a price is designed to make you look for the wrong number.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Discuss how asset-liability management strategies can help a bank hedge against interest rate risk.
questions.reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
questions.question: A Treasury bill with a face value of USD 100 is purchased for USD 88 and matures in 120 days. Its bank discount rate is 36.00%. Which of the following correctly states the yield-to-maturity equivalent yield on this bill, together with the correct explanation of why the two measures differ?

options.text: 36.00%, and the discount rate overstates the true return because it uses the purchase price as the base.
40.91%, and the discount rate understates the true return because it uses the face value as the base and a 360-day year.
41.48%, and the discount rate understates the true return because it uses the face value as the base and a 360-day year.
41.48%, and the discount rate overstates the true return because it uses the purchase price as the base and a 365-day year.

questions.solution:
$$\text{YTM equivalent yield} = \left[ \frac{100 - \text{purchase price}}{\text{purchase price}} \right] \times \left[ \frac{365}{\text{days to maturity}} \right]$$

**Step 1.** Base the return on what was actually invested:
$$(100 - 88) \div 88 = 0.136364$$

**Step 2. Annualise on a 365-day basis:**
$$365 \div 120 = 3.041667$$
$$\text{Equivalent yield} = 0.136364 \times 3.041667 = 0.41477, \text{ or } 41.48\%$$

**Step 3.** Compare with the discount rate:
$$DR = (12 \div 100) \times (360 \div 120) = 36.00\%$$

The equivalent yield is 5.48 percentage points higher, and both conventions push in the same direction:

| Convention | Discount rate (100) | Equivalent yield (88) | Effect on the reported figure |
|---|---|---|---|
| Base | Face value | Purchase price | A larger base gives a smaller ratio, so the discount rate is lower |
| Day count | 360 | 365 | A shorter assumed year gives a smaller annualisation factor, so the discount rate is lower again |

Conclusion: the bank discount rate systematically understates the true return on a money market instrument. As the reading states, the purchase price rather than the face amount is a much better base for calculating an instrument's true rate of return.

a.reason: 36.00% is the discount rate itself, not the equivalent yield, and the explanation misassigns the base: the discount rate uses face value, and it understates rather than overstates.

b.reason: The explanation is right but the number is wrong. 40.91% = (12 ÷ 88) × (360 ÷ 120), which correctly switches the base to the purchase price but leaves the 360-day count in place.

c.reason: 41.48%, and the discount rate understates because of both the face-value base and the 360-day year.

d.reason: The number is right but both halves of the explanation are transposed. The purchase price and the 365-day year belong to the equivalent yield, and the bias runs the other way.

trap.explanation: This is a two-part conjunction, so being right on the arithmetic is only half the job. Option B is the numerical near-miss produced by switching one convention and not the other, and it comes attached to the correct explanation, which makes it very attractive. Option D is the mirror image: right number, transposed explanation. The safe route is to compute the number and independently reason out the direction of bias before reading any option.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe the mechanics of repurchase agreements (repos) and calculate the settlement for a repo transaction.
questions.reading: LR2025: Repurchase Agreements and Financing
questions.question: During a presentation on quarterly performance, a risk manager at a securities dealer explains the difference between repurchase agreements (repos) and reverse repurchase agreements (reverse repos) to a group of newly hired analysts. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: In a repo, the seller of the securities agrees to buy them back at a later date at a slightly lower price, the difference representing the repo rate.
In a reverse repo, the buyer of the securities agrees to sell them back at a later date at a slightly lower price, so the cash lender earns the repo rate.
Repos are typically used to raise cash, while reverse repos are typically used to invest cash.
A repo is initiated by the buyer of the securities and a reverse repo by the seller, which is why the two names describe the same transaction from a single perspective.

questions.solution:
**Concept tested:** The two sides of a single repo transaction: who borrows, who lends, and which label attaches to each perspective.

A repo is a single transaction described from two sides. The same trade is a repo to one counterparty and a reverse repo to the other.

| | Repo (cash borrower) | Reverse repo (cash lender) |
|---|---|---|
| Leg one | Sells securities and receives cash | Buys securities and pays cash |
| Leg two | Repurchases the securities at a higher fixed price | Resells them at that higher fixed price |
| Economic role | Borrows on a collateralised basis; raises cash | Lends against collateral; invests cash |
| Repo rate | Pays it | Earns it |
| Perspective | The term 'repo' is used from the point of view of the initial security seller | The term 'reverse repo' is used from the point of view of the initial security buyer |

The repurchase price is fixed in advance, at the outset. That is what makes the transaction a loan rather than a pair of market trades: neither side is exposed to the security's price on the second leg, because the price is contractual rather than market determined.

$$\text{Repo rate} = \frac{\text{repurchase price} - \text{sale price}}{\text{sale price}} \text{, annualised}$$

a.reason: Polarity flip. The seller repurchases at a higher price. A lower repurchase price would mean the cash borrower was paid to borrow.

b.reason: Same polarity flip, restated from the lender's side. The buyer resells at a higher price, which is how the cash lender earns the repo rate.

c.reason: The cash borrower sells securities to raise cash; the cash lender buys them to put cash to work on a secured basis.

d.reason: Role misassignment. The repo label attaches to the initial security seller and the reverse repo label to the initial buyer, which is the opposite of what the option states. The closing clause is also wrong: the two names exist precisely because there are two perspectives.

trap.explanation: Options A and B are the same polarity flip on the repurchase price, presented from each side so a candidate holding the direction backwards finds confirmation either way. Option D is a role misassignment and is the more instructive miss, because the mapping of label to counterparty is tested directly on this exam. Anchor it with the cash: whoever ends leg one holding cash is doing the repo.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe the mechanics of repurchase agreements (repos) and calculate the settlement for a repo transaction.
questions.reading: LR2025: Repurchase Agreements and Financing
questions.question:
Ludska Bank has entered into a repo agreement with SKA Bank under which Ludska sells government bonds to SKA on the following terms:

| Term | Value |
|---|---|
| Face amount | USD 1,000,000 |
| Invoice price | USD 1,100,000 |
| Repo rate | 4.00% per annum |
| Term to settlement | 90 days |

Assuming a 360-day convention, which of the following is closest to the amount Ludska Bank will pay to repurchase the bonds on the settlement date?
questions.solution:
**Concept tested:** The repurchase price as the invoice price grown at the repo rate over the actual term, on a 360-day basis.

$$\text{Repurchase price} = \text{invoice price} \times \left[1 + \left(\text{repo rate} \times \frac{\text{repo term in days}}{360}\right)\right]$$

where the invoice price is the cash actually advanced on leg one, being the full or dirty price of the collateral after any haircut.

**Step 1.** Pro-rate the annual repo rate to the 90-day term:
$$0.04 \times \frac{90}{360} = 0.01 = 1.00\%$$

**Step 2.** Apply it to the invoice price, not to the face amount. The repo rate is interest on cash lent, and the cash lent is USD 1,100,000:
$$1{,}100{,}000 \times 1.01 = \text{USD } 1{,}111{,}000$$

Interpretation: SKA Bank advanced USD 1,100,000 and receives USD 1,111,000 back 90 days later. The USD 11,000 difference is the interest on a secured 90-day loan. The face amount of USD 1,000,000 never enters the calculation; it matters only for identifying the collateral.

a.reason: USD 1,100,000 is the invoice price with the repo interest term dropped altogether. It is the leg-one cash amount, not the leg-two settlement.

b.reason: USD 1,110,000 applies the repo rate to the face amount of USD 1,000,000 rather than to the invoice price: $1{,}100{,}000 + (1{,}000{,}000 \times 0.04 \times 90 \div 360)$. This is the wrong input twin.

d.reason: USD 1,144,000 = $1{,}100{,}000 \times 1.04$, applying the full annual rate to a 90-day term. This is a time-conversion error and overstates the interest by a factor of four.

trap.explanation: Option B is the wrong input twin and the one worth rehearsing, because a repo stem always supplies both a face amount and an invoice price and only one of them belongs in the formula. The repo rate is interest on cash, so it attaches to the cash advanced. Option D is the classic failure to de-annualise, and it is easy to spot because the answer moves by a suspiciously round 4%.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe the mechanics of repurchase agreements (repos) and calculate the settlement for a repo transaction.
questions.reading: LR2025: Repurchase Agreements and Financing
questions.question:
Three months after purchasing a bond on its coupon payment date, ABC Bank enters into a repurchase agreement on that bond to generate immediate liquidity. The bond and repo terms are:

| Term | Value |
|---|---|
| Notional | GBP 10,000,000 |
| Annual coupon, paid semiannually | 3.50% |
| Current clean price of the bond | 97.00 |
| Repo interest rate | 2.00% |
| Repo haircut | 3.50% |
| Repo term | 6 months |

Which of the following is closest to ABC Bank's anticipated cash outflow when the repo contract reaches expiration?
questions.solution:
**Concept tested:** The full repo settlement chain: clean price plus accrued interest, reduced by the haircut to give the cash advanced, then grown at the repo rate over the term.

$$\text{Cash outflow at expiry} = \Big[(\text{clean price} + \text{accrued interest}) \times (1 - \text{haircut})\Big] \times \big[1 + (\text{repo rate} \times t)\big]$$

**Step 1. Accrued interest.** The bond was bought on a coupon date and the repo is struck three months later, so three months of the annual coupon has accrued:
$$10{,}000{,}000 \times 0.035 \times \frac{3}{12} = \text{GBP } 87{,}500$$

**Step 2. Full (dirty) value of the collateral:**
$$(10{,}000{,}000 \times 0.97) + 87{,}500 = 9{,}700{,}000 + 87{,}500 = \text{GBP } 9{,}787{,}500$$

**Step 3.** Apply the haircut to obtain the cash actually advanced. The haircut is the lender's protection against a fall in collateral value, so the borrower receives less than the collateral is worth:
$$9{,}787{,}500 \times (1 - 0.035) = 9{,}787{,}500 \times 0.965 = \text{GBP } 9{,}444{,}937.50$$

**Step 4.** Grow the advance at the repo rate over the six-month term:
$$9{,}444{,}937.50 \times [1 + (0.02 \times 0.5)] = 9{,}444{,}937.50 \times 1.01 = \text{GBP } 9{,}539{,}386.88$$

Interpretation: ABC Bank receives GBP 9,444,938 today against collateral worth GBP 9,787,500, and repays GBP 9,539,387 in six months. The GBP 342,563 gap between collateral value and cash received is the haircut, which the bank does not get back; it is over-collateralisation, not a cost.

a.reason: GBP 9,444,938 is the cash advanced on leg one, before any repo interest. This is the intermediate-result trap: a legitimate quantity computed on the way to the answer.

c.reason: GBP 9,624,669 uses a full semiannual coupon of GBP 175,000 as accrued interest instead of the three months elapsed.

d.reason: GBP 9,885,375 = $9{,}787{,}500 \times 1.01$, omitting the haircut entirely. A dropped term, and the tell is that the outflow exceeds the dirty value of the collateral.

trap.explanation: Four distinct failure modes, one per option. Option A stops one step early (intermediate-result trap); option C mis-sizes accrued interest (unit and time conversion); option D drops the haircut (dropped term). Build the chain in the fixed order every time: clean, add accrued, subtract haircut, add repo interest. Note also the structural check that catches option D instantly, since a repo borrower can never repay more than the dirty value of the collateral it pledged on a short-dated trade at a low repo rate.

questions.reading: LR2025: Repurchase Agreements and Financing
questions.question: Bright Bank lends USD 10,000 of cash in the repo market at a spread of 0.26% for 150 days. Using the actual/360 day count convention, which of the following is closest to the value of that lending to the bank?

options.text: USD 1.08

questions.solution:
**Concept tested:** Valuing the benefit of lending cash at a spread over a stated term, using the money market actual/360 convention.

$$\text{Value of lending} = \text{cash amount} \times \text{spread} \times \frac{\text{days}}{360}$$

**Step 1.** Pro-rate the spread to the 150-day term:
$$\frac{150}{360} = 0.416667$$

**Step 2.** Apply to the cash amount:
$$10{,}000 \times 0.0026 \times 0.416667 = \text{USD } 10.83$$

Interpretation: the spread is the compensation for lending cash rather than holding it, and over 150 days on USD 10,000 it is worth USD 10.83, or about 10.8 basis points of the principal. The figure is small per unit of cash, which is precisely why repo desks operate at very large notionals and why small errors in the day count matter at portfolio scale.

Note the convention. Money market instruments, including repo, use actual/360. Using 365 would understate the value, because a longer assumed year makes each day a smaller fraction of it.

a.reason: USD 1.08 treats the spread as 0.026% rather than 0.26%, a decimal slip of one order of magnitude.

b.reason: USD 10.68 = $10{,}000 \times 0.0026 \times (150 \div 365)$, using a 365-day year. Money market conventions use actual/360.

d.reason: USD 26.00 = $10{,}000 \times 0.0026$, applying the full annual spread without pro-rating it to the 150-day term.

trap.explanation: Option B is the day-count twin and is the sharpest distractor here, because 10.68 and 10.83 differ by only 1.4% and neither looks obviously wrong. Fix the convention before computing: repo, Treasury bills and other money market instruments use 360. Option D is the failure to de-annualise and option A a decimal slip; both are caught by a rough order-of-magnitude check against the principal.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk

questions.reading: LR2025: Repurchase Agreements and Financing
questions.question: A repo trader is valuing the financing advantage embedded in an on-the-run government bond. The bond was issued on 31 March and currently trades at a special spread of 0.30% below general collateral (GC) rates. The trader expects it to trade at GC rates from 30 September onward. Using the actual/360 convention, which of the following is closest to the financing value per USD 100 of market value?
questions.solution:
**Concept tested:** The financing value of a bond trading special, being the special spread earned over the period for which the bond is expected to remain special.

A bond is on special when demand to borrow that specific issue is high, so its owner can finance it in the repo market at a rate below the general collateral rate. That discount is the special spread, and it is a real economic benefit to whoever owns the bond.

$$\text{Financing value} = \text{market value} \times \text{special spread} \times \frac{\text{days special}}{360}$$

**Step 1.** Establish the period over which the bond stays special. It is issued 31 March and is expected to trade at GC rates from 30 September, so the special period runs from 31 March to 30 September:
$$\text{April } 30 + \text{May } 31 + \text{June } 30 + \text{July } 31 + \text{August } 31 + \text{September } 30 = 183 \text{ days}$$

**Step 2.** Apply the spread over that period:
$$100 \times 0.0030 \times \frac{183}{360} = 100 \times 0.0015250 = \text{USD } 0.1525$$

Interpretation: owning this bond is worth about 15 cents per USD 100 of market value, purely from the cheaper financing it commands, and that advantage is normally already embedded in its price. On-the-run issues therefore trade rich to otherwise comparable off-the-run bonds, and the richness decays as the issue ages toward GC.

a.reason: USD 0.075 uses roughly 90 days rather than the 183 days for which the bond is expected to remain special, halving the period.

b.reason: USD 0.150 uses a 180-day half year rather than the actual 183 days between the two dates. This is a 30/360 assumption applied where the stem specifies actual/360.

d.reason: USD 0.300 applies the full annual special spread without pro-rating it to the special period.

trap.explanation: Option B is the discriminating trap and is only 2% away from the answer: 180 days feels like a half year and 183 is the actual day count between 31 March and 30 September. The stem names the convention, so count the days. Option A is the more damaging error conceptually, since it truncates the special period rather than mis-counting it; the period runs to the date the bond is expected to go GC, not to the next quarter end.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe the mechanics of repurchase agreements (repos) and calculate the settlement for a repo transaction.
questions.reading: LR2025: Repurchase Agreements and Financing
questions.question: A repo trader at Alameda Bank is looking to lend cash against bonds that are trading special. Which of the following best describes what the trader is looking for, and the consequence for the repo rate?

options.text: Bonds in particularly high demand in the securities lending market, which finance at a repo rate below the general collateral rate.
Bonds in particularly high demand in the securities lending market, which finance at a repo rate above the general collateral rate.
Any bond issued by the sovereign, since sovereign paper always finances more cheaply than corporate collateral of the same maturity.
Bonds accepted interchangeably as collateral without regard to the specific issue, which is what makes them cheap to finance.

questions.solution:
**Concept tested:** The distinction between special collateral and general collateral, and the direction in which the repo rate moves when an issue goes special.

| | General collateral (GC) | Special |
|---|---|---|
| What the cash lender wants | Any bond from an accepted class; the specific issue is irrelevant | One particular issue, usually because it is needed to cover a short or to deliver |
| Who has bargaining power | The cash lender | The collateral owner, because the issue is scarce |
| Repo rate | The GC rate | Below the GC rate, by the special spread |
| Consequence | Ordinary secured funding | The owner finances the position cheaply; the benefit is capitalised into the bond's price |

The direction is the whole point and is worth deriving rather than memorising. Cash lenders compete to obtain a scarce issue, and the only price lever they have is the interest they charge on the cash. Competition therefore pushes the repo rate down. In extreme cases a special can trade at or near zero, or even at a negative repo rate.

Note the role reversal against ordinary intuition: scarcity of the collateral benefits the borrower of cash, not the lender, because the borrower is the one supplying the scarce item.

a.reason: A special is the issue most in demand, and its repo rate sits below the general collateral rate.

b.reason: Polarity flip on the repo rate. High demand for a specific issue pushes its financing rate down, not up.

c.reason: Scope error stated as an absolute. Sovereign issuance is not automatically special; most sovereign paper trades as general collateral. Specialness attaches to a particular issue at a particular time, not to an issuer.

d.reason: Sibling swap. Interchangeable acceptance without regard to the specific issue is the definition of general collateral, which is exactly what a special is not.

trap.explanation: Option B is the polarity flip and it catches candidates who reason that high demand raises price and therefore raises the rate. The rate here is the price of cash, not of the bond, and the scarce item is the bond, so the cash side gets worse terms. Option D is a clean sibling swap between the two collateral categories.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Discuss common motivations for entering into repos, including their use in cash management and liquidity management.
questions.reading: LR2025: Repurchase Agreements and Financing
questions.question: Aluvia Bank has excess cash and has decided to place it with another bank under a repurchase agreement rather than deploy it in other short-term instruments. Which of the following best explains that preference?

options.text: A repo transaction is risk free, since the collateral eliminates any possibility of loss to the cash lender.
A repo transaction is more secure than an unsecured placement, because the cash is backed by collateral that can be sold if the counterparty fails.
A repo transaction guarantees a higher return than unsecured money market alternatives of the same maturity.
A repo transaction settles faster than other money market products, which is the principal reason cash-rich institutions prefer it.

questions.solution:
**Concept tested:** The security motivation for repo: it converts an unsecured credit exposure into a collateralised one, which is why cash-rich institutions use it.

The defining feature of repo from the cash lender's side is that the exposure is collateralised. If the counterparty fails to repurchase, the lender already owns the securities outright and can sell them to recover the cash. That is a materially better position than holding an unsecured claim.

The reading groups the motivations for entering repos as follows:

| Motivation | Which side | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Cash management | Cash lender | Put surplus cash to work overnight or for a few days on a secured basis, rather than leaving it unremunerated |
| Liquidity management | Cash borrower | Monetise a securities portfolio without selling it, retaining the economic exposure and any coupon |
| Security | Cash lender | Convert an unsecured credit exposure into a collateralised one, with margin maintenance throughout the term |
| Monetary policy | Central banks | Add or drain reserves from the banking system by conducting repo and reverse repo operations |

Note what repo is not good for. Because the exposure is secured, the repo rate is typically lower than the unsecured rate for the same counterparty and maturity. A cash lender chooses repo to reduce risk, accepting a lower return, not to raise return.

a.reason: Absolute-claim trap. Collateral reduces loss given default; it does not eliminate risk. The lender remains exposed to the collateral falling in value, to difficulty liquidating it, and to legal or operational failure in enforcing the claim.

b.reason: The transaction converts an unsecured exposure into a secured one, which is the stated attraction for a cash-rich institution.

c.reason: Polarity flip on the return. Secured lending earns less than unsecured lending to the same counterparty for the same term, precisely because the risk is lower.

d.reason: Scope error. Settlement speed is not the principal motivation identified in the reading, and repo is not distinctively faster than other money market instruments.

trap.explanation: Option A is the absolute-claim trap ('risk free', 'eliminates any possibility') and on this exam an absolute is nearly always the wrong answer. Option C is the more instructive miss because it gets the risk-return relationship backwards: if you are choosing repo, you are buying safety and paying for it in yield.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Discuss common motivations for entering into repos, including their use in cash management and liquidity management.
questions.reading: LR2025: Repurchase Agreements and Financing
questions.question: After modelling daily cash flows, the treasurer of BBB Bank concludes that the bank will be unable to meet its day-to-day funding requirements in about one year's time, and needs to secure funding of matching tenor now. The bank holds high-quality US Treasury bonds. Should the treasurer raise the funds by placing those bonds into a repo?

options.text: Yes, because US Treasury bonds are highly marketable and therefore attract the finest repo terms available in the market.
No, because repo financing is predominantly short term, so it would not match the tenor of the identified need and would introduce rollover risk.
Yes, because the repo market is deep enough that a one-year need can always be funded by rolling overnight trades.
No, because repo borrowing must be secured by collateral of similar value, and the bank cannot pledge Treasury bonds it intends to hold to maturity.

questions.solution:
**Concept tested:** Matching the tenor of a funding source to the tenor of the need, and the rollover risk created when short-term repo is used to fund a longer-dated requirement.

The identified need is a shortfall arising in about one year and persisting. Repo financing is predominantly overnight or a few days, occasionally extending to weeks or months, and only rarely beyond a year. Funding a one-year need with overnight repo means rolling the trade repeatedly, and each roll is a point at which the market can decline to renew, or renew only at a wider haircut.

$$\text{Short-dated funding against a longer-dated need} = \text{rollover risk} = \text{the Northern Rock and dealer-bank failure mechanism}$$

The mismatch is the point, and it is the same lesson that runs through the funding liquidity material. A treasurer who has correctly identified a need one year out should be looking at term funding, term deposits, or longer-dated debt issuance, not at a rolling overnight book.

Note that the quality of the collateral is not the issue. Treasury bonds are the best collateral there is and would attract the finest haircut and rate available. Excellent collateral does not fix a tenor mismatch, because the constraint is the maturity of the borrowing, not the credit standing of what secures it.

a.reason: True premise, wrong conclusion. The bonds would indeed attract fine terms, but collateral quality does not lengthen the tenor of the funding it secures.

b.reason: Repo is short-term funding, so it does not match a need arising a year out, and rolling it creates exactly the rollover exposure the treasurer is trying to avoid.

c.reason: Absolute-claim trap. 'Can always be funded by rolling' is precisely the assumption that failed for dealer banks in 2007 and 2008, when overnight repo markets closed to certain names and certain collateral.

d.reason: The premise about collateral is true but the reasoning is spurious. Pledging a bond in a repo is entirely compatible with holding it to maturity, since the bank repurchases it on the second leg and retains the economic exposure throughout.

trap.explanation: Option C is the dangerous one, because rolling short-dated funding does work right up until it does not, and the option describes normal market conditions accurately. The absolute 'always' is the tell. Option A is a scope error: it answers a question about collateral quality when the question asked about tenor.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Discuss common motivations for entering into repos, including their use in cash management and liquidity management.
questions.reading: LR2025: Repurchase Agreements and Financing
questions.question: A treasurer at a mid-sized commercial bank is explaining to the asset-liability committee why the bank appears on both sides of the repo market in the same week. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: When the bank enters a reverse repo it is pursuing a liquidity management objective, since it is converting securities into cash without selling them.
When the bank enters a repo it is pursuing a cash management objective, since it is deploying surplus cash on a secured basis for a short period.
When the bank enters a repo it is pursuing a liquidity management objective, monetising its securities portfolio without disposing of it and retaining the coupon and price exposure throughout.
Central banks conduct repo operations to alter the level of reserves in the banking system, and this is the only motivation for which the transaction is not economically a secured loan.

questions.solution:
**Concept tested:** Mapping each side of a repo transaction to its underlying motivation, and the distinction between raising cash against securities and deploying surplus cash.

The two sides of the market answer two different problems, and the same institution can face both in a single week.

| Position | Objective | What the institution is solving |
|---|---|---|
| Repo (sells securities, receives cash) | Liquidity management | It holds securities and needs cash. Repo monetises the portfolio without disposing of it: the bank keeps the coupon, keeps the price exposure, and buys the bonds back on leg two. |
| Reverse repo (buys securities, pays cash) | Cash management | It holds surplus cash and needs a short-dated, secured home for it rather than leaving it unremunerated. |

The advantage over an outright sale is worth stating precisely. Selling the bonds would also raise cash, but it would crystallise any gain or loss, remove the coupon income, and require the bank to buy back into the market at an unknown price if it wanted the exposure again. Repo separates the funding decision from the investment decision, which is why it is the standard tool for a securities portfolio that the bank intends to keep.

On central banks: they conduct repo and reverse repo operations to add or drain reserves as a monetary policy instrument. The transaction remains economically a collateralised loan; only the motivation differs.

a.reason: Role misassignment. A reverse repo means the bank is buying securities and paying cash, so it is deploying cash, not converting securities into it.

b.reason: The same swap in the other direction. Entering a repo means selling securities and receiving cash, so the bank is raising cash rather than deploying surplus cash.

c.reason: Repo raises cash against the portfolio while leaving coupon and price exposure with the bank, which is the liquidity management motivation.

d.reason: The first clause is right and the second is wrong. A central bank repo is still economically a collateralised loan; the policy objective sits on top of that structure rather than replacing it.

trap.explanation: Options A and B are a matched pair of role misassignments, so a candidate who has the repo and reverse repo labels transposed will find a consistent-looking answer either way. The reliable check is to follow the cash on leg one. Option D is a scope error that attaches a false exception to a true fact, which is the standard four-statement audit construction.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Explain how counterparty risk and liquidity risk can arise through the use of repo transactions.
questions.reading: LR2025: Repurchase Agreements and Financing
questions.question: Briggs Bank has bought US Treasury bonds from Roland Bank under a repo agreement that includes standard margin maintenance provisions. Before the settlement date, the market value of the bonds falls significantly. Which of the following actions is Briggs Bank most likely to take?

options.text: Terminate the agreement immediately, since the collateral no longer supports the cash advanced.
Demand accelerated maturity of the contract, so that the cash is returned before the collateral loses further value.
Take no action, since the repurchase price was fixed at the outset and is unaffected by the market value of the collateral.
Call for additional collateral from Roland Bank, so that the total value pledged again covers the cash advanced plus the agreed margin.

questions.solution:
**Concept tested:** Margin maintenance in repo: how a fall in collateral value is remedied during the life of the trade, and which party bears the obligation.

Briggs Bank is the cash lender: it paid cash and holds the bonds. A fall in the value of those bonds erodes its protection, because if Roland Bank failed to repurchase, the proceeds of selling the collateral might no longer cover the cash advanced.

Repo agreements address this with margin maintenance, which runs in both directions over the life of the trade:

| Collateral value | Who is exposed | Remedy |
|---|---|---|
| Falls | The cash lender, whose protection has eroded | The cash borrower delivers additional collateral |
| Rises | The cash borrower, who is now over-collateralised | The cash borrower may withdraw the excess collateral |

Note where the obligation sits. The cash borrower (Roland Bank) supplies extra collateral in a declining market and withdraws it in an advancing one. The lender calls, the borrower delivers.

This mechanism is also the channel through which repo transmits stress. A general fall in collateral values triggers margin calls across the market simultaneously, forcing borrowers to find cash or sell assets, which pushes collateral values down further. That is the repo version of the positive feedback loop.

a.reason: Unilateral termination is not the contractual remedy and would breach the agreement. Termination rights arise on default, not on a fall in collateral value that the margin mechanism is designed to handle.

b.reason: Repo terms are fixed at the outset and cannot be accelerated unilaterally. The agreement already contains a remedy for this situation.

c.reason: Scope error built on a true fact. The repurchase price is indeed fixed, but that is exactly why the lender needs the collateral to hold its value: the fixed price is what it is owed, and the collateral is what secures it. Inaction leaves the exposure unhedged.

d.reason: Additional collateral restores the agreed level of over-collateralisation, which is the standard margin maintenance remedy.

trap.explanation: Option C is the trap worth naming, because it uses a correct piece of knowledge (the repurchase price is fixed) to reach the wrong conclusion. The fixed price is the lender's claim, not its protection. Options A and B both assume rights the contract does not confer, which is a scope error about what a repo agreement actually permits.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Explain how counterparty risk and liquidity risk can arise through the use of repo transactions.
questions.reading: LR2025: Repurchase Agreements and Financing
questions.question: Voynet Bank has bought a security from Bornet Bank under a repo agreement that includes margin maintenance provisions. In the period before settlement, the market value of the security rises significantly. Which of the following is Bornet Bank most likely to do?

options.text: Request that the amount of collateral pledged be reduced, so as to release the excess value back to its own balance sheet.
Request that the repurchase price be reduced, so that it captures the appreciation in the security.
Terminate the agreement and sell the security into the market at the higher price.
Take no action, since the appreciation accrues to Voynet Bank as the current legal owner of the security.

questions.solution:
**Concept tested:** The symmetry of margin maintenance, and the fact that price exposure on the collateral remains with the cash borrower throughout the trade.

Bornet Bank is the cash borrower: it sold the security and received cash. The margin mechanism is symmetric, so the same provision that would require Bornet to post more collateral in a falling market permits it to withdraw collateral in a rising one.

$$\text{Collateral falls} \rightarrow \text{borrower posts more} \quad|\quad \text{Collateral rises} \rightarrow \text{borrower withdraws the excess}$$

Why the borrower and not the lender benefits: although Voynet Bank holds legal title to the security for the term of the trade, the economic exposure never leaves Bornet Bank. Bornet has contracted to repurchase at a fixed price, so any appreciation between the two legs accrues to it. That is the defining feature that makes a repo a secured loan rather than a sale.

The practical consequence is a balance sheet one. Collateral pledged is encumbered and cannot be used elsewhere, so releasing the excess frees assets for other funding or for the liquidity buffer.

a.reason: Margin maintenance permits the cash borrower to withdraw collateral in an advancing market, releasing the encumbered excess.

b.reason: The repurchase price is fixed at inception and is a function of the cash advanced and the repo rate. It does not move with the market value of the collateral, which is precisely what makes the transaction a loan.

c.reason: Bornet Bank does not hold the security and has a contractual obligation to repurchase it. Unilateral termination to capture a price move is not available and would breach the agreement.

d.reason: Role misassignment on the economics. Legal title sits with Voynet Bank, but the price exposure sits with Bornet Bank, which has locked in its repurchase price. The appreciation belongs to the borrower.

trap.explanation: Option D is the sharp one and it turns on a genuine distinction between legal title and economic exposure. Legal ownership transfers in a repo, which is what makes the lender's position better than a pledge, but the fixed repurchase price leaves all price risk and reward with the borrower. Option B is a scope error that would convert the repo into a market trade.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Explain how counterparty risk and liquidity risk can arise through the use of repo transactions.
questions.reading: LR2025: Repurchase Agreements and Financing
questions.question: A regulator is preparing a note on the role played by repo transactions in the failures of several firms during the financial crisis of 2007 and 2008. Which of the following best describes the mechanism?

options.text: Firms borrowed at relatively high interest rates against high-quality collateral, so that the cost of funding rose faster than the yield on their assets.
Firms borrowed at relatively low interest rates against low-quality collateral, and when doubts about that collateral emerged, funding was withdrawn or repriced abruptly.
The US government defaulted on a portion of its Treasury obligations, which destroyed the value of the collateral underpinning the market.
The repo market was entirely unregulated, and the absence of any legal framework meant that collateral could not be enforced on default.

questions.solution:
**Concept tested:** How repo transmitted stress in 2007 and 2008: cheap short-term funding secured on collateral whose quality was not what it appeared, withdrawn through haircuts and refusal to roll.

The mechanism has three stages and each is separately testable.

| Stage | What happened |
|---|---|
| 1. Build-up | Firms financed large positions in structured and mortgage-related securities using short-term repo, at low rates. The low rate reflected the market's belief that the collateral was safe. |
| 2. Doubt | Once the quality of the collateral came into question, cash lenders responded in two ways: raising haircuts, which forced borrowers to find more collateral or repay part of the loan, and declining to roll the trade at all. |
| 3. Spiral | Borrowers sold assets to meet the shortfall, which depressed prices, which raised haircuts further. Because the funding was overnight, the entire book had to be refinanced daily, so there was no time to react in an orderly way. |

Two features of repo turned a valuation problem into a funding failure: the tenor, since overnight funding must be renewed every day, and the haircut, which is not fixed and rises precisely when the borrower can least afford it. This is the same wrong-way pattern seen in Ashanti and Metallgesellschaft, where the demand for cash arrives exactly when cash is hardest to find.

a.reason: Polarity flip on both variables. Borrowing was cheap, not expensive, and the collateral was of low quality rather than high. The cheapness is central: it is what made the leverage attractive.

b.reason: Low rates on low-quality collateral, followed by abrupt withdrawal through wider haircuts and refusal to roll.

c.reason: Factually false. The US government did not default on its Treasury obligations. The collateral in question was private-label structured product, not sovereign paper.

d.reason: Absolute-claim trap. The repo market is lightly regulated in some respects, but 'entirely unregulated' with 'no legal framework' is false: repos operate under master agreements with enforceable close-out and collateral provisions, and enforceability was not the failure point.

trap.explanation: Option A is a double polarity flip and it is superficially attractive because 'firms got into trouble borrowing' primes the reader toward expensive funding. The opposite is true and it is the cheapness that created the problem. Option D is an absolute claim that also misidentifies the failure mode: the collateral was enforceable, it was simply worth much less than assumed.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Explain how counterparty risk and liquidity risk can arise through the use of repo transactions.
questions.reading: LR2025: Repurchase Agreements and Financing
questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a broker-dealer is briefing the board on how a securities financing book generates liquidity risk as distinct from counterparty credit risk. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Because a repo is fully collateralised, the transaction converts liquidity risk into counterparty credit risk, so a dealer funding itself entirely through repo has no residual liquidity exposure.
A rise in haircuts requires the dealer to fund a larger share of each position from its own resources, so an unchanged securities book can generate a cash demand without any trade being executed.
Haircuts are fixed at the inception of a master agreement and cannot be varied for the life of the relationship, so the dealer's funding requirement per unit of collateral is known in advance.
Liquidity risk in a repo book arises principally from the cash lender's exposure to a fall in collateral value, since it is the lender that must find replacement funding on a default.

questions.solution:
**Concept tested:** How the haircut, rather than default, is the channel through which a repo book generates funding liquidity risk.

The haircut determines how much cash a given pool of collateral raises:

$$\text{Cash raised} = \text{collateral market value} \times (1 - \text{haircut})$$

The complement, the haircut itself, is the portion the dealer must fund from its own equity or from other borrowing. Two variables therefore drive the dealer's cash need, and only one of them is under its control:

| Change | Effect on cash raised | Who controls it |
|---|---|---|
| Collateral market value falls | Falls proportionately | The market |
| Haircut rises | Falls, on an unchanged book | The cash lender |

Worked illustration. A dealer finances GBP 1 billion of collateral at a 2% haircut and raises GBP 980 million. If lenders move to a 5% haircut, the same collateral raises only GBP 950 million. The dealer must find GBP 30 million of cash overnight, without having bought or sold anything.

This is why haircut risk is a liquidity exposure and not a credit exposure. No counterparty has defaulted; the terms on which the market will lend have simply moved. And the movement is wrong way: haircuts widen in exactly the conditions in which asset values are falling and alternative funding is scarcest, so the demand for cash arrives at the worst possible moment.

a.reason: Absolute-claim trap. Collateralisation reduces credit exposure but does not remove liquidity exposure; it relocates it into the haircut and the rollover. A dealer funded entirely overnight has a great deal of residual liquidity risk, which is the dealer bank failure mechanism.

b.reason: A haircut increase reduces the cash raised against an unchanged book, generating a funding requirement with no transaction taking place.

c.reason: Factually reversed. Haircuts are not fixed for the life of a relationship; they are set trade by trade and were raised sharply and repeatedly during 2007 and 2008.

d.reason: Role misassignment. It is the cash borrower, the dealer, that faces the funding problem, since it must replace the cash if the trade is not rolled. The lender's exposure to a fall in collateral value is a credit and market exposure, not a funding one.

trap.explanation: Option A is the absolute-claim trap and it encodes a genuinely common misconception, that collateral solves everything. Option D is a role misassignment that sounds analytical because it correctly identifies collateral value as a risk, then attaches the funding consequence to the wrong party. Follow the cash: whoever needs to replace it is the one with the liquidity problem.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Evaluate the characteristics of sound Early Warning Indicators (EWI) measures.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 3: Early Warning Indicators
questions.question: A liquidity risk manager is selecting metrics for the bank's early warning indicator dashboard. She wants measures that provide information about potential stress before an actual event occurs. Which type of indicator is she describing?

options.text: A lagging indicator, which confirms a stress event after it has begun and is therefore the more reliable class of measure.
A leading indicator, which signals potential stress ahead of the event and so allows management action while options remain open.
A sharp indicator, which is defined by the breadth of the data set it draws on rather than by its timing.
A coincident indicator, which moves at the same time as the event and is preferred because it carries no false positives.

questions.solution:
**Concept tested:** The timing dimension of early warning indicators, and why leading measures are what an EWI framework requires.

Early warning indicators are classified along two dimensions, and the exam tests both.

| Dimension | Types | What an EWI framework needs |
|---|---|---|
| Timing | Leading: signals stress before the event. Lagging: confirms stress after it has begun. | Leading. A lagging measure tells you what has already happened, by which point the range of available responses has narrowed. |
| Granularity | Sharp: highly granular, drawn from a specific subset of data. Broad: aggregated across the institution. | Both, in combination. Sharp measures locate the problem; broad measures show its scale. |

The purpose of an EWI is to initiate management discussion and necessary corrective action while there is still time to act. That objective is what makes the leading property essential rather than merely desirable: an indicator that only confirms a problem after the fact cannot serve the purpose the framework exists for.

Note also that leading indicators are inherently noisier than lagging ones. They will generate false positives, which is why the framework attaches escalation and cost-benefit decisions to a trigger rather than automatic action.

a.reason: Polarity flip on the timing, with a spurious justification attached. Lagging indicators confirm rather than anticipate, and greater reliability after the event is of no use to a framework designed to prompt action before it.

b.reason: A leading indicator signals potential stress ahead of the event, which is what the manager described.

c.reason: Sibling swap between the two classification dimensions. Sharp describes granularity, not timing, so it does not answer the question asked.

d.reason: A coincident measure by definition provides no advance warning, and the claim that it carries no false positives is an absolute claim with no support in the reading.

trap.explanation: Option C is the sibling swap and the one that separates candidates who have read the material from those who recognise the vocabulary, because 'sharp' is a genuine term from the same reading applied to the wrong axis. Option A pairs the reversed answer with a plausible-sounding merit (reliability) to make the flip harder to see.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Evaluate the characteristics of sound Early Warning Indicators (EWI) measures.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 3: Early Warning Indicators
questions.question: A consultant reviewing a bank's liquidity dashboard recommends the addition of several sharp early warning indicators. Which of the following best describes what she is recommending?

options.text: Indicators drawn from a highly granular subset of the bank's data, capable of isolating stress in a specific product, entity or currency.
Indicators reported to the highest level of aggregation, so that the board sees the position of the group as a whole.
Indicators that summarise past performance, so that the trend over prior reporting periods is visible alongside the current reading.
Indicators whose interpretation requires specialist quantitative expertise, so that they cannot be misread by non-specialists.

questions.solution:
**Concept tested:** Sharpness as a granularity property of an EWI, and why granular measures are needed alongside aggregate ones.

A sharp early warning indicator is a highly granular measure, drawn from a specific subset of data rather than from an institution-wide aggregate.

The reason granularity matters is that aggregation conceals. A group-level funding metric can sit comfortably within appetite while a single legal entity, a single currency book or a single product line is already under acute strain. Because liquidity is not freely transferable across entities, currencies and jurisdictions, a problem that is small in group terms can still be fatal where it sits.

| Property | Sharp indicator | Broad indicator |
|---|---|---|
| Data | A specific subset: one entity, currency, product or counterparty group | Aggregated across the institution |
| Strength | Locates the problem | Sizes the problem |
| Weakness | Noisy; many indicators to monitor | Conceals concentration |

A sound framework uses both. Sharpness is about where the measure looks, not about how difficult it is to compute or how far back it looks.

a.reason: Sharp means highly granular, based on a subset of the data.

b.reason: Polarity flip on the granularity axis. Aggregation to the highest level is the opposite of sharpness, and it is the property that lets concentrations hide.

c.reason: Sibling swap onto the timing axis. Summarising past performance describes a lagging indicator, which is a separate classification and is the property an EWI framework is trying to avoid.

d.reason: Misdefines the term. Sharpness concerns the granularity of the data, not the technical difficulty of interpreting the output. An indicator only a specialist can read is a governance weakness, not a design feature.

trap.explanation: Option B is the direct polarity flip and is attractive because 'sharp' colloquially suggests high-level clarity. It means the opposite: narrow and detailed. Option C imports the timing axis, which is the same sibling swap seen in the preceding question run in reverse. Keep the two axes separate: timing is leading against lagging, granularity is sharp against broad.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Evaluate the characteristics of sound Early Warning Indicators (EWI) measures.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 3: Early Warning Indicators
questions.question: A supervisor asks a risk analyst to compile a list of sound early warning indicators of a potential liquidity problem at the bank. Which of the following sets contains only genuine warning signals?

options.text: Negative publicity concerning an asset class the institution holds; a decline in the share price; widening spreads on the institution's debt and credit default swaps; significant deterioration in the institution's financial condition.

Negative publicity concerning an asset class the institution holds; a decline in the share price; an increase in credit lines extended to the institution; an increase in the weighted average maturity of liabilities.
A decline in the share price; widening credit default swap spreads; an increase in credit lines extended to the institution; significant deterioration in the institution's financial condition.

Widening credit default swap spreads; an increase in credit lines extended to the institution; significant deterioration in financial condition; an increase in the weighted average maturity of liabilities.

questions.solution:
**Concept tested:** Discriminating genuine early warning signals from developments that improve rather than threaten the liquidity position.

Every candidate item in the option set is a real observable. The task is to sort them by direction: does the development make a liquidity problem more likely, or less?

| Observable | Signal | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Negative publicity about an owned asset class | Warning | Counterparties reassess the institution's exposure and may withdraw funding or widen haircuts |
| Share price decline | Warning | A market-based view that the institution's prospects have deteriorated; often precedes funding withdrawal |
