| Widening debt and CDS spreads | Warning | The direct market price of the institution's credit; the clearest single signal that funding is repricing |
| Significant deterioration in financial condition | Warning | The fundamental driver behind the market signals |
| Increase in credit lines extended to the institution | Not a warning | More committed funding available is an improvement. It is a drop in credit lines that signals trouble |
| Increase in the weighted average maturity of liabilities | Not a warning | Longer-dated funding reduces rollover risk. It is a shortening of liability maturity that signals trouble |

Option A is the only set containing four genuine warning signals. The other three each import at least one of the two improvements.

a.reason: All four items are genuine warning signals identified in the reading.

b.reason: Contains two improvements: an increase in credit lines extended to the institution, and lengthening liability maturity.

c.reason: Contains one improvement, the increase in credit lines extended to the institution.

d.reason: Contains two improvements, the increase in credit lines and the lengthening of liability maturity.

trap.explanation: Both planted items are polarity flips of genuine indicators: a drop in credit lines and a shortening of liability maturity are warning signs, so their opposites have been inserted. The efficient technique on a list-selection item is to identify the one or two items that are clearly wrong and eliminate every option containing them, rather than validating each set in full. Here, spotting the credit lines item alone removes three of the four options.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Evaluate the characteristics of sound Early Warning Indicators (EWI) measures.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 3: Early Warning Indicators
questions.question: An investment bank maintains a set of parameters and processes designed to identify probable liquidity risks at a nascent stage. Each of the following would be treated as an early warning sign EXCEPT:

options.text: A rapid rise in the leverage ratio combined with heavy reliance on short-term repo funding.
An increase in currency mismatches across the funding book.
A narrowing of the spreads on the institution's debt and credit default swaps.
An increase in redemptions of certificates of deposit before maturity.

questions.solution:
**Concept tested:** Directional screening of early warning indicators: identifying which movement in a metric constitutes deterioration.

Each option names a metric that appears in EWI frameworks. The exception is the one whose stated direction represents improvement.

| Metric | Deterioration is | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Leverage plus short-term repo reliance | A rise | More assets funded by borrowing that must be renewed continually; the dealer bank failure pattern |
| Currency mismatches | An increase | Liquidity is not freely transferable across currencies; a surplus in one does not cure a deficit in another |
| Debt and CDS spreads | A widening | The market repricing the institution's credit; narrowing spreads mean the market's view is improving |
| Early CD redemptions | An increase | Depositors accepting a penalty to exit early is a strong behavioural signal of lost confidence |

Spreads are the single most closely watched market-based EWI because they are continuously observable and directly price the institution's own credit. That is precisely why the direction has to be held firmly: widening is the warning, narrowing is the reassurance.

The early CD redemption item deserves a note of its own. A depositor breaking a term deposit before maturity forfeits interest, so the behaviour reveals a preference for certainty of access over return. That makes it a leading behavioural indicator rather than a lagging balance sheet one.

a.reason: Rising leverage funded by short-term repo is a warning sign, and the combination is the canonical pre-failure profile for a dealer bank.

b.reason: Increasing currency mismatches are a warning sign, since liquidity cannot be assumed transferable across currencies.

c.reason: Narrowing spreads indicate the market's assessment of the institution's credit is improving. It is widening spreads that constitute the warning.

d.reason: An increase in early CD redemptions is a warning sign, indicating that depositors will accept a penalty to obtain access to their funds.

trap.explanation: This is a negative-qualifier item in which the exception is created by a single polarity flip on one metric while the other three are stated in the correct direction. The reading past the EXCEPT is the mechanical risk; the substantive risk is knowing which way spreads move on bad news. Anchor it with the price: a wider spread means investors demand more compensation to hold your paper.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Evaluate the characteristics of sound Early Warning Indicators (EWI) measures.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 3: Early Warning Indicators
questions.question: A newly appointed head of liquidity risk is deciding when the bank's early warning indicator metrics should be established and actively tracked. Which of the following is most appropriate?

options.text: During a business-as-usual environment, so that normal ranges are understood and a departure from them is meaningful.
During periods of institution-specific stress, when the metrics carry the most information and management attention is highest.
After an industry-wide decline in performance, so that the calibration reflects genuinely stressed conditions rather than benign ones.
After a loss-causing event has occurred, so that the indicators can be calibrated against a known outcome.

questions.solution:
**Concept tested:** Why an early warning framework must be established and baselined in normal conditions if its signals are to mean anything under stress.

An early warning indicator works by signalling a departure from normal. That requires two things that can only be obtained in calm conditions: a baseline of what normal looks like, and thresholds calibrated against it.

$$\text{No baseline} \rightarrow \text{no threshold} \rightarrow \text{no signal}$$

Three further reasons the business-as-usual answer is the right one:

| Requirement | Why it needs calm conditions |
|---|---|
| Baseline and threshold calibration | A range observed only under stress is not a normal range, so a threshold set from it will not trigger until the stress is already severe |
| Data and systems build | Sourcing granular data across entities, currencies and products takes time that a stressed institution does not have |
| Governance and escalation | Triggers, owners and escalation routes must be agreed and documented before they are needed, not negotiated during an event |

The general principle carries across the whole liquidity syllabus, and it is the same one behind contingency funding plans and break-glass testing: the instrument has to exist and be understood before the event, because during the event there is no time to build it and no capacity to interpret an uncalibrated reading.

a.reason: Establishing and tracking metrics in normal conditions produces the baseline against which a stressed reading becomes meaningful.

b.reason: A framework first established under stress has no baseline, so its readings cannot be interpreted as departures from normal. It also arrives too late to give warning of the stress already underway.

c.reason: Same defect, deferred to a market-wide trigger. Calibrating thresholds against stressed conditions sets them so wide that they will not signal the next episode until it is severe.

d.reason: This inverts the purpose entirely. An indicator established after a loss event is by construction a lagging measure, and an early warning framework exists to act before the loss.

trap.explanation: Options B, C and D form a ladder of increasing lateness, and each carries a superficially sensible justification about information content or calibration realism. The scope error common to all three is treating an EWI as a diagnostic tool applied to a known problem rather than a monitoring tool that must already be running. Option D is the clearest case: it converts a leading indicator into a lagging one.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Evaluate the characteristics of sound Early Warning Indicators (EWI) measures.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 3: Early Warning Indicators
questions.question: A bank's liquidity policy states that breaching an early warning indicator trigger initiates management discussion and formally documented action. The head of treasury is reviewing how those decisions should be taken. Which of the following is least consistent with sound practice?

options.text: Increasing the stock of highly liquid assets, weighed against the earnings forgone by holding them.
Setting a minimum standard for the liquidity buffer consistent with the bank's stated risk appetite.
Continuing to comply with the liquidity coverage ratio requirement, assessed alongside the cost of the assets held to meet it.
Applying a set-and-forget approach, under which triggers agreed at implementation are left unchanged so that decisions remain consistent over time.

questions.solution:
**Concept tested:** EWI triggers as the entry point to a documented, recalibrated cost-benefit decision rather than to an automatic or static response.

The purpose of a trigger is to initiate management discussion and necessary corrective action. It is the start of a decision, not the decision itself. Almost every response available to management involves a trade-off between resilience and earnings:

| Action | Benefit | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Increase highly liquid assets | Greater capacity to absorb an outflow | Lower yield on the asset base |
| Lengthen liability maturity | Less rollover risk | Higher funding cost through the term liquidity premium |
| Hold a larger buffer than the LCR requires | Headroom above the regulatory minimum | Cost of carrying assets that earn less than the alternatives |

A set-and-forget approach fails on two counts. First, it is not a cost-benefit decision at all, since nothing is weighed. Second, thresholds calibrated at implementation become stale as the balance sheet, the business mix and market conditions change, so a trigger left untouched will eventually fire constantly or never fire at all. Both outcomes destroy the framework's usefulness, the first by generating alert fatigue and the second by going silent.

Sound practice is periodic recalibration of thresholds, documented rationale for each trigger response, and clear ownership of the escalation route.

a.reason: This is a genuine cost-benefit decision: more resilience against forgone earnings.

b.reason: Setting a minimum buffer standard against stated risk appetite is sound practice and is itself a calibrated trade-off.

c.reason: Weighing continued LCR compliance against the cost of the qualifying assets held is a legitimate cost-benefit assessment.

d.reason: A set-and-forget approach weighs nothing and leaves thresholds uncalibrated as conditions change. It is the least consistent with sound practice.

trap.explanation: The qualifier is 'least consistent', so three options are sound practice and one is not, which inverts the usual reading. The distractor's appeal is the word 'consistent': stability of decision criteria sounds like good governance. It is a scope error, because consistency of process is sound while rigidity of calibration is not.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Identify EWI guidelines from banking regulators and supervisors (OCC, BCBS, Federal Reserve).
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 3: Early Warning Indicators
questions.question: A regulatory affairs analyst is preparing a memorandum on supervisory expectations for early warning indicators, drawing on guidance from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) and the Federal Reserve. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: The BCBS Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management require a bank to design a set of indicators to identify the emergence of increased risk or vulnerabilities in its liquidity risk position, and to consider potential negative events across both firm-specific and market-wide dimensions.

The OCC's guidance places responsibility for designing and calibrating a bank's early warning indicators with the examination team, which sets the thresholds the bank is then required to monitor against.

Federal Reserve supervisory guidance treats early warning indicators as a substitute for a contingency funding plan, on the basis that a bank detecting stress early will not require a pre-agreed emergency playbook.
Supervisory guidance across the three bodies converges on a single prescribed list of mandatory indicators, so that positions are directly comparable between institutions.

questions.solution:
**Concept tested:** What supervisory guidance on early warning indicators actually requires, and where responsibility for design and calibration sits.

Three features run consistently through supervisory guidance on early warning indicators, and each is a candidate for a role misassignment or scope distractor.

| Feature | What the guidance says |
|---|---|
| Ownership | The bank designs, calibrates and monitors its own indicator set. Supervisors assess whether the framework is adequate and intervene where it is not. This mirrors BCBS Principle 1, under which the bank is responsible for sound liquidity risk management while supervisors assess and act. |
| Coverage | Indicators must span both firm-specific and market-wide dimensions, and both should be considered individually and in combination, mirroring the scenario requirement in the stress testing principle. |
| Relationship to the CFP | Early warning indicators feed the contingency funding plan by identifying when it should be invoked. They are a complement, not a substitute: the CFP is a separate requirement with its own invocation and escalation procedures and its own testing obligation. |

On comparability: guidance is deliberately principles-based rather than prescriptive on the specific indicators, because the relevant measures depend on the institution's business model, funding profile, currencies and role in the system. A bank funded by retail deposits and a dealer funded by overnight repo need materially different dashboards.

The ownership and coverage points above are supported directly by the BIS Principles reproduced in the source text; statements about the specific OCC and Federal Reserve documents are drawn from the broader curriculum.

a.reason: The bank designs the indicator set, and coverage spans firm-specific and market-wide events.

b.reason: Role misassignment. Supervisors assess the adequacy of a bank's framework and intervene where it is deficient; they do not design or calibrate the bank's indicators for it.

c.reason: Scope error. Early warning indicators and contingency funding plans are complementary requirements. The indicators signal when the plan may need to be invoked; they do not remove the need for a plan.

d.reason: Guidance is principles-based rather than a prescribed mandatory list, precisely because the relevant indicators depend on the institution's business model and funding profile.

trap.explanation: Option B is the role misassignment, and governance items on this exam are decided by the actor far more often than by the action. Option C is a scope error that would be attractive to anyone who has not held the CFP and the EWI framework apart as separate obligations. Option D uses 'single prescribed list' and 'directly comparable', which are absolute-flavoured claims about principles-based supervision and are almost always wrong.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Discuss the process of liquidity transfer pricing (LTP) and identify best practices for the governance and implementation of an LTP process.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 17: Liquidity Transfer Pricing
questions.question: A treasury analyst is documenting the components that a bank's liquidity transfer pricing framework must charge out to its business lines. Each of the following is a cost component of liquidity transfer pricing EXCEPT:

options.text: Funding liquidity costs, being the term liquidity premium embedded in the bank's marginal cost of funds.
The cost of the liquidity cushion held against contingent outflows.
Contingent liquidity risk costs arising from undrawn commitments and other off-balance-sheet exposures.
General operating and administrative expenses of the business lines that originate the assets.

questions.solution:
**Concept tested:** What liquidity transfer pricing charges for, and the boundary between liquidity costs and other costs of doing business.

Liquidity transfer pricing is the mechanism by which a bank allocates the cost of liquidity to the business lines whose activities create the need for it. The components it charge are all liquidity costs:

| Component | What it prices |
|---|---|
| Funding liquidity cost | The term liquidity premium in the bank's marginal cost of funds, charged according to the tenor of the asset being funded |
| Cost of the liquidity cushion or buffer | The earnings forgone by holding high-quality liquid assets rather than higher-yielding ones |
| Contingent liquidity risk cost | The cost of standing ready to fund undrawn commitments, credit lines and other off-balance-sheet exposures if they are drawn |

General operating and administrative expenses are a cost of running the business, not a cost of liquidity. They are allocated through the bank's ordinary cost allocation and management accounting processes. Including them in the LTP charge would blur the price signal that LTP exists to send.

That price signal is the whole purpose. If a business line can write long-dated, illiquid assets or grant large undrawn commitments without being charged for the liquidity they consume, it will write too many of them. LTP aligns the incentives of individual business lines with the liquidity risk their activities create for the bank as a whole, which is the same objective as BIS Principle 4 on internal pricing.

a.reason: Funding liquidity cost is the primary LTP component and is the one the matched-maturity marginal cost of funds approach is designed to measure.

b.reason: The cost of carrying the liquidity cushion is a stated LTP component.

c.reason: Contingent liquidity risk cost, arising from undrawn commitments and similar exposures, is a stated LTP component.

d.reason: General operating and administrative expenses are a cost of doing business, allocated through ordinary management accounting, not a liquidity cost.

trap.explanation: This is a negative-qualifier item whose exception is created by scope rather than by a reversal: every option is a genuine cost the bank incurs, and only one of them is a liquidity cost. The test to apply is whether the item would disappear if the bank's funding were free and instantaneous. Operating expenses would not, so they are not an LTP component.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Discuss the process of liquidity transfer pricing (LTP) and identify best practices for the governance and implementation of an LTP process.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 17: Liquidity Transfer Pricing
questions.question: A risk analyst is discussing with her supervisor the alternative approaches to liquidity transfer pricing and the consequences each produces for the bank's balance sheet. Which of the following statements is most likely correct?

options.text: Under a matched-maturity marginal cost of funds approach, the bank's fixed-rate borrowing cost is converted into a floating-rate borrowing cost for the purpose of the internal charge.

Where management remuneration is based on net income, both an average cost-of-funds approach and a zero cost-of-funds approach correctly align the maturity of the bank's lending and borrowing activities.
Under a zero cost-of-funds approach, a bank typically ends up holding long-dated illiquid assets financed by stable long-term liabilities.
The largest maturity transformation on a bank's balance sheet typically arises under an average cost-of-funds approach.

questions.solution:
**Concept tested:** The mechanics of the matched-maturity marginal cost of funds approach and the distortions produced by the average-cost and zero-cost alternatives.

The three approaches differ in what the business line is charged, and the differences drive predictable balance sheet distortions.

| Approach | What is charged | Distortion produced |
|---|---|---|
| Matched-maturity marginal cost of funds | The marginal cost of funding of the same tenor as the asset, which converts the bank's fixed-rate borrowing cost into a floating-rate internal charge | None by design; this is best practice |
| Average cost of funds | A single blended rate regardless of tenor | Long-dated assets are undercharged and short-dated assets overcharged, so the bank writes too many long assets against short funding |
| Zero cost of funds | Nothing at all | The most extreme case: liquidity appears free, so business lines accumulate long-dated illiquid assets funded by whatever is cheapest, which is short-term wholesale money. This produces the largest maturity transformation |

The ranking matters and is the substance of the question. Zero cost of funds produces the greatest maturity transformation, because the internal price signal is entirely absent. The average cost approach sits between the two: it charges something, but the same something regardless of tenor, so it still systematically favours long assets.

The remuneration point is a governance amplifier rather than a correction. Where managers are paid on net income, an approach that undercharges long-dated assets makes those assets look unusually profitable, so the incentive reinforces the distortion instead of offsetting it.

a.reason: The matched-maturity marginal cost of funds approach converts the fixed-rate borrowing cost into a floating-rate internal charge matched to the asset's tenor.

b.reason: Reverses the effect. Neither approach aligns maturities; both understate the cost of long-dated assets, and remuneration based on net income amplifies the resulting misallocation rather than correcting it.

c.reason: Polarity flip on the funding side. Under a zero cost-of-funds approach the bank accumulates long-dated illiquid assets financed by short-term funding, which is precisely why the approach is dangerous.

d.reason: Sibling swap between the two flawed approaches. The largest maturity transformation arises under the zero cost-of-funds approach, not the average cost approach.

trap.explanation: Option D is the sibling swap and is the most likely miss, because a candidate who knows that flawed LTP causes maturity transformation still has to rank the two flawed methods. Order them by how much price signal survives: zero cost sends none, average cost sends a distorted one, matched-maturity sends the right one. Option C flips the funding leg while keeping the asset leg correct, which makes it read as half-familiar.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Discuss the process of liquidity transfer pricing (LTP) and identify best practices for the governance and implementation of an LTP process.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 17: Liquidity Transfer Pricing
questions.question: A consultant is advising a bank that is upgrading its liquidity transfer pricing framework toward current best practice. Which of the following recommendations is most consistent with that objective?

options.text: Move wholesale funding from decentralised regional funding desks to a centrally controlled treasury function, so that a single owner sets and applies the internal price.
Devolve responsibility for setting internal liquidity charges to each business line, so that the charge reflects the commercial realities the line faces.
Apply a uniform funding rate to all net funding needs regardless of size, so that no business line can claim it has been treated inconsistently.
Exclude off-balance-sheet exposures from the LTP framework, on the ground that they consume no funding until they are drawn.

questions.solution:
**Concept tested:** Governance of the LTP process: central ownership, independence of the price setter, and the scope of what must be priced.

Best practice on LTP governance rests on a single structural idea: the internal price must be set by a party with no interest in the outcome, and applied consistently across the whole bank.

| Best practice | Why |
|---|---|
| Central treasury ownership of wholesale funding and of the LTP price | A single owner with a bank-wide view sets the price. Decentralised funding desks price to their own local conditions and incentives, which reintroduces exactly the misalignment LTP exists to remove |
| Independence of the price setter from the business lines | A business line that sets its own charge will set it low |
| Escalating rates on net funding needs beyond agreed limits | Discourages over-trading and concentration by making the marginal unit of funding progressively more expensive |
| Coverage of on- and off-balance-sheet activities | Undrawn commitments consume contingent liquidity and must be charged for it, which is the contingent liquidity cost component |
| Senior management engagement and documented policy | LTP reallocates profitability between business lines, so it will be contested; it needs authority behind it |

Option A captures the central structural move. The others each reverse one of the remaining principles.

a.reason: Centralising wholesale funding under treasury gives a single independent owner of the internal price, applied consistently across the bank.

b.reason: Role misassignment, and the most damaging of the four. A business line setting its own liquidity charge has every incentive to set it too low, which recreates the misalignment LTP is designed to correct.

c.reason: Scope error. Best practice applies higher funding rates once net funding needs breach agreed limits, precisely to discourage over-trading. A flat rate regardless of size removes that brake.

d.reason: Reverses the contingent liquidity principle. Undrawn commitments consume contingent liquidity from the moment they are granted, because the bank must stand ready to fund them, which is why they carry an LTP charge.

trap.explanation: Option B is the role misassignment and it is dressed in a genuinely appealing argument about commercial realism. Ask who benefits from a lower charge: if the answer is the party setting it, the governance is wrong. Option D is a scope error resting on a true observation, since undrawn lines really do consume no funding until drawn, but they consume contingent liquidity throughout, and that is what is being priced.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Discuss challenges that may arise for banks during the implementation of LTP.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 17: Liquidity Transfer Pricing
questions.question: The treasurer of a bank that is introducing a formal liquidity transfer pricing framework is briefing the executive committee on the difficulties the project is likely to encounter. Which of the following is most accurate?

options.text: Because the framework reallocates profitability between business lines rather than changing the bank's aggregate earnings, it is largely uncontroversial internally and the principal challenges are technical.

Charging for the liquidity consumed by long-dated and off-balance-sheet business will make parts of the existing book appear unprofitable, so the framework requires senior management authority and clear policy to survive business-line resistance.

The behavioural assumptions needed to price non-maturing deposits and undrawn commitments can be read directly from contractual terms, so the main obstacle is the volume of data rather than its interpretation.
Once thresholds and rates have been agreed at implementation, they should be held constant, since frequent recalibration would undermine the comparability of business-line performance over time.

questions.solution:
**Concept tested:** Why LTP implementation is a governance problem before it is a technical one, and the specific obstacles that arise.

The mechanical difficulty of LTP is real but secondary. The binding constraint is that the framework redistributes measured profitability, and the losers under the new regime are usually the businesses that were most profitable under the old one.

| Challenge | Nature of the problem |
|---|---|
| Business-line resistance | Long-dated lending and commitment-heavy businesses were previously subsidised by an undercharged liquidity cost. Correct pricing makes some of that book look marginal or loss-making, and the affected lines will contest the methodology rather than the conclusion |
| Behavioural assumptions | Non-maturing deposits, undrawn commitments and prepayable loans have no contractual maturity that reflects their actual behaviour. Their effective tenor and draw probability must be modelled, and the assumptions materially change the charge, so they become the focus of dispute |
| Data and systems | Charges must be applied at transaction level across products, entities and currencies, which many legacy systems were never built to support |
| Choice of curve and recalibration | The term liquidity premium moves, sharply so in stress. A framework calibrated once and left alone will send a stale price signal |
| Transition | Applying the new charge to legacy business written under the old regime raises questions of fairness and of contract economics |

Because the obstacles are institutional rather than technical, the remedies are governance ones: explicit senior management sponsorship, a documented and independently owned methodology, and a transition plan agreed in advance.

a.reason: Scope error resting on a true premise. Aggregate earnings are indeed roughly unchanged, which is exactly why the internal distributional fight is intense. Zero-sum reallocation is more contested than growth, not less.

b.reason: Reallocated profitability generates resistance, which is why the framework requires senior authority and clear policy behind it.

c.reason: Factually reversed. The items that are hardest to price are precisely those whose contractual terms do not describe their behaviour, so the assumptions must be modelled and are inherently contestable. Interpretation is the obstacle, not volume.

d.reason: Same set-and-forget error that appears in the EWI material. The term liquidity premium moves materially over time, so holding rates constant sends an increasingly stale price signal. Comparability of reported performance is not a reason to price liquidity wrongly.

trap.explanation: Option A is the trap for the analytically minded: it correctly observes that LTP does not change aggregate profit and then draws precisely the wrong inference about how contested it will be. Option C inverts the difficulty of behavioural modelling, and option D repeats the set-and-forget scope error, which recurs across this syllabus wherever a calibrated parameter is involved.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Distinguish between the various sources of non-deposit liabilities at a bank.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 14: Managing Nondeposit Liabilities
questions.question: A treasury analyst is classifying the bank's non-deposit funding by instrument. Which of the following best describes commercial paper?

options.text: Short-term unsecured notes with maturities from a few days to nine months, issued by well-known corporations and financial firms on the strength of the issuer's own name.
Short-term notes secured by a pool of the issuer's receivables, which is what allows non-investment grade issuers to access the market.
Interest-bearing time deposits issued in bearer form and tradeable in a secondary market before maturity.
US dollar denominated deposits held at banks located outside the United States, priced off the domestic federal funds rate.

questions.solution:
**Concept tested:** Distinguishing commercial paper from the neighbouring non-deposit funding instruments by security, form and market.

The non-deposit funding sources are tested by discrimination rather than by definition, so it is worth holding them as a set:

| Instrument | Secured? | Typical maturity | Distinguishing feature |
|---|---|---|---|
| Commercial paper | Unsecured | A few days to 9 months | Issued on the strength of the issuer's own name, so access depends on credit standing |
| Asset-backed commercial paper | Secured by a receivables pool | Similar | The collateral, not the sponsor's name, supports the rating |
| Negotiable CDs | Unsecured | Days to a year | Bearer form and tradeable before maturity in a secondary market |
| Eurocurrency deposits | Unsecured | Overnight to a year | Denominated in one currency but held at banks outside that currency's home jurisdiction |
| Repurchase agreements | Secured | Overnight upward | Collateralised by securities, so the cheapest of the group |

The unsecured, name-dependent character of commercial paper is what made it fragile in 2007. When doubts about issuers emerged there was no collateral to fall back on, so the market simply closed to affected names, which is why securitisation and ABCP conduits are cited as a source of liquidity that disappeared almost overnight.

a.reason: Unsecured short-term notes issued on the issuer's own name, with maturities from a few days to nine months.

b.reason: Sibling swap. Backing by a receivables pool describes asset-backed commercial paper, which is a distinct instrument.

c.reason: Sibling swap. Bearer form and secondary market tradeability describe negotiable certificates of deposit.

d.reason: Sibling swap. Dollar deposits held at banks outside the United States are Eurocurrency (Eurodollar) deposits.

trap.explanation: Every wrong option is a correct definition of a different instrument from the same list, which is the standard construction for a 'distinguish between' objective and means plausibility screening is useless. Hold the set by their discriminating attribute: paper is unsecured and name-based, ABCP is collateral-based, CDs are tradeable, Eurodeposits are offshore, repo is secured.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Distinguish between the various sources of non-deposit liabilities at a bank.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 14: Managing Nondeposit Liabilities
questions.question: Gift Bank is a financially sound institution with an immediate reserve shortfall. Its management agrees to take a very short-term loan from the Federal Reserve at a rate set above the federal funds target rate. Which facility is the bank using?

options.text: Primary credit, available to sound institutions at a rate above the federal funds target, with minimal administrative burden.
Secondary credit, available to sound institutions at a rate above the federal funds target, with minimal administrative burden.
Seasonal credit, available to institutions of any condition to smooth predictable annual swings in deposits and loan demand.
Primary credit, available only to institutions that have exhausted all private funding sources and priced below the federal funds target as a concession.

questions.solution:
**Concept tested:** Distinguishing the three Federal Reserve discount window programmes by eligibility, pricing and purpose.

| Facility | Who qualifies | Pricing | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| Primary credit | Institutions in sound financial condition | Above the federal funds target | Very short-term backup funding, with minimal administrative requirements and few questions asked |
| Secondary credit | Institutions that do not qualify for primary credit | Above the primary credit rate | Short-term liquidity, or resolution of severe financial difficulties, with close supervisory scrutiny of the borrower's condition |
| Seasonal credit | Smaller institutions with recurring intra-year swings | A market-based rate | Smoothing predictable seasonal patterns in deposits and loan demand, typically agricultural or tourism driven |

Two features decide the answer. The bank is described as sound, which rules out secondary credit, and the need is an immediate one-off shortfall rather than a predictable annual pattern, which rules out seasonal credit.

Note the pricing logic, which is deliberate and is tested. All three facilities sit above or at market, never below. Pricing the window at a penalty keeps it a genuine backstop rather than a cheap funding source, and it is the same stigma consideration that surfaced in the Northern Rock case: banks avoid the window because using it signals distress.

a.reason: Primary credit is the facility for sound institutions, priced above the federal funds target and administered with minimal burden.

b.reason: Sibling swap on eligibility. Secondary credit is for institutions that do not qualify for primary credit and comes with close supervisory scrutiny, not minimal administration.

c.reason: Sibling swap on purpose. Seasonal credit addresses predictable recurring swings, not an immediate one-off reserve shortfall.

d.reason: Right facility, wrong description. Primary credit is not restricted to institutions that have exhausted private sources, and it is priced above the federal funds target rather than below it.

trap.explanation: Option D is the sharpest distractor because it names the correct facility and then attaches two false conditions, so a candidate who has matched the name will still be caught. The polarity flip on pricing is the tell: a central bank backstop priced below market would be used routinely, which defeats its purpose. Options B and C are eligibility and purpose swaps.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Distinguish between the various sources of non-deposit liabilities at a bank.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 14: Managing Nondeposit Liabilities
questions.question: The treasurer of a mid-sized bank is reviewing the bank's non-deposit funding options ahead of a large loan drawdown. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Federal funds purchased are secured by the borrowing bank's Treasury holdings, which is why they price below repurchase agreements of the same tenor.
Repurchase agreements are secured by the transfer of specific securities, which is why they typically price below unsecured federal funds of the same tenor.
Eurocurrency deposits are subject to the same reserve requirements as domestic transaction deposits, which removes any cost advantage over onshore funding.
Negotiable certificates of deposit cannot be sold before maturity, so the bank must hold them on its balance sheet for the full term.

questions.solution:
**Concept tested:** The security, reserve treatment and marketability characteristics that differentiate the main non-deposit funding sources and drive their relative cost.

Relative pricing across non-deposit sources is driven by three attributes, and each generates a standard distractor.

| Attribute | Effect on cost | Where it bites |
|---|---|---|
| Security | Collateralised funding prices below unsecured funding of the same tenor and counterparty | Repo below federal funds; federal funds are an unsecured interbank borrowing of reserve balances |
| Reserve treatment | Funding exempt from reserve requirements has a lower all-in cost, because every dollar raised is investable | Eurocurrency deposits and most non-deposit borrowings escape the reserve requirement that applies to domestic transaction deposits |
| Marketability | An instrument the holder can sell commands a lower yield, because the holder is not locked in | Negotiable CDs trade in a secondary market; ordinary time deposits do not |

The reserve point deserves emphasis because it links back to the deposit multiplier material. If a 10% reserve requirement applies, only 90 cents of each dollar of that funding can be invested, so the effective cost of the funding is its stated rate divided by 0.90. Non-deposit sources that escape the requirement avoid that grossing up entirely, which is a large part of why banks shifted toward them.

a.reason: Federal funds purchased are unsecured borrowings of reserve balances between banks. The option also reverses the pricing conclusion that would follow if they were secured.

b.reason: Repo is secured by the transfer of specific securities, so it prices below unsecured federal funds of comparable tenor.

c.reason: Reversed. Eurocurrency deposits sit outside the domestic reserve requirement regime, and that exemption is a significant part of their cost advantage.

d.reason: Reversed. Negotiability is the defining feature of a negotiable CD: the holder can sell it in a secondary market before maturity.

trap.explanation: Option A is a polarity flip on the security attribute dressed as a pricing argument, and it is tempting because federal funds sound institutional and safe. They are unsecured. Options C and D each invert the defining attribute of an instrument, which is the standard way a 'distinguish between' objective is corrupted: keep the attribute, flip the direction.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Differentiate between deterministic and stochastic cash flows and provide examples of each.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 7: Monitoring Liquidity
questions.question: A risk analyst is classifying the bank's projected cash flows for the liquidity monitoring framework. Which of the following accurately describes a deterministic cash flow?

options.text: It occurs at a future instant known with certainty at the reference date, in an amount also known with certainty at that date.
It occurs at a future instant known with certainty at the reference date, but in an amount that cannot be fully determined.
It occurs at a random future instant, in an amount known with certainty at the reference date.
It is unpredictable in both timing and amount, which is why it must be modelled rather than scheduled.

questions.solution:
**Concept tested:** The two-dimensional taxonomy of cash flows by time and by amount, and what qualifies as fully deterministic.

The taxonomy classifies every cash flow on two independent dimensions, always assessed from a stated reference date such as today.

| Dimension | Deterministic | Stochastic |
|---|---|---|
| Time | The instant of occurrence is known with certainty | The instant is random |
| Amount | The amount is known with certainty; the reading labels these simply as fixed, being set by the contract | The amount cannot be fully determined |

A cash flow described without qualification as deterministic is deterministic on both dimensions. Options B and C each describe a genuine category from the taxonomy, but a mixed one: deterministic in one dimension and stochastic in the other.

Two properties of the classification are separately examinable. First, it is relative to the reference point: a cash flow can change category when the point of view shifts to a future date, because uncertainty resolves over time. Second, on the asset side a flow qualifies as fixed amount and deterministic time only if the obligor or issuer is risk free, since a credit event would otherwise alter the contractual schedule.

a.reason: Certain in timing and certain in amount is the fully deterministic case.

b.reason: This is deterministic time with a stochastic amount, a mixed category rather than a deterministic cash flow.

c.reason: This is stochastic time with a deterministic amount, the reverse mixed category. The reading gives contracts providing for a given sum payable at an uncertain date as the example.

d.reason: Unpredictable in both dimensions is the fully stochastic case, the opposite of what was asked.

trap.explanation: Options B and C are the two mixed categories, and both are real classifications from the same figure in the reading, which makes them far more attractive than an invented distractor would be. The discipline is to check both dimensions before answering: an unqualified 'deterministic' requires certainty in time and in amount.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Differentiate between deterministic and stochastic cash flows and provide examples of each.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 7: Monitoring Liquidity
questions.question: An instructor describes a class of cash flows as arising from financial contracts such as fixed-rate bonds, fixed-rate mortgages and loans, including bonds issued and loans received by the bank and held among its liabilities, and as being produced by periodic interest payments and periodic capital instalments where the asset amortises. Assuming the obligor is risk free, into which category do these cash flows fall?

options.text: Deterministic amount at deterministic times.
Behavioural cash flows.
Credit-related cash flows.
New business cash flows.

questions.solution:
**Concept tested:** Mapping a described instrument onto the cash flow taxonomy, including the risk-free obligor condition that the classification depends on.

Fixed-rate instruments with contractual coupon dates and a defined amortisation schedule are the textbook case of certainty on both dimensions. The contract fixes when each payment falls and how large it is.

Two points in the description are doing real work:

| Feature in the stem | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| Both assets and liabilities are included | The classification is symmetric. Bonds issued and loans received by the bank generate deterministic outflows in exactly the way its own holdings generate deterministic inflows |
| The obligor is risk free | Without this, a credit event could alter the schedule, and the flows would fall into the credit-related stochastic-amount subcategory instead |

The three wrong options are the stochastic-amount subcategories, and each has a defining trigger:

$$\text{Credit related} \rightarrow \text{a default event} \quad|\quad \text{Indexed or contingent} \rightarrow \text{a market variable such as a Libor fixing} \quad|\quad \text{Behavioural} \rightarrow \text{a client decision} \quad|\quad \text{New business} \rightarrow \text{contracts not yet written}$$

A fixed-rate loan from a risk-free obligor has none of those triggers.

a.reason: Contractual timing and contractual amounts, with the risk-free condition removing the credit trigger.

b.reason: Behavioural flows depend on decisions made by the bank's clients or counterparties, such as prepayment or early withdrawal, which can only be loosely predicted. A fixed-rate contract with no embedded option has no such dependency.

c.reason: Credit-related flows carry amount uncertainty arising from credit events. The stem removes that by specifying a risk-free obligor.

d.reason: New business flows arise from contracts to be dealt in the future. The stem describes contracts already in place.

trap.explanation: Option C is the trap that rewards close reading, because without the risk-free qualifier it would be a defensible answer: a fixed-rate loan to a risky borrower genuinely does have a stochastic amount. The qualifier is the whole difference, and it is the kind of single-condition hinge this exam is built on. Option B catches anyone who associates loans with prepayment behaviour without noticing the contract described has no option in it.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Differentiate between deterministic and stochastic cash flows and provide examples of each.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 7: Monitoring Liquidity
questions.question: A liquidity analyst is assigning the bank's cash flows to the four subcategories of stochastic-amount flows. Which of the following assignments is correct?

options.text: A floating-rate loan whose coupon resets to a published benchmark is a behavioural cash flow, because the client chooses when to reset.
A non-maturing retail deposit that customers may withdraw at any time is an indexed or contingent cash flow, because its balance depends on market rates.
The projected drawdown on loans the bank plans to originate next year is a new business cash flow, because the contracts generating it have not yet been dealt.
The expected recovery on a defaulted corporate exposure is a new business cash flow, because the recovery amount is negotiated after the original contract has lapsed.

questions.solution:
**Concept tested:** Discriminating the four stochastic-amount subcategories by what actually drives the uncertainty in each.

When the amount of a cash flow is stochastic, the reading identifies four subcategories, each defined by the source of the uncertainty rather than by the instrument type.

| Subcategory | Uncertainty driven by | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Credit related | Credit events, such as the default of one or more clients | Expected recovery on a defaulted exposure; loan repayments from a risky obligor |
| Indexed or contingent | Market variables, such as Libor fixings | Coupons on a floating-rate loan or note |
| Behavioural | Decisions made by clients or counterparties, only loosely predictable and sometimes based on information the bank does not hold | Non-maturing deposit withdrawals; mortgage prepayment; drawdown of a committed line |
| New business | Contracts to be dealt in the future and more or less planned by the bank | Projected originations in next year's business plan |

The efficient way to assign a flow is to ask a single question: whose decision or which variable makes the amount uncertain. If it is a published rate, the flow is indexed. If it is a client exercising a choice, it is behavioural. If it is a default, it is credit related. If the contract does not yet exist, it is new business.

a.reason: Sibling swap. A reset to a published benchmark is driven by a market variable, so the flow is indexed or contingent. The client does not choose the reset.

b.reason: Sibling swap. A non-maturing deposit is the standard behavioural example, since the uncertainty comes from the customer's decision to withdraw. Rates influence that decision but do not determine the flow.

c.reason: Flows from contracts the bank plans to write but has not yet dealt are new business flows.

d.reason: Sibling swap. Recovery on a defaulted exposure is credit related, since the uncertainty arises from a credit event, not from a contract that has yet to be written.

trap.explanation: All three wrong options are sibling swaps between adjacent subcategories, which is the only sensible way to test a four-way taxonomy. Option B is the most instructive because both labels are arguable on the surface: deposit balances do respond to rates. The classification follows the proximate driver, and that is the customer's decision, which makes it behavioural.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Differentiate between various types of liquidity, including funding, operational, strategic, contingent, and restricted liquidity.
questions.reading: LR2025: Liquidity Stress Testing
questions.question: A liquidity risk manager is explaining to the risk committee why the bank's headline stock of liquid assets overstates what would actually be available in a stress scenario. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Operational liquidity is the cash needed to fund the business day to day and to ensure orderly clearing of payment transactions, and it is therefore unavailable to meet financial obligations under a liquidity stress test.
Restricted liquidity comprises the very high quality assets that can be converted into cash without material loss of value, and measuring it is the principal objective of the liquidity stress test.
Contingent liquidity consists of liquid assets that may be used only for specifically defined purposes, such as collateralising particular wholesale borrowings.
Strategic liquidity is held primarily to support the bank during periods of stress, which is why it is counted alongside the liquid asset buffer in the stress test.

questions.solution:
**Concept tested:** The four purposes for which an institution holds liquidity, and which of them may be counted as available in a liquidity stress test.

As a source of funding liquidity, institutions hold liquidity for four purposes. The distinction matters because only one of the four is genuinely available to absorb stressed outflows.

| Purpose | What it is | Available in a stress test? |
|---|---|---|
| Operational | Cash to fund the business daily and ensure orderly clearing of payments, plus a cushion for the unpredictability of daily settlement | No. It must be maintained to keep the institution operating |
| Restricted | Liquid assets usable only for specifically defined purposes, for example collateralising particular wholesale borrowings | No for general obligations, but it should be applied against the specific assumed outflows it supports |
| Contingent | The liquid asset buffer: very high quality assets convertible into cash without real loss of market value | Yes. Measuring the contingent liquidity required to cover stressed outflows is the principal objective of the stress test |
| Strategic | Cash held for future business needs arising outside normal operations, such as an acquisition | Not primarily. It is not aimed at supporting the bank during stress |

The practical consequence is the point of the briefing. A bank reporting a large headline liquid asset figure may have far less genuinely available capacity once operational balances, encumbered or earmarked assets and strategic reserves are removed. Only the contingent layer answers the question the stress test asks.

a.reason: Operational liquidity funds the daily business and payment clearing and is therefore unavailable to meet obligations under a stress test.

b.reason: Sibling swap. The high-quality convertible buffer whose measurement is the principal objective of the stress test is contingent liquidity, not restricted liquidity.

c.reason: The mirror image of the same swap. Liquid assets usable only for specifically defined purposes are restricted liquidity.

d.reason: Reverses the purpose. Strategic liquidity is held for future business needs outside normal operations and is not primarily aimed at supporting the bank during stress, so counting it in the buffer would overstate capacity.

trap.explanation: Options B and C are a matched pair of sibling swaps between contingent and restricted liquidity, so a candidate holding those two labels the wrong way round finds confirmation either way. Anchor them by function rather than by name: restricted means ring-fenced for something specific, contingent means reserved for the contingency, which is the stress itself.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Differentiate between various types of liquidity, including funding, operational, strategic, contingent, and restricted liquidity.
questions.reading: LR2025: Liquidity Stress Testing
questions.question: A bank reports total liquid assets of EUR 12 billion. Of that, EUR 2 billion is working cash needed to clear daily payment obligations, EUR 3 billion is pledged as collateral against specific wholesale borrowings, and EUR 1 billion has been set aside by the board to fund a planned acquisition. Which of the following best describes the amount that should be treated as available to meet general financial obligations in the bank's liquidity stress test?

options.text: EUR 12 billion, since all of the assets are liquid and could in principle be monetised under sufficient stress.
EUR 10 billion, since only the working cash needed for daily payment clearing must be excluded.
EUR 6 billion, being the contingent liquidity remaining once operational, restricted and strategic liquidity are removed.
EUR 9 billion, since pledged collateral remains the bank's property and can be recalled by substituting other assets.

questions.solution:
**Concept tested:** Applying the four-purpose liquidity taxonomy to a reported liquid asset stock to isolate the contingent layer.

Only contingent liquidity is available to meet general financial obligations under a stress scenario. The other three layers must be stripped out.

| Layer | Amount | Treatment |
|---|---|---|
| Operational: working cash for daily payment clearing | EUR 2bn | Excluded; must be maintained to keep the bank operating |
| Restricted: pledged against specific wholesale borrowings | EUR 3bn | Excluded from general availability; applied instead against the specific outflows it supports |
| Strategic: earmarked for a planned acquisition | EUR 1bn | Excluded; held for business needs outside normal operations, not for stress support |
| Contingent: the residual buffer | EUR 6bn | Available |

$$12 - 2 - 3 - 1 = \text{EUR } 6 \text{ billion}$$

Interpretation: the headline figure overstates genuinely available capacity by a factor of two. That gap is the reason the taxonomy exists. A stress test run against the EUR 12 billion headline would conclude the bank could absorb twice the outflow it can actually absorb, and the error would only become visible during the event.

Note the treatment of the restricted layer in particular. It is not simply deleted from the analysis: it should be applied against the assumed outflows it supports, so the EUR 3 billion offsets the wholesale borrowings it collateralises rather than disappearing.

a.reason: Treats the headline stock as fully available, which is precisely the error the taxonomy exists to prevent. Liquidity being liquid is not the same as its being available.

b.reason: Removes only the operational layer, leaving restricted and strategic liquidity counted as available for general obligations.

c.reason: 12 minus 2 operational, 3 restricted and 1 strategic leaves EUR 6 billion of contingent liquidity.

d.reason: Removes operational and strategic but retains the pledged collateral, on a substitution argument the framework does not accept. Encumbered assets are restricted precisely because they cannot be freely redeployed, and the BIS principles require the buffer to be unencumbered with no legal, regulatory or operational impediment to its use.

trap.explanation: Options B and D are partial deductions, each retaining one layer that should have come out, and they are ordered either side of the answer so magnitude alone will not rescue you. Option D is the most dangerous because its substitution argument sounds operationally sophisticated; it collides directly with the unencumbered requirement in BIS Principle 12.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe best practices for the reporting of a bank's liquidity position.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 13: Liquidity Risk Reporting and Stress Testing
questions.question: A treasury reporting analyst is documenting the suite of liquidity reports produced for the asset-liability committee. Which of the following most accurately describes the mismatch report?

options.text: It sets out the maturity gap between all assets and liabilities for each time bucket, adjusted for holdings of liquid securities.
It reports the bank's end-of-day liquidity position across settlement systems and currencies.
It lists the bank's marketable asset holdings at a granular level so that the eligibility of each for the liquidity buffer can be assessed.
It tracks month-end actuals and forecasts for deposits and loans by customer type.

questions.solution:
**Concept tested:** Distinguishing the standard liquidity reports by what each measures and at what frequency.

The reporting suite is tested by discrimination, so it is worth holding the reports as a set:

| Report | What it shows | Typical frequency |
|---|---|---|
| Mismatch report | The maturity gap between all assets and liabilities in each time bucket, with an adjustment for liquid securities, which can be monetised ahead of their contractual maturity | Regular, and the basis for the cash flow horizon report |
| Liquidity buffer qualifying securities report | Granular analysis of marketable asset holdings and their eligibility for the buffer | Monthly, submitted within 15 business days of month end |
| Deposit tracker | Month-end actuals, month-on-month changes and month-end forecasts for deposits and loans by customer type | Monthly |
| Daily flows report | Cash movements and the end-of-day position | Daily |
| Large depositor concentration report | Depositors holding above a threshold, commonly 5% of total liabilities | Regular |

The liquid securities adjustment is the distinguishing feature of the mismatch report and the reason it is more useful than a raw contractual maturity ladder. A five-year government bond has a five-year contractual maturity but can be sold or repoed tomorrow, so placing it in the five-year bucket without adjustment would understate near-term capacity.

a.reason: Maturity gap for all assets and liabilities per time bucket, with an adjustment for liquid securities.

b.reason: Sibling swap. The end-of-day position across systems and currencies belongs to the daily flows and intraday reporting, not the mismatch report.

c.reason: Sibling swap. Granular analysis of marketable holdings is the liquidity buffer qualifying securities report, produced monthly within 15 business days of month end.

d.reason: Sibling swap. Month-end actuals and forecasts by customer type describe the deposit tracker.

trap.explanation: Every wrong option correctly describes a different report from the same suite, so the item cannot be answered by recognising plausible language. The mismatch report is the only one organised by time bucket, which is the single word that identifies it.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe best practices for the reporting of a bank's liquidity position.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 13: Liquidity Risk Reporting and Stress Testing
questions.question: A reporting analyst is compiling the off-balance-sheet section of the bank's liquidity report, which captures potential stress points for funding. Each of the following belongs in that section EXCEPT:

options.text: Undrawn liquidity lines committed to clients.
Letters of credit issued on behalf of clients.
Revolving credit facilities granted but not yet drawn.
The bank's own holdings of high-quality liquid assets.

questions.solution:
**Concept tested:** Which exposures constitute off-balance-sheet stress points for funding, and the distinction between a contingent claim on the bank and an asset it owns.

Off-balance-sheet items matter for liquidity because each represents a potential future outflow the bank has already committed to but has not yet funded. The common feature is that a third party, not the bank, decides when the obligation crystallises.

| Item | Nature | Liquidity consequence |
|---|---|---|
| Liquidity lines | Committed backstop facilities | Drawn precisely when the client is under stress, which is often when the bank is too |
| Letters of credit | Contingent payment obligation | Crystallises into a cash outflow if the underlying obligation is called |
| Revolving credit facilities | Committed but undrawn lending | The client chooses when to draw; drawdowns on lines of credit are an explicit component of the LCR stress scenario |

High-quality liquid assets are the opposite kind of item. They sit on the balance sheet, they are owned by the bank, and they are a source of liquidity rather than a claim on it. They appear in the liquidity report as part of the buffer and in the LCR numerator, not among the off-balance-sheet stress points, and they are equally not part of the liability profile, which breaks down the share of each type of liability at the bank.

a.reason: Liquidity lines are a committed off-balance-sheet exposure and a recognised stress point.

b.reason: Letters of credit are contingent obligations that can convert into cash outflows.

c.reason: Undrawn revolving credit facilities are off-balance-sheet commitments, and their drawdown is a named component of the LCR stress scenario.

d.reason: Liquid assets are on-balance-sheet holdings owned by the bank and are a source of liquidity rather than a contingent claim on it.

trap.explanation: The negative qualifier is the mechanical risk. The conceptual test is direction of flow: the three genuine items are all things that could take cash out at somebody else's option, while the exception is something the bank can turn into cash at its own option. Ask of each item who holds the option and which way the cash moves.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe best practices for the reporting of a bank's liquidity position.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 13: Liquidity Risk Reporting and Stress Testing
questions.question: Following a stress test, a supervisor compares ABC Bank's funding yield curve with the curves of its peer group and observes that ABC's curve has risen materially above them. What is the most likely implication?

options.text: ABC Bank is experiencing funding stress, since the market is demanding a higher return to lend to it than to comparable institutions.
ABC Bank is holding an unusually high level of liquidity, which has depressed its need to compete for funds.
ABC Bank's liabilities exceed its assets, which is the definition of a funding curve above the peer group.
ABC Bank has a high level of solvency, since a steeper curve reflects the term premium investors attach to a well-capitalised borrower.

questions.solution:
**Concept tested:** Reading the funding yield curve as a market-based indicator of an institution's own funding cost relative to peers.

A funding yield curve plots what the bank must pay to raise funds at each tenor. It is a price the market sets for that specific institution, so its level relative to peers is a direct market judgement on the bank's credit and funding position.

$$\text{Curve above peers} \rightarrow \text{the market demands more to lend to this bank} \rightarrow \text{funding stress}$$

This is the same signal as widening debt and credit default swap spreads, expressed on the funding side rather than the traded credit side, and it belongs to the same family of market-based early warning indicators. Its particular value is the tenor dimension: a curve that has risen mainly at the short end suggests an acute funding concern, while a uniform shift suggests a general reassessment of the bank's credit.

Comparison against peers is what makes the reading meaningful. A rise in the absolute level of the curve may simply reflect a rise in market rates generally; a rise relative to peers isolates the institution-specific component.

a.reason: A funding curve above the peer group means the market requires a higher return to lend to this bank, which is a funding stress signal.

b.reason: Polarity flip. A bank holding ample liquidity and under no funding pressure would show a curve at or below the peer group, not above it.

c.reason: Liabilities exceeding assets is insolvency, which is a different concept entirely, and it is not what a funding curve measures. The curve prices funding cost, not balance sheet arithmetic.

d.reason: Polarity flip. Strong capitalisation lowers the cost of funds. A higher curve indicates a weaker perceived credit, not a stronger one.

trap.explanation: Options B and D are both polarity flips that attach a favourable interpretation to an unfavourable signal, which is the standard corruption for any price-based indicator. Option C is the solvency-liquidity confusion appearing again in a new costume. The reliable reading is to treat the curve as a price: a higher price for your funding is bad news, not good.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe best practices for the reporting of a bank's liquidity position.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 13: Liquidity Risk Reporting and Stress Testing
questions.question: A newly appointed head of treasury reporting is setting principles for how the bank's liquidity position should be reported. Which of the following is most consistent with best practice?

options.text: Reporting should be produced at the consolidated group level only, since liquidity surpluses in one entity offset deficits in another and entity-level reporting creates unnecessary noise.

Reporting frequency should be matched to the volatility of the underlying exposure, so that a clearing member with substantial trading activity reports intraday while a stable retail deposit book is tracked monthly.
Behavioural assumptions should be avoided in favour of contractual maturities throughout, since contractual terms are objective and auditable.
Once thresholds have been agreed with the regulator, reports should present the position against those thresholds without commentary, so that management judgement does not colour the numbers.

questions.solution:
**Concept tested:** Principles governing liquidity reporting: granularity, frequency, treatment of behavioural items, and the role of qualitative commentary.

Four principles run through the reporting material, and each of the wrong options reverses one of them.

| Principle | Practice |
|---|---|
| Frequency matched to volatility | A clearing member at a derivatives exchange faces intraday liquidity demands and needs an intraday dashboard. A stable retail deposit book is adequately tracked monthly through the deposit tracker. Uniform frequency either wastes effort or misses the exposure |
| Granularity below the group | Reports must be produced by entity, currency and jurisdiction, because liquidity is not freely transferable across them. Consolidation conceals trapped liquidity |
| Behavioural treatment where it is evidenced | Overnight balances may be treated as long-term where they can be demonstrated to behave that way, and a proportion of stable deposits may be treated as long-term funds where stability is evident. Contractual maturity alone would classify all current accounts as overnight, which nobody believes |
| Qualitative reporting alongside quantitative | Regular qualitative reporting covers movements in retail deposits, growth or shrinkage of asset books and the average day-to-day cash position, giving the numbers their context |

Option B states the frequency principle correctly, including the two ends of the range the reading illustrates.

a.reason: Reverses the granularity principle. Group-level netting assumes liquidity moves freely between entities and currencies, which is exactly what legal, regulatory and operational restrictions prevent.

b.reason: Frequency should track the volatility of the exposure, from intraday for a trading-intensive clearing member to monthly for a stable deposit book.

c.reason: Reverses the behavioural principle. Evidenced behavioural treatment is expressly permitted and is necessary, since non-maturing deposits have no contractual maturity that reflects how they actually behave.

d.reason: Removes the qualitative layer. Regular qualitative reporting on deposit movements, asset book growth and the average cash position is part of the standard reporting set, not an intrusion of judgement into it.

trap.explanation: Each wrong option promotes a genuine virtue, simplicity, objectivity or freedom from bias, and reaches a wrong conclusion by applying it where it does not belong. Option A is the most costly in practice, since consolidated reporting is what allows trapped liquidity in a subsidiary or a currency to go unnoticed until it is needed.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Differentiate between the mechanics of foreign exchange (FX) swaps and cross-currency swaps.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 20: Covered Interest Rate Parity Lost
questions.question: A derivatives analyst is comparing FX swaps and cross-currency swaps as tools for managing foreign currency funding. Which of the following correctly identifies what the two instruments have in common?

options.text: Both involve an exchange of one currency for another at inception and a re-exchange at maturity.
Both involve periodic exchanges of interest payments in the two currencies over the life of the trade.
Both are used principally to manage long-term interest rate risk rather than funding needs.
Both are transacted principally by central banks in the management of foreign currency reserves.

questions.solution:
**Concept tested:** The shared structure of FX swaps and cross-currency swaps, and the interest payment feature that distinguishes them.

The two instruments share their principal exchange structure and differ on everything else.

| | FX swap | Cross-currency swap |
|---|---|---|
| Exchange of principal at inception | Yes | Yes |
| Re-exchange of principal at maturity | Yes, at a rate agreed at inception | Yes, normally at the original spot rate |
| Periodic interest payments during the life | No. The interest differential is embedded in the difference between the near and far leg rates | Yes. Each party pays interest on the currency it received, periodically, at a floating or fixed rate |
| Typical maturity | Short, usually under one year | Long, commonly several years |
| Principal use | Short-term funding and liquidity management across currencies | Longer-term funding and the transformation of debt from one currency to another |

The interest treatment is the discriminator and the source of most distractors. An FX swap has no interest leg at all: it is a spot transaction paired with an offsetting forward, and the interest rate differential between the two currencies is expressed entirely through the forward points. A cross-currency swap makes that differential explicit as a stream of payments.

a.reason: Both structures exchange currencies at inception and re-exchange at maturity.

b.reason: This is the feature that distinguishes the two. A cross-currency swap has periodic interest exchanges; an FX swap does not, since the differential is embedded in the forward rate.

c.reason: Reverses the purpose for one of the pair. FX swaps are short-dated funding and liquidity instruments, not long-term interest rate management tools.

d.reason: Central banks do transact FX swaps, notably in the crisis-era swap lines, but both instruments are overwhelmingly used by commercial banks and corporates. The claim overstates a narrow case.

trap.explanation: Option B is the intended trap and is the single most important distinction in this objective: it names a real feature of one instrument and asserts it of both. If you can state which of the two has an interest leg, you can answer almost any question on this pair. Option C is a scope error that swaps the tenor and purpose of the FX swap for those of the cross-currency swap.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Differentiate between the mechanics of foreign exchange (FX) swaps and cross-currency swaps.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 20: Covered Interest Rate Parity Lost
questions.question: A treasurer is deciding between an FX swap and a cross-currency swap to fund a five-year US dollar asset from a euro liability base. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: An FX swap would carry no rollover risk over the five years, because the far leg rate is fixed at inception and can be extended on the same terms.
Under a cross-currency swap the parties exchange principal at inception and re-exchange at maturity, and each pays interest on the currency it received during the life of the trade.
An FX swap expresses the interest rate differential through periodic payments, while a cross-currency swap embeds it in the forward rate.
The cross-currency basis is the difference between the spot and forward rates on an FX swap, and it is zero whenever covered interest parity holds.

questions.solution:
**Concept tested:** The cash flow mechanics of a cross-currency swap and the rollover consequence of using short-dated FX swaps to fund a long-dated asset.

Trace the cash flows of a cross-currency swap in three stages:

| Stage | Cash flows |
|---|---|
| Inception | Party A pays EUR and receives USD at the spot rate |
| Each payment date | Party A pays interest on the USD it received; Party B pays interest on the EUR it received |
| Maturity | The principals are re-exchanged, normally at the original spot rate |

The tenor point is what decides the treasurer's question. An FX swap is a short-dated instrument, so funding a five-year asset with FX swaps means rolling the position repeatedly. Each roll is a point at which the market can decline to renew, or renew only at a wider cross-currency basis. That is precisely the exposure that materialised for non-US banks during the dollar shortage, when the cost of obtaining dollars through FX swaps rose sharply.

$$\text{Short-dated FX swaps funding a long-dated asset} = \text{currency and tenor mismatch} = \text{rollover risk}$$

The cross-currency basis is a separate concept: the spread added to one leg of a cross-currency swap that makes the two legs of equal value. Under textbook covered interest parity it would be zero, and its persistent departure from zero after 2008 is the subject of the next objective.

a.reason: Absolute-claim trap resting on a false premise. An FX swap is short dated, so funding a five-year asset requires repeated rollover, and there is no right to extend on the original terms.

b.reason: Principal exchanged at inception and re-exchanged at maturity, with each party paying interest on the currency it received.

c.reason: The two instruments are transposed. The FX swap embeds the differential in the forward rate; the cross-currency swap expresses it through periodic payments.

d.reason: Misdefines the basis. The cross-currency basis is the spread applied to one leg of a cross-currency swap to equalise the value of the two legs, not the spot-to-forward difference on an FX swap. The second clause is true of the textbook case and does not rescue the first.

trap.explanation: Option C is the transposition of the discriminating feature and is the same trap as in the preceding question run in reverse, which makes the pair worth drilling together. Option A is an absolute claim whose appeal is that the far leg rate genuinely is fixed; what is not fixed is the availability or price of the next swap.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Assess the causes of covered interest rate parity violations after the financial crisis of 2008.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 20: Covered Interest Rate Parity Lost
questions.question: John Paul, chief investment officer at Herald Advisors, is concerned about the cross-currency basis that has persisted since the global financial crisis. Which of the following is the most suitable explanation for the continued presence of a non-zero basis between two currencies?

options.text: Regulatory change has expanded the scope for speculative proprietary trading by US banks, increasing the capital devoted to closing the basis.
Given the general decline in global interest rates, the inclusion of a liquidity risk cost in swap pricing is no longer necessary.
The basis increasingly incorporates the financing and balance sheet costs incurred by arbitrageurs in maintaining the positions that would otherwise close it.
Because arbitrage positions largely eliminate counterparty exposure, the associated credit valuation adjustment costs have risen.

questions.solution:
**Concept tested:** Why covered interest parity ceased to hold after 2008: the arbitrage that enforces it is no longer free, so the basis reflects the cost of executing it.
