Covered interest parity is an arbitrage relationship, not a law of nature. It holds only for as long as someone stands ready to trade any deviation away at negligible cost.

$$\text{CIP holds} \iff \text{the arbitrage is costless and unconstrained}$$

Before 2008, dealer balance sheets were cheap and lightly constrained, so even a small deviation attracted enough capital to close it. Afterwards, several changes made carrying the position expensive:

| Change | Effect on the arbitrage |
|---|---|
| Leverage ratio and risk-based capital requirements | The position consumes balance sheet regardless of how low its market risk is, so it must earn a return on that capital |
| Higher and more differentiated bank funding costs | The arbitrageur must fund the position, and that funding is no longer available at a uniform risk-free rate |
| Counterparty credit charges | Credit valuation adjustment and margin requirements add a further carrying cost |
| Reduced proprietary risk taking | Less capital is available to be deployed against deviations in the first place |

The result is a persistent equilibrium rather than a persistent mispricing. The basis settles at roughly the cost of holding the position, so it is not an unexploited profit: it is the price of the balance sheet required to exploit it. Structural demand for dollar funding by non-US banks, the dollar funding gap, then determines the sign and size of that basis.

a.reason: Reversed. Post-crisis regulation, including the Volcker rule and higher capital requirements, reduced the capital available for speculative proprietary trading. Less arbitrage capital is part of why the basis persists.

b.reason: Reversed. Liquidity and funding risk costs became more significant in swap pricing after the crisis, not less, and the level of interest rates does not determine whether such a cost is warranted.

c.reason: The basis has come to reflect the financing and balance sheet costs of carrying the arbitrage position, which is why it no longer converges to zero.

d.reason: Internally contradictory. If arbitrage positions largely eliminated counterparty exposure, credit valuation adjustment costs would fall rather than rise. The premise and the conclusion point in opposite directions.

trap.explanation: Options A and B are polarity flips on post-crisis regulatory and pricing developments, and each would, if true, argue for the basis closing rather than persisting, which is a useful internal check. Option D is self-contradicting: read the causal chain in a distractor and confirm the premise actually supports the conclusion.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Assess the causes of covered interest rate parity violations after the financial crisis of 2008.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 20: Covered Interest Rate Parity Lost
questions.question: A macro strategist is briefing clients on why covered interest rate parity has failed to hold since 2008. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Deviations from covered interest parity are largest at quarter and year ends, because banks reduce balance sheet usage for regulatory reporting dates, which withdraws precisely the capacity the arbitrage requires.
Deviations are largest in the most liquid currency pairs, since high turnover makes the basis more volatile and therefore wider on average.
The persistence of the basis indicates a straightforward unexploited arbitrage, and its size measures the risk-free profit available to any institution willing to take the trade.
Because covered interest parity is a no-arbitrage identity derived from spot and forward rates alone, a non-zero basis can only reflect an error in the quoted forward rate.

questions.solution:
**Concept tested:** The empirical signature of post-crisis CIP violations, and why the basis is a price for balance sheet rather than an unexploited arbitrage.

The reporting-date pattern is the strongest single piece of evidence that the basis is a balance sheet phenomenon rather than a pricing error.

$$\text{Quarter end approaches} \rightarrow \text{banks shrink balance sheet for reporting} \rightarrow \text{arbitrage capacity withdrawn} \rightarrow \text{basis widens sharply} \rightarrow \text{normalises after the date passes}$$

If the deviation were a genuine free profit, it would not appear and disappear on a calendar schedule tied to when banks report their leverage ratios. That it does is direct evidence that the binding constraint is the availability of balance sheet, not the absence of anyone who has noticed the trade.

The other empirical regularities point the same way. The basis is generally wider for currencies whose banking systems have the largest structural dollar funding needs, because demand for dollars through the swap market is greatest there, and it widens in periods of market stress when balance sheet is scarcest and dollar demand highest. Both are demand-and-capacity effects, not information effects.

The conceptual point to carry into the exam: covered interest parity is enforced by arbitrage, and arbitrage requires a balance sheet. Once the balance sheet has a price, so does the parity relationship.

a.reason: The reporting-date pattern is the characteristic signature, and it identifies balance sheet capacity as the binding constraint.

b.reason: Reverses the relationship. Deviations are widest where structural dollar funding demand is greatest and where balance sheet is scarcest, not where turnover is highest. Liquidity narrows a basis rather than widening it.

c.reason: Misreads the persistence. The basis approximates the cost of carrying the position, so it is not a risk-free profit. If it were, the reporting-date pattern would not exist.

d.reason: Scope error. Covered interest parity involves spot rates, forward rates and the two interest rates, and it is a no-arbitrage relationship only under the assumption of costless, unconstrained arbitrage. Relaxing that assumption, rather than any quotation error, explains the basis.

trap.explanation: Option C is the trap that catches strong candidates, because the textbook framing of covered interest parity really does present a deviation as an arbitrage. The post-crisis lesson is that the arbitrage has a cost, so the deviation is a price rather than a profit. Option D is a scope error that treats a conditional no-arbitrage result as an unconditional identity.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Discuss the process of liquidity transfer pricing (LTP) and identify best practices for the governance and implementation of an LTP process.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 17: Liquidity Transfer Pricing
questions.question: A line of credit granted to a corporate customer has a limit of USD 80 million, of which USD 24 million has already been drawn. The bank assumes a 45% probability that the customer will draw the remaining balance, and the cost of term funding the assets held in the liquidity cushion is 24 basis points. Which of the following is closest to the rate the bank should charge for the contingent liquidity risk of this facility?

options.text: 7.56 bps

questions.solution:
**Concept tested:** Pricing the contingent liquidity risk of an undrawn commitment, as the undrawn proportion of the facility weighted by the draw probability and the cost of carrying the cushion.

$$\text{Contingent liquidity charge} = \frac{\text{undrawn amount}}{\text{total limit}} \times \text{probability of drawdown} \times \text{cost of term funding the cushion}$$

**Step 1.** Undrawn amount:
$$80 - 24 = \text{USD } 56 \text{ million}$$

**Step 2.** Undrawn proportion of the facility. The charge is expressed as a rate on the whole facility, so the undrawn amount is scaled by the limit:
$$56 \div 80 = 0.700$$

**Step 3.** Weight by the probability that the balance is drawn, and by the cost of holding the cushion that must stand behind it:
$$0.700 \times 0.45 \times 24 = 7.56 \text{ basis points}$$

Interpretation: the bank must hold liquid assets against the possibility of the customer drawing the remaining USD 56 million, and those assets earn less than the alternatives. The 7.56 basis point charge passes that carrying cost to the business line that granted the facility, so the commitment is priced rather than given away. Without the charge, undrawn lines look free to the originating line and are granted too freely, which is exactly the exposure that crystallised through drawdowns on lines of credit in the LCR stress scenario.

a.reason: 0.756 bps is the correct figure divided by ten, a decimal slip.

b.reason: $0.70 \times 0.45 \times 24 = 7.56$ basis points.

c.reason: 10.80 bps = $0.45 \times 24$, omitting the undrawn proportion. This charges as though the entire facility were undrawn.

d.reason: 16.80 bps = $0.70 \times 24$, omitting the draw probability. This charges as though drawdown were certain.

trap.explanation: Options C and D are each a dropped term, and the two together define the calculation: the charge scales by both how much of the facility is still available and how likely it is to be taken. Dropping either one overstates the charge, so any answer above the correct figure should prompt a check that both weights were applied.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Discuss the process of liquidity transfer pricing (LTP) and identify best practices for the governance and implementation of an LTP process.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 17: Liquidity Transfer Pricing
questions.question: A four-year amortizing loan is to be charged for funding liquidity risk under the matched-maturity marginal cost of funds approach. The annual term liquidity premiums applying to each year of the loan's life are 12, 17, 24 and 30 basis points respectively. Which of the following is closest to the charge for funding liquidity risk on this loan?
questions.solution:
**Concept tested:** Applying the matched-maturity marginal cost of funds approach to an amortizing loan by weighting each year's term liquidity premium by its maturity.

The matched-maturity approach charges each slice of the loan the term liquidity premium appropriate to that slice's maturity, then combines them into a single rate weighted by term:

$$\text{Charge} = \frac{\sum_t (\text{TLP}_t \times t)}{\sum_t t}$$

**Step 1.** Weight each year's premium by its maturity:

| Year $t$ | TLP (bps) | TLP $\times\, t$ |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 12 | 12 |
| 2 | 17 | 34 |
| 3 | 24 | 72 |
| 4 | 30 | 120 |
| Total | 83 | 238 |

**Step 2.** Divide by the sum of the weights:
$$\sum t = 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10$$
$$\text{Charge} = 238 \div 10 = 23.80 \text{ basis points}$$

Interpretation: the charge of 23.8 basis points sits well above the simple average of 20.75, because the longer-dated slices carry both the higher premiums and the heavier weights. That is the point of the method. A flat average would undercharge the long end of the loan, which is exactly the distortion the average cost-of-funds approach produces at the level of the whole balance sheet.

a.reason: 17.70 bps applies the weights in reverse (4, 3, 2, 1), charging the shortest slice most heavily. This inverts the term structure.

b.reason: 20.75 bps is the simple unweighted average of the four premiums, 83 divided by 4. It ignores the maturity weighting entirely.

c.reason: $238 \div 10 = 23.80$ basis points.

d.reason: 83.00 bps is the sum of the four premiums with no averaging at all.

trap.explanation: Option B is the intended trap and is the most natural wrong move, since 'average' is doing the work in the method's name and a simple mean feels like the obvious construction. The weighting is what makes it matched-maturity. Option A is a reversed weighting that produces a figure below the simple average, which is a useful signal: because the premium curve rises with term, any correct term-weighted answer must exceed the simple mean.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Discuss the process of liquidity transfer pricing (LTP) and identify best practices for the governance and implementation of an LTP process.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 17: Liquidity Transfer Pricing
questions.question:
A bank recorded the following term liquidity premiums and average costs of funds, in basis points, before the global financial crisis and more recently:

| Term in years | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pre-crisis: term liquidity premium | 1 | 3 | 5 | 7 | 10 |
| Pre-crisis: average cost of funds | 3 | 3 | 3 | 3 | 3 |
| Current: term liquidity premium | 5 | 8 | 10 | 18 | 35 |
| Current: average cost of funds | 10 | 10 | 10 | 10 | 10 |

A one-year non-amortizing bullet loan has a principal of USD 5 million. Under the matched-maturity marginal cost of funds approach, which of the following is closest to the charge transferred to the business unit writing the loan, pre-crisis and currently respectively?

options.text: USD 100 and USD 500
USD 500 and USD 2,500
USD 1,500 and USD 5,000
USD 2,000 and USD 7,500

questions.solution:
**Concept tested:** Translating a term liquidity premium into a currency charge on a specific loan, and the distinction between the term liquidity premium and the average cost of funds.

$$\text{Charge} = \text{principal} \times \text{term liquidity premium at the loan's maturity}$$

**Step 1.** Select the correct row and column. The loan is a one-year bullet, so it takes the one-year term liquidity premium. The average cost of funds row is not used: it is the benchmark the matched-maturity approach replaces, not an input to it.

$$\text{Pre-crisis: 1 basis point} \quad|\quad \text{Current: 5 basis points}$$

**Step 2.** Apply each to the principal:
$$\text{Pre-crisis} = 5{,}000{,}000 \times 0.0001 = \text{USD } 500$$
$$\text{Current} = 5{,}000{,}000 \times 0.0005 = \text{USD } 2{,}500$$

Interpretation: the charge for the same loan has risen fivefold. That is the central empirical point of the liquidity transfer pricing material. Before the crisis, term liquidity premiums were so small that the difference between charging them properly and ignoring them was almost invisible, which is why weak LTP practices survived. Afterwards, the premiums widened sharply and at the long end dramatically, from 10 to 35 basis points at five years, so an institution still using an average or zero cost-of-funds approach was mispricing its long-dated lending by a wide and growing margin.

a.reason: USD 100 and USD 500 apply the correct premiums to a principal of USD 1 million rather than USD 5 million.

c.reason: USD 1,500 and USD 5,000 use the average cost of funds figures of 3 and 10 basis points instead of the term liquidity premium. This is the wrong input twin, and it is the very substitution the matched-maturity approach exists to correct.

d.reason: USD 2,000 and USD 7,500 add the term liquidity premium to the average cost of funds (1 + 3 = 4 bps and 5 + 10 = 15 bps), double-counting the funding cost.

trap.explanation: Option C is the wrong input twin and is the substantive trap: the table deliberately supplies both a term liquidity premium row and an average cost of funds row, and only the first belongs in a matched-maturity charge. Option D compounds the error by adding them. Identify which row the method requires before reading any numbers off the table.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Distinguish between the various sources of non-deposit liabilities at a bank.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 14: Managing Nondeposit Liabilities
questions.question: A commercial bank has a new loan request meeting its quality standards of USD 660 million, expects to purchase USD 330 million of newly issued Treasury securities later in the week, and expects drawings on credit lines from its best corporate customers of USD 358 million. Deposits and other customer funds received today total USD 456 million, and a further USD 265 million is expected during the coming week. The current funding gap is zero. Which of the following is closest to the bank's estimated available funds gap for the coming week?

options.text: USD 326 million
USD 347 million
USD 423 million
USD 627 million

questions.solution:
**Concept tested:** The available funds gap as the excess of planned uses of funds over expected sources over a defined horizon.

$$\text{Available funds gap} = (\text{loans} + \text{investments}) - (\text{deposits} + \text{other funds available})$$

**Step 1.** Total planned uses of funds. All three are commitments of cash during the week, including the drawings on credit lines, which the bank must stand ready to fund:
$$660 + 330 + 358 = \text{USD } 1{,}348 \text{ million}$$

**Step 2.** Total expected sources over the same horizon:
$$456 + 265 = \text{USD } 721 \text{ million}$$

**Step 3.** The gap:
$$1{,}348 - 721 = \text{USD } 627 \text{ million}$$

Interpretation: the bank must raise USD 627 million from non-deposit sources during the week, which is exactly the decision that leads into the choice among federal funds, negotiable CDs, Eurodollars, commercial paper and the discount window. The available funds gap sizes the requirement; the effective cost rate comparison then chooses the source.

Note that the credit line drawings belong in uses even though the bank did not choose to make them. A committed line is a use of funds at the customer's option, which is precisely why it carries a contingent liquidity charge under the liquidity transfer pricing framework.

a.reason: USD 326 million omits both the Treasury purchases and part of the sources, leaving an incoherent subset of the inputs.

b.reason: USD 347 million omits the drawings on credit lines from uses: $660 + 330$ minus 721 gives 269, and no consistent treatment of the remaining items reaches the correct figure.

c.reason: USD 423 million omits the USD 265 million of funds expected later in the week, understating sources and, in this construction, the gap.

d.reason: $1{,}348$ minus $721 = \text{USD } 627$ million.

trap.explanation: The dropped term is the recurring error, and the item most often dropped is the drawings on credit lines, because they read as a contingent item rather than a planned use. They are a use of funds over the horizon and must be included. Build the two totals separately and in full before subtracting.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Distinguish between the various sources of non-deposit liabilities at a bank.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 14: Managing Nondeposit Liabilities
questions.question:
A bank holding company plans to raise USD 1 billion of short-term funds. The current annual market interest rates and non-interest costs of the alternative sources are shown below. Assume a reserve requirement of 10% applies, so that only 90% of the funds raised are investable.

| Source | Market interest rate | Non-interest cost |
|---|---|---|
| Federal funds | 2.10% | 0.42% |
| Negotiable CDs | 2.25% | 0.42% |
| Eurodollars | 2.15% | 0.52% |
| Commercial paper | 2.20% | 0.67% |

Which of the following is closest to the effective cost rate of federal funds and of negotiable CDs respectively?
questions.solution:
**Concept tested:** The effective cost rate of a funding source, combining interest and non-interest costs and grossing up for the proportion of funds that cannot be invested.

$$\text{Effective cost rate} = \frac{\text{interest cost} + \text{non-interest cost}}{\text{net investable funds as a proportion of funds raised}}$$

**Step 1.** Total cost of federal funds, adding the two cost components:
$$2.10\% + 0.42\% = 2.52\%$$

**Step 2.** Gross up for the reserve requirement. Only 90 cents of each dollar raised can be invested in earning assets, so the cost must be spread over that smaller base:
$$2.52\% \div 0.90 = 2.80\%$$

**Step 3.** Repeat for negotiable CDs:
$$(2.25\% + 0.42\%) \div 0.90 = 2.67\% \div 0.90 = 2.97\%$$

Interpretation: the headline market rates differ by only 15 basis points, but the effective rates differ by 17 basis points once both adjustments are made. The grossing up amplifies every difference by a factor of $1 \div 0.90$, which is why the reserve treatment of a funding source matters as much as its quoted rate. A source exempt from the reserve requirement avoids the grossing up entirely.

a.reason: 2.10% and 2.25% are the quoted market rates alone, with both the non-interest cost and the reserve grossing up dropped.

b.reason: 2.52% and 2.67% add the non-interest cost correctly but omit the grossing up for non-investable funds.

d.reason: 3.11% and 3.30% divide by 0.81 rather than 0.90, applying the reserve adjustment twice.

trap.explanation: Option B is the intermediate-result trap and the most likely miss, because adding the two cost components feels like the whole calculation. The second step is the one that distinguishes an effective cost rate from a total cost rate: the denominator is investable funds, not funds raised. Option D applies the same adjustment twice, which is what happens when the grossing up is remembered as a rule rather than derived from the definition.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Assess the causes of covered interest rate parity violations after the financial crisis of 2008.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 20: Covered Interest Rate Parity Lost
questions.question: The EUR/USD spot rate is USD 1.32 per euro and the one-year forward rate is USD 1.22 per euro. The one-year US dollar interest rate is 6.00%. Which of the following is closest to the one-year euro interest rate implied by covered interest rate parity?
questions.solution:
**Concept tested:** Solving the covered interest parity relationship for an unknown interest rate, with the base and quote currencies correctly identified.

$$\frac{F}{S} = \frac{1 + r_{\text{quote}}}{1 + r_{\text{base}}}$$

where $S$ and $F$ are the spot and forward rates expressed as units of the quote currency per unit of the base currency. Here the quotation is USD per EUR, so the euro is the base currency and the dollar is the quote currency.

**Step 1.** Form the forward-to-spot ratio:
$$1.22 \div 1.32 = 0.92424$$

The euro is at a forward discount against the dollar, which under parity requires the euro interest rate to be higher than the dollar rate. That direction check disposes of two options before any algebra.

**Step 2.** Substitute and solve for the euro rate:
$$0.92424 = \frac{1.06}{1 + r_{\text{EUR}}}$$
$$1 + r_{\text{EUR}} = 1.06 \div 0.92424 = 1.14689$$
$$r_{\text{EUR}} = 14.69\%$$

Interpretation: an investor borrowing dollars at 6%, converting at spot, investing at 14.69% in euros and selling the proceeds forward at 1.22 ends with exactly what a dollar deposit would have returned. That equality is what covered interest parity asserts, and the persistent post-crisis failure of the relationship is the subject of the two questions immediately preceding the set-aside section.

a.reason: 10.24% would leave the euro rate only modestly above the dollar rate, which is inconsistent with a forward discount of nearly 8%.

b.reason: 12.42% likewise understates the required differential.

d.reason: 29.32% inverts the forward-to-spot ratio, treating the dollar as the base currency: $1.06 \times (1.32 \div 1.22)$ overstates the differential by roughly a factor of two.

trap.explanation: Option D is the base and quote inversion, which is the dominant error on every covered interest parity question and produces an answer roughly twice too large here. Guard against it with the direction check before computing: the currency trading at a forward discount must be the higher-yielding one. The euro is at a discount, so the euro rate must exceed 6%, and it must exceed it by roughly the size of the discount.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Compare various money market and capital market instruments and discuss their advantages and disadvantages.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 4: The Investment Function in Financial Services Management
questions.question: A treasury analyst at a commercial bank is classifying the securities in the bank's investment portfolio for a training session. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: Treasury bills are long-term debt obligations of the federal government and are therefore capital market instruments.
Securities reaching maturity within one year are money market instruments, and they are held principally for liquidity and stability of income rather than for yield.
Capital market instruments carry shorter maturities than money market instruments, which is why they exhibit less price volatility.
Bankers' acceptances are capital market instruments, since the underlying trade obligation typically extends beyond one year.

questions.solution:
The classification is purely a maturity one, and everything else follows from it.

| | Money market instruments | Capital market instruments |
|---|---|---|
| Maturity | One year or less | More than one year |
| Examples | Treasury bills, short-term federal agency notes, certificates of deposit, Eurocurrency deposits, commercial paper, bankers' acceptances | Treasury notes and bonds, municipal bonds, corporate bonds, asset-backed securities |
| Price volatility | Low, because short duration limits sensitivity to rate changes | Higher, and rising with maturity |
| Why the bank holds them | Liquidity and stability of income | Yield, and diversification of the earning asset base |

The reading is explicit that investment securities are expected to help stabilise the institution's income, particularly when loan revenues fall. That role is what distinguishes the investment portfolio from the loan book: loans are the higher-yielding but less liquid and more cyclical asset, and securities are the counterweight.

Treasury bills specifically are the shortest-dated federal obligation, issued at a discount with maturities of one year or less, and are the archetypal money market instrument.

a.reason: Polarity flip on maturity. Treasury bills are short-term obligations of one year or less. Treasury notes and bonds are the longer-dated instruments.

b.reason: The one-year boundary defines the money market, and the portfolio's role is liquidity and income stability.

c.reason: Reverses the definition and then draws a conclusion that would follow from it. Capital market instruments have longer maturities, and therefore greater price volatility, not less.

d.reason: Sibling swap on classification. Bankers' acceptances are short-dated money market instruments arising from trade transactions, typically well under a year.

trap.explanation: Option A is the single most testable fact in this objective and is corrupted by one word: bills against bonds. Option C is a double reversal that is internally consistent, which makes it dangerous, since a candidate who has the maturity definition backwards will find the volatility claim confirms it. Fix the anchor: bills are short, notes and bonds are long, and the one-year line is the boundary.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Compare various money market and capital market instruments and discuss their advantages and disadvantages.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 4: The Investment Function in Financial Services Management
questions.question: Joshua is a portfolio manager considering adding bankers' acceptances to his firm's short-term investment portfolio. Which of the following correctly pairs the instrument's defining characteristic with a genuine disadvantage of holding it?

options.text: It is a bank's commitment to pay a stated sum on a stated future date under stated conditions, and its disadvantage is that it cannot be traded before maturity.
It is a bank's commitment to pay a stated sum on a stated future date under stated conditions, and its disadvantage is that it is issued in odd denominations and is not available in all maturities.
It is an unsecured note issued by a corporation on the strength of its own name, and its disadvantage is a yield below that of Treasury bills.
It is a deposit denominated in one currency and held outside that currency's home jurisdiction, and its disadvantage is that it cannot be discounted at the central bank.

questions.solution:
A bankers' acceptance is a money market instrument representing a bank's commitment to pay a specified amount of money on a specified future date under specified conditions. It arises from trade finance: a bank accepts, and so guarantees, a customer's payment obligation on an import or export transaction.

| Advantages | Disadvantages |
|---|---|
| Among the safest money market instruments, because the accepting bank stands behind the obligation | Issued in odd denominations, reflecting the underlying trade transaction rather than a standard issue size |
| Yields exceed Treasury bills, though they sit below Eurocurrency deposits | Not available in every maturity, again because supply depends on trade flows rather than an issuance calendar |
| Eligible for discount at the Federal Reserve, which supports their liquidity | The market is thinner than for Treasury bills |

The structural point behind both disadvantages is the same: supply is a by-product of international trade, not of a funding programme. An investor cannot simply ask for USD 50 million at six months; the instrument exists in whatever size and tenor the underlying commercial transaction created.

a.reason: The definition is right but the disadvantage is false. Bankers' acceptances trade in a secondary market and can also be discounted at the Federal Reserve.

b.reason: Correct definition, and both stated disadvantages follow from supply being driven by trade transactions.

c.reason: Sibling swap on the definition. An unsecured note issued on the issuer's own name is commercial paper. The yield claim is also reversed, since acceptances yield more than Treasury bills, not less.

d.reason: Sibling swap on the definition. A deposit held outside its currency's home jurisdiction is a Eurocurrency deposit, and the eligibility claim is reversed since acceptances can be discounted at the Federal Reserve.

trap.explanation: This is a two-part conjunction, so a candidate can hold the definition and still be caught by the disadvantage. Option A is the most dangerous because it pairs the correct definition with a plausible-sounding illiquidity claim, and illiquidity is the disadvantage most investors would guess at. The real disadvantages are practical rather than structural: odd sizes and patchy maturities.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Compare various money market and capital market instruments and discuss their advantages and disadvantages.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 4: The Investment Function in Financial Services Management
questions.question: Peter Jones, chief financial officer at a commercial bank, wants to diversify the bank's investment portfolio by adding securities with different risk profiles. Which of the following is generally regarded as carrying an implicit rather than an explicit guarantee of the federal government?

options.text: Commercial paper issued by highly rated industrial corporations.
Securities issued by government-sponsored enterprises.
Eurocurrency deposits placed with branches of major international banks.
Short-term Treasury notes issued directly by the federal government.

questions.solution:
The gradation is the examinable point, and it maps onto yield.

| Security | Government support | Yield consequence |
|---|---|---|
| Treasury bills, notes and bonds | Explicit. Direct full faith and credit obligations of the federal government | Lowest yield of the group |
| Securities of government-sponsored enterprises | Implicit. Not formally guaranteed, but the market has long assumed support would be forthcoming | A modest spread over Treasuries, reflecting that the guarantee is assumed rather than contractual |
| Commercial paper | None. Unsecured obligation of the issuing corporation | Wider spread, varying with the issuer's credit |
| Eurocurrency deposits | None. Obligation of the accepting bank, outside the domestic deposit insurance regime | Highest of the four |

The word implicit is doing all the work. An implicit guarantee is a market expectation, not a legal obligation, which is precisely why it can be tested in a crisis. The 2008 conservatorship of the two largest housing GSEs is the event that converted the assumption into action and confirmed the market's reading, but the securities were not formally guaranteed beforehand.

For a bank building an investment portfolio, agency paper sits in a useful middle ground: more yield than Treasuries, materially less credit risk than corporate paper, and generally eligible as high-quality collateral.

a.reason: Commercial paper is an unsecured corporate obligation with no government support of any kind, implicit or explicit.

b.reason: Government-sponsored enterprise securities carry an implicit expectation of federal support without a formal guarantee.

c.reason: Eurocurrency deposits are obligations of the accepting bank and sit outside the domestic guarantee and insurance framework entirely.

d.reason: Right direction, wrong degree. Treasury notes carry an explicit full faith and credit guarantee, not an implicit one, so they do not answer the question as asked.

trap.explanation: Option D is the scope trap and the one most likely to catch a well-prepared candidate, because Treasuries obviously carry government backing and the reader supplies 'guarantee' without checking whether the qualifier was implicit or explicit. The stem's single adjective is the whole question. Read the qualifier before scanning the options.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Identify and discuss various factors that affect the choice of investment securities by a bank.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 4: The Investment Function in Financial Services Management
questions.question: A bank's investment committee is documenting the risks that bear on its choice of investment securities. Which of the following correctly identifies the risk described?

options.text: The risk that the bank must sell part of its portfolio before maturity and realise a capital loss is prepayment risk.
The risk that loans pooled as collateral behind a security are repaid ahead of schedule, which is particularly acute for residential mortgages, is call risk.
The risk that the bank must sell part of its portfolio before maturity and realise a capital loss is liquidity risk.
The risk that rising prices for goods and services erode the purchasing power of interest income and repaid principal is business risk.

questions.solution:
The reading names a specific set of risks, and each has a precise trigger. The exam tests the mapping, not the definitions in isolation.

| Risk | Trigger |
|---|---|
| Liquidity risk | The bank must sell part of the portfolio before maturity and accepts a capital loss to do so |
| Prepayment risk | Loans behind a security are terminated or paid off ahead of schedule; acute for pooled residential mortgages and consumer loans |
| Call risk | The issuer exercises a contractual right to redeem the security early, typically after rates have fallen |
| Inflation risk | Rising prices erode the purchasing power of interest income and repaid principal |
| Credit or default risk | The issuer fails to pay |
| Business risk | The local economy the bank serves deteriorates, hitting loan and deposit business simultaneously |
| Tax exposure | The after-tax return differs from the gross yield, which drives the municipal against corporate comparison |

Prepayment and call risk are the pair most often confused, and the discriminator is who exercises the option. In a call, the issuer redeems. In a prepayment, the underlying borrowers repay. Both hurt the holder in the same circumstances, when rates have fallen and reinvestment is unattractive, which is why the consequence does not distinguish them.

a.reason: Sibling swap. Selling before maturity at a loss is liquidity risk; prepayment risk concerns early repayment by underlying borrowers.

b.reason: Sibling swap in the other direction. Early repayment of pooled loans is prepayment risk; call risk is the issuer's contractual right to redeem.

c.reason: Forced sale before maturity with a capital loss is the definition of liquidity risk in this context.

d.reason: Sibling swap. Erosion of purchasing power by rising prices is inflation risk. Business risk concerns deterioration in the local economy the bank serves.

trap.explanation: Every wrong option is a correct definition attached to the wrong label, which is the standard construction for a risk-taxonomy item. Option B is the sharpest because prepayment and call risk have identical consequences and differ only in who holds the option. Sort by the actor: issuer redeems is a call, borrowers repay is a prepayment.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Identify and discuss various factors that affect the choice of investment securities by a bank.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 4: The Investment Function in Financial Services Management
questions.question: A treasury analyst notes that the bank cannot accept deposits from federal, state and local government units unless it posts securities acceptable to those units as backing. Which factor affecting the choice of investment securities does this describe?

options.text: Pledging requirements, which constrain the composition of the portfolio because only certain securities qualify as acceptable collateral.
Statutory requirements, which cap the proportion of the portfolio that may be held in any single issuer.
Regulatory capital requirements, which set the risk weight applied to each security class.
Operational requirements, which govern the custody and settlement arrangements for securities held in the portfolio.

questions.solution:
Pledging requirements exist to safeguard public funds. Depository institutions in the United States cannot accept deposits from federal, state and local government units unless they post collateral acceptable to those units.

The consequence for portfolio construction is direct and often binding:

| Effect | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| Only certain securities qualify | Typically Treasury and agency paper, so the bank must hold those regardless of whether they offer the best risk-adjusted return |
| Pledged securities are encumbered | They cannot simultaneously serve as the bank's liquidity buffer, which links directly to the restricted liquidity category and to the unencumbered requirement in BIS Principle 12 |
| The requirement scales with public deposits | Winning a large government deposit mandate mechanically increases the securities the bank must hold and pledge |

This is why pledging appears in the list of factors affecting the choice of investment securities rather than in a chapter on collateral. It is a constraint on what the bank buys, sitting alongside expected rate of return, tax exposure, interest rate risk, credit risk, business risk, liquidity risk, call risk, prepayment risk, inflation risk and collateral requirements.

a.reason: Posting acceptable securities to back government unit deposits is the pledging requirement.

b.reason: Misdescribes the concept. Statutory requirements is not the term used for collateralising public deposits, and single-issuer concentration limits are a different constraint.

c.reason: Capital requirements determine how much capital a holding consumes, not whether securities must be posted against a deposit.

d.reason: Custody and settlement arrangements are operational matters and do not determine which securities the bank must hold to accept a class of deposit.

trap.explanation: The distractors are all real constraints that a bank genuinely faces, so recognition of the term alone will not settle it. The discriminator in the stem is the conditional structure: the bank cannot accept a specific type of deposit unless it posts collateral. That is a pledging requirement, and its second-order effect, encumbering the securities posted, is the part worth carrying into the liquidity material.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Identify and discuss various factors that affect the choice of investment securities by a bank.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 4: The Investment Function in Financial Services Management
questions.question: ABC Bank is enjoying unusually high loan revenues following a surge in loan demand. Management decides to sell lower-yielding securities at a loss in order to reduce the bank's current taxable income, replacing them with securities of similar quality and maturity. Which technique is the bank using?

options.text: A tax swap, which realises a loss to offset taxable income while leaving the portfolio's risk and maturity profile substantially unchanged.
A tax shelter, which defers recognition of income to a later period without any sale of securities.
Portfolio immunisation, which protects the realised return on the portfolio against movements in interest rates.
A rate expectation strategy, which shifts the maturity structure of the portfolio in anticipation of a change in interest rates.

questions.solution:
A tax swap sells securities carrying an unrealised loss and reinvests the proceeds in similar instruments. The loss becomes deductible against current income while the portfolio's economic position is largely preserved.

Sell at a loss $\rightarrow$ deduct the loss against high current taxable income $\rightarrow$ reinvest in comparable securities $\rightarrow$ risk and maturity profile broadly unchanged

Why the timing matters: the value of the deduction depends on the marginal tax rate applied to it. A year of unusually high loan revenue is exactly when that rate is highest, so the same realised loss is worth more then than in a lean year. Tax exposure is a listed factor affecting the choice of investment securities precisely because the bank's own tax position, not the security's characteristics, drives the decision.

The related computation, which appears in the set-aside section, is the tax-equivalent yield used to compare a tax-exempt municipal bond against a taxable alternative:

$\text{Tax-equivalent yield} = \dfrac{\text{tax-exempt yield}}{1 - \text{marginal tax rate}}$

a.reason: Selling at a loss to shelter current income while maintaining the portfolio profile is the tax swap.

b.reason: The stem describes an actual sale realising an actual loss, not a deferral arrangement. The mechanism does not match.

c.reason: Sibling swap onto a different strategy. Immunisation protects the realised return against interest rate movements and has no tax objective.

d.reason: Sibling swap. A rate expectation strategy repositions maturities on a rate view; the stem's transaction is explicitly motivated by taxable income and preserves the maturity profile.

trap.explanation: Options C and D are genuine portfolio strategies from the same chapter, which makes them plausible to anyone matching on 'sells and replaces securities'. The discriminator is the stated motive: the stem says the purpose is to reduce current taxable income, and only one technique in the chapter has a tax objective.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Identify and discuss various factors that affect the choice of investment securities by a bank.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 4: The Investment Function in Financial Services Management
questions.question: A bank's investment officer is comparing maturity management strategies for the securities portfolio. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: The barbell strategy is the most aggressive approach, requiring the bank to shift maturities continually in response to interest rate forecasts.
The rate expectation strategy is the most aggressive approach, requiring the bank to shift the maturities of its securities continually in response to forecast changes in interest rates.
Portfolio immunisation protects the bank against credit deterioration in the securities held, regardless of the direction of interest rates.
A front-end load maturity policy places the portfolio predominantly in long-dated securities, which maximises income while sacrificing liquidity.

questions.solution:
| Strategy | Structure | Character |
|---|---|---|
| Front-end load maturity policy | Securities concentrated at the short end | Conservative; emphasises liquidity over income |
| Back-end load maturity policy | Securities concentrated at the long end | Emphasises income over liquidity |
| Barbell strategy | Holdings at both ends, little in the middle | Combines liquidity from the short leg with income from the long leg |
| Rate expectation strategy | Maturities shifted continually according to the rate forecast | The most aggressive. Its success depends entirely on forecasting accuracy |
| Portfolio immunisation | Duration matched to the planning horizon | Protects the realised return against interest rate movements in either direction |

The aggression ranking follows from what each strategy bets on. The load and barbell policies take a structural position and hold it. The rate expectation strategy takes an active directional view and must be right repeatedly, which is why the reading singles it out and why the same chapter stresses that consistent rate forecasting is close to impossible.

On immunisation: it neutralises the offsetting effects of price risk and reinvestment risk, so the realised return is protected whichever way rates move. It does nothing whatever about credit risk.

a.reason: Sibling swap. The barbell is a structural allocation to both ends of the maturity spectrum, not an actively traded rate view.

b.reason: The rate expectation strategy shifts maturities on a rate forecast and is the most aggressive of the approaches.

c.reason: Scope error. Immunisation protects against interest rate movements, not against credit deterioration, which is a separate risk requiring separate management.

d.reason: Polarity flip. A front-end load policy concentrates holdings at the short end and emphasises liquidity. The description given is the back-end load policy.

trap.explanation: Option C is the substantive trap because immunisation sounds like comprehensive protection and the word carries a medical connotation of general immunity. It is specific: rate risk only. Option D is a polarity flip on the front-end and back-end labels, which are easy to transpose since neither name states which end it loads.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Calculate a bank's net liquidity position and explain factors that affect the supply and demand of liquidity at a bank.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 5: Liquidity and Reserves Management
questions.question:
ABC Bank Limited projects the following cash inflows and outflows over the next day, in USD millions:

| Item | Amount | Item | Amount |
|---|---|---|---|
| Deposit withdrawals | 129 | Sales of bank assets | 61 |
| Deposit inflows | 119 | Stockholder dividend payments | 172 |
| Scheduled loan repayments | 122 | Revenues from sale of non-deposit services | 118 |
| Acceptable loan requests | 90 | Repayments of bank borrowings | 84 |
| Borrowings from the money market | 110 | Operating expenses | 70 |

Which of the following is closest to the bank's projected net liquidity position over the next day?

options.text: A deficit of USD 15 million
A deficit of USD 23 million
A surplus of USD 15 million
A surplus of USD 23 million

questions.solution:
$\text{Net liquidity position} = \text{total supplies of liquidity} - \text{total demands for liquidity}$

Step 1. Assign each item. The test is simply the direction of the cash flow.

| Supplies (cash in) | Amount | Demands (cash out) | Amount |
|---|---|---|---|
| Deposit inflows | 119 | Deposit withdrawals | 129 |
| Scheduled loan repayments | 122 | Acceptable loan requests | 90 |
| Sales of bank assets | 61 | Stockholder dividend payments | 172 |
| Revenues from non-deposit services | 118 | Repayments of bank borrowings | 84 |
| Borrowings from the money market | 110 | Operating expenses | 70 |
| Total supplies | 530 | Total demands | 545 |

Step 2. Net:

$530 - 545 = -\text{USD }15\text{ million}$

Interpretation: the bank faces a liquidity deficit of USD 15 million over the day and must cover it, most obviously by increasing money market borrowings or selling additional assets. Note that the two largest single items sit on opposite sides and are both discretionary in nature: the USD 172 million dividend is a demand the bank chooses to create, and the USD 110 million of money market borrowing is a supply it chooses to raise. A deficit of this size is a management decision as much as a forecast.

The four pairings in the table are worth memorising as pairs, since GARP constructs distractors by moving one item across the line: inflows against withdrawals, repayments received against new loans granted, asset sales against borrowings repaid.

a.reason: 530 supplies less 545 demands gives a deficit of USD 15 million.

b.reason: A deficit of USD 23 million results from misclassifying one item, most commonly placing scheduled loan repayments among demands rather than supplies.

c.reason: The magnitude is right but the sign is reversed, which happens when demands are subtracted from supplies in the wrong order.

d.reason: Both the misclassification and the sign error, compounded.

trap.explanation: The dominant error is a misclassification rather than arithmetic, and the item most often moved to the wrong side is scheduled loan repayments, because the word repayment reads as an outflow. It is cash coming in from borrowers. Sort every line by asking which way the money travels before totalling anything. Option C is the pure sign error and is caught by asking whether the answer should be a surplus or a deficit before you compute it.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Calculate a bank's net liquidity position and explain factors that affect the supply and demand of liquidity at a bank.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 5: Liquidity and Reserves Management
questions.question: Prime Savings projects a net liquidity surplus of USD 31 million for the coming week. Its total supply of liquidity for the week is USD 122 million. Its demands for liquidity, excluding stockholder dividend payments, total USD 89 million. Which of the following is closest to the expected stockholder dividend payments for the week?

options.text: USD 2 million
USD 3 million
USD 7 million
USD 11 million

questions.solution:
$\text{Net liquidity position} = \text{total supplies} - \text{total demands}$

Step 1. Total demands must equal supplies less the surplus:

$\text{Total demands} = 122 - 31 = \text{USD }91\text{ million}$

Step 2. Dividends are the component of demand not yet counted:

$\text{Dividends} = 91 - 89 = \text{USD }2\text{ million}$

Check by reconstructing the position: 122 supplies less 91 demands gives the stated surplus of USD 31 million.

Interpretation: the bank's dividend is small relative to the week's flows, so the surplus is driven by the operating position rather than by discretionary distributions. The identity is worth holding in a form you can rearrange in any direction, because GARP will supply any three of the four quantities and ask for the fourth.

Note that stockholder dividend payments belong unambiguously to demands. They are a cash outflow the bank has committed to, and their inclusion on that side is the whole basis of the question.

a.reason: (122 minus 31) minus 89 = USD 2 million.

b.reason: USD 3 million results from an arithmetic slip in the second subtraction and does not reconcile: 89 plus 3 gives demands of 92, implying a surplus of 30 rather than 31.

c.reason: USD 7 million treats the surplus as USD 26 million or otherwise mis-states one input; it fails the reconstruction check.

d.reason: USD 11 million results from adding the surplus to supplies rather than subtracting it, which is a sign error in the first step: (122 plus 31) minus 89 less an offsetting slip.

trap.explanation: The sign error in step one is the trap worth guarding: a surplus means supplies exceed demands, so demands are found by subtracting the surplus from supplies, not adding it. The reconstruction check disposes of every wrong option in about fifteen seconds, and it is the discipline to build on any reverse-solve item.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Calculate a bank's net liquidity position and explain factors that affect the supply and demand of liquidity at a bank.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 5: Liquidity and Reserves Management
questions.question:
XYZ Bank forecasts the following balances over the coming months, in USD millions:

| Month | Checkable deposits | Time and savings deposits | Commercial loans | Consumer loans |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| January | 219 | 639 | 729 | 209 |
| February | 216 | 591 | 731 | 267 |
| March | 203 | 593 | 783 | 265 |
| April | 189 | 580 | 785 | 213 |

Using the sources and uses of funds approach, which of the following correctly identifies the month with the largest liquidity deficit and the month showing a liquidity surplus?

options.text: February shows the largest deficit and April shows a surplus.
February shows the largest deficit and March shows a surplus.
March shows the largest deficit and April shows a surplus.
April shows the largest deficit and February shows a surplus.

questions.solution:
The approach rests on a single relationship. Deposits are the bank's source of funds and loans are its use of them, so the liquidity gap over a period is:

$\text{Estimated liquidity gap} = \Delta\text{total deposits} - \Delta\text{total loans}$

Step 1. Total each side by month:

| Month | Total deposits | Total loans | Change in deposits | Change in loans | Liquidity gap |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| January | 858 | 938 | | | |
| February | 807 | 998 | -51 | +60 | -111 (deficit) |
| March | 796 | 1,048 | -11 | +50 | -61 (deficit) |
| April | 769 | 998 | -27 | -50 | +23 (surplus) |

Step 2. Read the result. February combines a fall in deposits with a rise in loans, which is the worst possible combination and produces the largest deficit at USD 111 million. April shows a surplus despite deposits also falling, because loans fell by considerably more.

The April result is the instructive one. A month in which deposits decline can still generate a liquidity surplus, because what matters is the relative movement of the two sides, not the direction of either alone. A bank shrinking its loan book faster than its deposit base frees liquidity even as its balance sheet contracts.

a.reason: February gives a gap of -111, the largest deficit; April gives +23, a surplus.

b.reason: The February identification is right, but March shows a deficit of USD 61 million, not a surplus. Loans rose by 50 while deposits fell by 11.

c.reason: March is a deficit but not the largest; February's is nearly double it. The April identification is correct.

d.reason: Both months are transposed. April is the surplus month and February the largest deficit.

trap.explanation: The recurring error is reading the deposit column alone and concluding that any month with falling deposits must be a deficit month, which produces the wrong answer for April. The gap is a difference of two changes, so both columns must be computed. A secondary trap is comparing deposits to loans in levels rather than changes; the levels show loans above deposits in every month, which says nothing about the period gap.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Calculate a bank's net liquidity position and explain factors that affect the supply and demand of liquidity at a bank.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 5: Liquidity and Reserves Management
questions.question: XYZ Bank forecasts a liquidity deficit for the coming month and is reviewing the actions available to close it. Each of the following would help cover the deficit EXCEPT:

options.text: Advertising aggressively to attract negotiable order of withdrawal deposits.
Selling a portion of the securities portfolio.
Expanding new lending aggressively to creditworthy borrowers.
Selling securities under agreements to repurchase.

questions.solution:
Every action available to a bank facing a projected deficit does one of two things: it increases supplies of liquidity or it reduces demands. Expanding the loan book does the opposite of both.

| Action | Effect | Side of the equation |
|---|---|---|
| Attract NOW deposits through advertising | Raises deposit inflows | Increases supply |
| Sell securities outright | Converts assets into cash | Increases supply |
| Sell securities under repurchase agreements | Raises cash against the portfolio without disposing of it, retaining the coupon and price exposure | Increases supply |
| Expand new lending | Funds must be advanced to borrowers | Increases demand, worsening the deficit |

Acceptable loan requests appear on the demand side of the net liquidity position, which is the direct link back to the preceding questions. Granting a loan is a use of liquidity, however profitable the loan may be. Profitability and liquidity are different questions, and a bank can lend itself into a funding crisis while every individual loan is sound.

Note the distinction between the two securities actions. An outright sale crystallises any gain or loss and removes the asset; a repurchase agreement raises the same cash while keeping the economic exposure. The choice between them is a portfolio decision, not a liquidity one, since both close the gap.

a.reason: Attracting deposits raises the supply of liquidity and helps close the deficit.

b.reason: Selling securities converts assets to cash, raising supply.

c.reason: New lending is a use of funds and appears among demands for liquidity. It widens the deficit rather than closing it.

d.reason: A repurchase agreement raises cash against the securities portfolio without selling it outright, raising supply.

trap.explanation: The negative qualifier is the mechanical risk, and the conceptual trap is the association between lending and revenue. Aggressive lending is unambiguously good for the income statement and unambiguously bad for a liquidity deficit, and the question tests whether the two are held apart. Apply the same direction test used on the net liquidity position: does the action bring cash in or send it out?

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Calculate a bank's net liquidity position and explain factors that affect the supply and demand of liquidity at a bank.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 5: Liquidity and Reserves Management
questions.question: A treasurer is explaining to the board why the bank's liquidity position tightens at predictable points in the year even when the balance sheet is stable. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Liquidity demands and supplies arrive at different times, so a bank can face a deficit in a period during which its total deposits and total loans are both unchanged.
Because every supply of liquidity is matched by a corresponding demand within the same period, a bank with a stable balance sheet cannot experience a timing deficit.
The principal source of liquidity demand is the maturity of the bank's own borrowings, and customer loan drawdowns are a supply of liquidity because they generate interest income.
Seasonal and cyclical patterns affect the demand for liquidity but not its supply, since deposit inflows are determined by the bank's pricing rather than by external conditions.

questions.solution:
The net liquidity position is a flow measure over a period, not a balance sheet ratio. That is why a bank whose stock of deposits and loans is unchanged over a month can still run out of cash within it: the inflows and the outflows do not arrive on the same days.

Stable stocks over a period $\neq$ matched flows within it

Three families of factors move the two sides, and they do not move them together:

| Factor | Effect on supply | Effect on demand |
|---|---|---|
| Seasonal, for example agricultural cycles, retail holiday periods or tax dates | Deposit inflows peak and trough on a calendar | Loan demand and withdrawals peak on a different calendar |
| Cyclical, tied to the economy | Deposit growth weakens in a downturn | Credit line drawdowns rise in a downturn, precisely when supply weakens |
| Trend, structural shifts in customer behaviour | Migration of retail balances to higher-yielding alternatives | Long-run growth in the loan book |

The cyclical row is the one worth carrying into the rest of the syllabus. Supply and demand for liquidity are negatively correlated across the cycle: the conditions that dry up funding are the conditions that trigger drawdowns. That wrong-way relationship is the same pattern seen in repo haircuts, in committed credit lines under the LCR stress scenario, and in the Ashanti and Metallgesellschaft cases.

a.reason: The position is a flow concept, so a timing mismatch produces a deficit even where the stocks are unchanged.

b.reason: Absolute-claim trap. Matching over a period does not imply matching within it, and the whole purpose of measuring a net liquidity position over short horizons is to expose exactly this.

c.reason: Role misassignment on the second clause. Customer loan drawdowns are a demand for liquidity, since cash must be advanced. Future interest income does not make a cash outflow a supply.

d.reason: Scope error. Seasonal and cyclical factors affect both sides, and deposit inflows respond to external conditions as well as to the bank's own pricing.

trap.explanation: Option C is the role misassignment that recurs throughout this objective: treating a profitable activity as a source of liquidity because it generates revenue. Cash advanced today is a demand regardless of what it earns tomorrow. Option B is an absolute claim that would, if true, make the entire net liquidity position framework unnecessary, which is a useful internal check.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 6: Intraday Liquidity Risk Management
questions.question: XYZ Bank obtains funds from the federal funds market during the day to settle amounts owed to another bank, and uses those funds to meet foreign exchange obligations falling due at its correspondent bank the following morning. Respectively, which source of intraday liquidity is the bank drawing on, and to which use is it putting the funds?

options.text: Cash balances, applied to outgoing wire transfers.
Liquid assets, applied to outgoing wire transfers.
Overnight borrowings, applied to funding for Nostro accounts.
Intraday credit, applied to settlements at payment, clearing and settlement systems.

questions.solution:
The reading separates where intraday liquidity comes from and what it is consumed by. Both lists must be held, because a question of this form asks for one of each.

| Sources of intraday liquidity | Uses of intraday liquidity |
|---|---|
| Cash balances held at the central bank | Settlements at payment, clearing and settlement (PCS) systems |
| Liquid assets that can be monetised during the day | Outgoing wire transfers on behalf of the bank and its clients |
| Intraday credit, including uncommitted lines from a clearing bank | Funding for Nostro accounts, meaning balances held at correspondent banks in other currencies |
| Overnight borrowings, such as federal funds purchased and Eurodollar deposits | Collateral pledging |
| Incoming funds flow from counterparties | Asset purchases and funding |

Step 1. Identify the source. Federal funds borrowed today and repaid the following morning are overnight borrowings, not intraday credit. Intraday credit is extended and extinguished within the same business day; an overnight borrowing survives the close.

Step 2. Identify the use. A Nostro account is the bank's own account held at a correspondent, typically in a foreign currency. Funding foreign exchange obligations falling due at a correspondent is funding for Nostro accounts.

a.reason: Wrong on both. Cash balances are a distinct source and were not used here, and the obligation is at a correspondent account rather than an outgoing wire transfer.

b.reason: Liquid assets are a genuine source but not the one described, and the use is again misidentified.

c.reason: Federal funds borrowed and repaid the next morning are overnight borrowings, and meeting obligations at a correspondent is funding for Nostro accounts.

d.reason: Sibling swap on the source. Intraday credit is extended and repaid within the same day; a borrowing repaid the following morning is not intraday. Settlement at a PCS system is also a different use from funding a correspondent account.

trap.explanation: Option D is the trap and it turns on the tenor of the borrowing. The word intraday in the objective primes candidates to select intraday credit as the source, but the stem says the funds are repaid the next morning, which makes them overnight. Read the repayment timing. The second discriminator is the destination: a correspondent account is a Nostro, not a wire transfer and not a PCS settlement.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 6: Intraday Liquidity Risk Management
questions.question: A bank treasurer is classifying an intraday exposure with the following characteristics: it settles once per day, generally in the late afternoon; it may act as either a source or a use of funds depending on the participant's net position on the day; and it is harder to forecast for same-day settlement activity than for securities settling over several days. Which category does the exposure belong to?

options.text: Outgoing wire transfers.
Funding for Nostro accounts.
Collateral pledging.
Settlements at payment, clearing and settlement systems.

questions.solution:
Each characteristic in the stem points to the same category.

| Characteristic | What it identifies |
|---|---|
| A single settlement per day, typically late afternoon | A netted settlement cycle rather than a stream of individual payments. Wire transfers occur continuously through the day |
| May be a source or a use, depending on the net position | Netting. A participant that is a net receiver on the day takes liquidity in; a net payer sends it out. Only a netted settlement has this two-way character |
| Harder to forecast for same-day than for multi-day settlement | Multi-day settlement gives advance visibility of the obligation; same-day activity does not |

Taken together these describe settlement at a payment, clearing and settlement system, where participants' obligations are netted and settled at defined times.

The two-way property is the strongest single clue and is worth generalising. Most uses of intraday liquidity are one-directional: an outgoing wire sends cash out, funding a Nostro sends cash out, pledging collateral encumbers an asset. Only a netted settlement position can flip between source and use from one day to the next, which is why financial market utilities invest in liquidity saving mechanisms such as bilateral and multilateral netting, net debit caps, throughput requirements and staggered settlement windows.

a.reason: Outgoing wire transfers occur throughout the day rather than in a single settlement cycle, and they are always a use of funds, never a source.

b.reason: Funding a Nostro account is a one-directional use tied to the bank's own correspondent balances, not a netted daily settlement.

c.reason: Collateral pledging encumbers assets and is one-directional. It has no daily netting cycle.

d.reason: A once-daily netted settlement that can be either a source or a use, with limited same-day forecastability, is settlement at a PCS system.

trap.explanation: The discriminating clue is the second characteristic, that the exposure can be either a source or a use. A candidate scanning for a familiar label will match on the first characteristic alone and may pick any of the uses. Read all three conditions: only one category satisfies the two-way property, and that alone identifies the answer.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 6: Intraday Liquidity Risk Management
questions.question: A bank's intraday liquidity dashboard includes a measure derived by comparing a client's peak daily intraday overdraft against the credit line established for that client. Which measure is this?

options.text: Client intraday credit usage.
Daily maximum intraday liquidity usage.
Payment throughput.
Total bank intraday credit lines available and usage.

questions.solution:
The measures are separated by whose exposure they capture and against what the figure is compared. Getting the actor right decides most questions on this material.

| Measure | Whose position | Construction |
|---|---|---|
| Client intraday credit usage | The bank's client | The client's peak daily intraday overdraft compared with the credit line established for that client |
| Daily maximum intraday liquidity usage | The bank's own | The largest net negative position the bank itself reaches during the day |
| Total bank intraday credit lines available and usage | The bank as borrower | Lines extended to the bank by its clearing banks, and how much is drawn |
| Total intraday credit lines to clients and counterparties | The bank as lender | Lines extended by the bank, in aggregate |
| Payment throughput | Operational | Outgoing payments as a proportion of total payments, or against time markers through the day |

Note the pairing of the third and fourth rows. The bank sits on both sides of the intraday credit market, receiving lines from its clearing banks and extending them to its clients, and the two exposures are monitored separately because they fail in opposite directions. A withdrawal of lines to the bank is a funding problem; a drawdown of lines by clients is a credit and liquidity problem.

Payment throughput is measured for three stated reasons: to track volume patterns and ensure the day's payments are processed on time, to meet financial market utility requirements to submit a target percentage of payments by a deadline, and to identify peak periods and their correlation with intraday liquidity on hand and credit usage.

a.reason: Peak client overdraft against the established client line is client intraday credit usage.

b.reason: Role misassignment. Daily maximum intraday liquidity usage measures the bank's own peak position, not a client's.

c.reason: Payment throughput measures the pace at which outgoing payments are released through the day, not any overdraft against a line.

d.reason: Direction reversed. This measures lines extended to the bank and the bank's use of them, whereas the stem describes a line the bank extended to a client.

trap.explanation: Options B and D are both role misassignments and between them cover the two ways to get this wrong: measuring the bank's own position instead of the client's, and measuring lines received instead of lines granted. On any intraday measure, identify the subject first: whose overdraft, and whose line?

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 6: Intraday Liquidity Risk Management
questions.question: XYZ Bank monitors its intraday and end-of-day settlement positions at every financial market utility in which it participates, capturing transaction-level detail wherever possible and storing it for later analysis. Which measure for understanding intraday flows is the bank employing?

options.text: Total payments.
Other cash transactions.
Settlement positions.
Total bank intraday credit lines available and usage.

questions.solution:
The measures for understanding intraday flows are distinguished by what is being counted:

| Measure | What it captures |
|---|---|
| Total payments | Payer and payee information, the payment system used, the time received or originated, routing information, any suspensions, and the credit status of the payment |
| Other cash transactions | Cash movements outside the main payment flows, such as internal book transfers and non-payment cash activity |
| Settlement positions | Intraday and end-of-day settlement positions at each financial market utility in which the bank participates, maximising transaction-level detail for analysis |

The stem matches the third row word for word: settlement positions, at every financial market utility, at transaction level. The identifying feature is that the measure is organised by venue, meaning the FMU, rather than by individual payment.

Why it is monitored separately: a bank's net settlement obligation at a given utility is the single largest intraday exposure it faces at that venue, and it can flip between a receipt and an obligation from day to day. Aggregating it into total payments would conceal the concentration.

a.reason: Total payments captures payer and payee detail, the system used, timing, routing and suspensions for individual payments. It is organised by payment, not by settlement venue.

b.reason: Other cash transactions covers cash movements outside the main payment flows, such as internal book transfers and non-payment cash activity, which does not match the stem's description of settlement positions at financial market utilities.

c.reason: Monitoring intraday and end-of-day settlement positions at each financial market utility, at transaction level, is the settlement positions measure.

d.reason: Sibling swap onto the risk-monitoring measures. Credit lines available and used is a measure for quantifying risk levels, not for understanding flows.

trap.explanation: Option D is the trap for a candidate reading carefully but confusing the two families of measures: those for understanding intraday flows against those for quantifying and monitoring risk levels. Hold them apart by purpose, since the first describes what moved and the second describes how much exposure was created.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Compare and contrast the major lines of business in which dealer banks operate and the risk factors they face in each line of business.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 8: The Failure Mechanics of Dealer Banks
questions.question: A large European dealer bank operates in both the primary and the secondary securities markets. Which of the following correctly describes the parties between which it intermediates in each?

options.text: In the primary market it intermediates between issuers and investors, and in the secondary market between sellers and buyers of already issued securities.
In the primary market it intermediates between sellers and buyers of already issued securities, and in the secondary market between issuers and investors.
In both markets it intermediates exclusively between other dealer banks, since retail and institutional clients access the market through separate channels.
In the primary market it intermediates between corporate clients only, and in the secondary market it acts solely as principal rather than as an intermediary.

questions.solution:
The distinction turns on whether the security is being created or changing hands.

| | Primary market | Secondary market |
|---|---|---|
| What happens | Securities are issued for the first time | Already issued securities are traded between holders |
| Parties intermediated | Issuers and investors | Sellers and buyers |
| Dealer's role | Underwriting and distribution: placing new paper with investors | Market making: standing ready to buy and sell, providing continuous liquidity |
| How the dealer earns | Underwriting fees and the distribution spread | The bid-ask spread on each transaction |
| Cash proceeds go to | The issuer | The selling investor |

The cash flow destination is the cleanest way to hold the pair. In a primary transaction the money reaches the issuer and finances the business. In a secondary transaction it reaches another investor, and the issuer receives nothing.

Both roles sit within the securities business, which is one of several lines in which a dealer bank operates alongside over-the-counter derivatives, repo intermediation, prime brokerage, asset management and its own proprietary positions. Each line generates a distinct risk profile, which is why the failure mechanics of a dealer bank run through several channels at once.

a.reason: Issuers and investors in the primary market, sellers and buyers in the secondary market.

b.reason: The two markets are transposed. New issuance is the primary market by definition.

c.reason: Absolute-claim trap. Dealer banks intermediate for issuers, institutional investors, corporates and other dealers alike; the interdealer market is one segment, not the whole.

d.reason: Scope error on both halves. Primary market activity is not confined to corporate clients, and dealers act as intermediaries in the secondary market as well as taking principal positions.

trap.explanation: Option B is the straight transposition and is the only distractor a prepared candidate is likely to reach, so the whole item turns on holding the two labels the right way round. Anchor on the word primary: it is the first time the security exists, so the issuer must be one of the two parties. Options C and D fail on absolutes and scope respectively.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Compare and contrast the major lines of business in which dealer banks operate and the risk factors they face in each line of business.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 8: The Failure Mechanics of Dealer Banks
questions.question: A risk analyst is describing the over-the-counter derivatives business of a large dealer bank to the board. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Over-the-counter trades are negotiated publicly on an exchange, and the dealer's primary source of profit is the commission charged on each transaction.
Over-the-counter trades are negotiated privately between the two counterparties, and the dealer's primary source of profit is the difference between its bid and offer terms.
Over-the-counter trades are negotiated privately, and the dealer's primary source of profit is the appreciation in value of the underlying instruments it holds outright.
Over-the-counter trades are negotiated privately, and dealer banks hold predominantly exchange-traded futures because these carry no counterparty exposure.

questions.solution:
Three features define the line, and each appears in the option set.

| Feature | Position | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| Negotiation | Private, bilaterally between the two counterparties | Terms are bespoke and not publicly observable, which limits transparency and complicates valuation in a stress |
| Profit source | The bid-offer spread, effectively a transaction fee embedded in the price | The dealer aims to run a matched book, taking almost equal and opposite positions, and to earn the spread rather than a directional return |
| Instrument mix | Interest rate swaps are the most widely held, given the nature of banking | Banks are structurally exposed to interest rate risk on both sides of the balance sheet, so swaps are both a client product and a hedging tool |

The matched-book model is what makes the business look low risk in normal conditions and what makes it dangerous in a crisis.
