The maturity management strategies available to a securities portfolio and what each does with the two ends of the curve.

| Strategy | Where the holdings sit | What it buys |
|---|---|---|
| Front-end load | Short end | Liquidity and low price volatility, at the cost of income when the curve is upward sloping |
| Back-end load | Long end | Income, at the cost of liquidity and greater price sensitivity |
| Barbell | Both ends, little in the middle | Liquidity from the short leg and income from the long leg simultaneously |
| Rate expectation | Shifted continually on the rate forecast | The most aggressive approach; its success depends entirely on forecasting accuracy |

How curve shape bears on the choice. With an upward-sloping curve the long end pays materially more, so a front-end load sacrifices real income and a barbell captures part of it while retaining a liquid short leg. With a flat curve there is little reward for extending, so the case for the long leg weakens. With an inverted curve, short rates exceed long rates and the front end is both the more liquid and the higher-yielding choice, which is the one configuration in which the conservative policy is also the profitable one.

The naming convention is the trap and is worth fixing deliberately: front end means short maturities and back end means long maturities, because the labels refer to position along the maturity spectrum rather than to when income arrives.

a.reason: Polarity flip on the label. A front-end load policy concentrates holdings at the short end, which sacrifices rather than maximises income under an upward-sloping curve.

b.reason: The barbell holds both ends with little in intermediate maturities, combining liquidity and income.

c.reason: The same label flip in the other direction. A back-end load policy concentrates at the long end. The observation about an inverted curve favouring short maturities is correct but is attached to the wrong policy.

d.reason: Reverses the strategy entirely. The rate expectation strategy shifts maturities continually in response to the rate outlook and is the most aggressive approach, not a fixed and conservative one.

trap.explanation: Options A and C are the same front-and-back label transposition applied in both directions, so a candidate holding the convention backwards finds confirmation either way. Option C is the more dangerous of the pair because it pairs the flipped label with a correct statement about inverted curves. Fix the convention before reading the options.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Apply investment maturity strategies and maturity management tools based on the yield curve and duration.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 4: The Investment Function in Financial Services Management
questions.question: A portfolio manager is considering whether to use duration rather than calendar maturity to manage the securities portfolio. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Duration equals calendar maturity for any security paying a fixed coupon, which is why the two measures can be used interchangeably for maturity management.

Portfolio immunisation sets the duration of the portfolio equal to the manager's planning horizon, so that price risk and reinvestment risk offset and the realised return is protected whichever way rates move.
Portfolio immunisation protects the realised return against both interest rate movements and credit deterioration in the securities held.
Because duration is fixed at purchase, an immunised portfolio requires no rebalancing for the remainder of the planning horizon.

questions.solution:
Immunisation as the duration-based maturity management tool, and the limits of what it protects.

Duration is a value- and time-weighted measure of maturity, and it is the operative measure for maturity management because it captures when cash is actually returned rather than when the contract ends.

Immunisation condition: portfolio duration = planning horizon

Why matching the horizon works. A rate rise imposes two offsetting effects. Market values fall, which is price risk, and coupons are reinvested at higher yields, which is a reinvestment gain. When duration equals the horizon the two effects cancel, so the realised return over the horizon is protected whichever way rates move.

| Property | Position |
|---|---|
| Duration against calendar maturity | Duration is less than maturity for any instrument paying out over time; the two are equal only for zero-coupon securities, single-payment loans and Treasury bills |
| What immunisation protects | Interest rate risk only; credit risk is untouched and must be managed separately |
| Stability of the position | Duration drifts as rates change and as instruments approach maturity, so an immunised portfolio requires continual and costly rebalancing |

a.reason: Factually wrong. Duration is below calendar maturity for any coupon-paying instrument, and equality holds only for zero-coupon and single-payment securities, which is precisely why the two measures are not interchangeable.

b.reason: Matching duration to the planning horizon offsets price risk against reinvestment risk and protects the realised return.

c.reason: Scope error. Immunisation addresses interest rate risk. It does nothing about credit deterioration, which requires separate management.

d.reason: Reverses the dynamic property. Duration changes as rates move and as instruments season, so immunisation is a continual rebalancing exercise rather than a one-off trade.

trap.explanation: Option C is the substantive trap, because immunisation carries a connotation of general protection and candidates over-extend it. It is specific to rate risk. Option D is the static-duration assumption, which is the same error that makes duration gap management costly in practice: a matched position does not stay matched.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Assess the key components of a contingency funding plan.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 11: Contingency Funding Planning
questions.question: A risk manager is documenting the components of the bank's contingency funding plan framework. Each of the following is a component of that framework EXCEPT:

options.text: Governance and oversight, defining roles, committees and decision rights.
Monitoring and escalation, including early warning indicators and defined escalation levels.
Scenario and liquidity gap analysis, aligned to the liquidity stress testing framework.
Liquidity monitoring, being the routine business-as-usual reporting of the bank's daily liquidity position.

questions.solution:
The structure of the CFP framework and the boundary between contingency planning and business-as-usual liquidity management.

The framework has four components, each answering a different question about a contingency:

| Component | Question answered |
|---|---|
| Governance and oversight | Who decides, through which committees, with what authority |
| Scenario and liquidity gap analysis | Which events are planned for, and how large is the gap under each |
| Monitoring and escalation | What signals a deteriorating position, and at which level of severity does each response engage |
| Contingent actions | What the bank can actually do, in what order, and how much each action raises |

Routine liquidity monitoring is a business-as-usual activity. It runs continuously regardless of whether any contingency is contemplated, and it belongs to the daily reporting suite rather than to the plan. The plan's monitoring component is narrower and different in kind: it concerns early warning indicators and escalation triggers, not the routine reporting of the daily position.

On the early warning indicators within the monitoring component, the factors considered are macro-environment, industry and institution-specific measures. A generic 'financial measures' category is not one of them, because every one of the three named categories is expressed through financial measures.

a.reason: Governance and oversight is a stated component of the CFP framework.

b.reason: Monitoring and escalation, including early warning indicators and escalation levels, is a stated component.

c.reason: Scenario and liquidity gap analysis is a stated component and is the link to the stress testing framework.

d.reason: Routine liquidity monitoring is business-as-usual reporting. The plan's monitoring component concerns early warning indicators and escalation, not the daily position report.

trap.explanation: The exception is a scope error rather than a fabrication: routine liquidity monitoring is a real and essential activity, simply not a component of the contingency plan. That makes it harder to reject than an invented item. The discriminating question is whether the activity exists only because a contingency is contemplated. Governance, scenarios, escalation and contingent actions do; daily position reporting does not.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Assess the key components of a contingency funding plan.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 11: Contingency Funding Planning
questions.question: Roy Jakes is designing a contingency funding plan and is identifying the stakeholders whose involvement the plan requires. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: The internal audit committee should be a decision-making stakeholder within the plan, since its independence makes it well placed to authorise contingent funding actions.
The corporate treasury function monitors the ongoing business, funding, risk and liquidity profile as part of its business-as-usual activities, and that monitoring is what feeds the plan.
Operations and technology should be excluded from the stakeholder group, since contingent funding decisions are financial rather than operational.
The plan should be designed by the risk function alone, so that its independence from the business is preserved and its conclusions cannot be contested.

questions.solution:
Which functions participate in contingency funding planning, and the distinction between executing the plan and providing independent assurance over it.

The plan requires participation from the functions that will have to act, and independent assurance from a function that will not.

| Function | Role in the plan |
|---|---|
| Corporate treasury | Monitors the ongoing business, funding, risk and liquidity profile as a business-as-usual activity; that monitoring is the plan's input, and treasury executes most contingent actions |
| Management committee | Decision-making authority at the higher escalation levels |
| Risk and capital committee | Oversight of the liquidity risk profile and of the limits framework |
| Operations and technology | Essential. Contingent actions require settlement, collateral movement, payment and system capability, and an action that cannot be operationally executed is not an action |
| Internal audit | Not a decision-making stakeholder. It provides independent assurance over the framework, which is incompatible with participating in the decisions it must later review |

The internal audit exclusion is a straightforward three-lines-of-defence point. Audit cannot independently assess a plan it helped design and execute, so its involvement is assurance rather than participation.

Operations and technology deserve emphasis in the other direction. A plan listing a contingent action the bank cannot operationally perform within the required timeframe is worse than no plan, because it creates false assurance. This is the reason for break-glass testing.

a.reason: Role misassignment. Internal audit provides independent assurance over the framework and is not a decision-making stakeholder within it; participating would compromise the independence the option relies on.

b.reason: Treasury's business-as-usual monitoring of the business, funding, risk and liquidity profile is the input the plan draws on.

c.reason: Scope error. Operations and technology are essential stakeholders, because contingent actions must be executable through the bank's systems and settlement capability.

d.reason: Reverses the design principle. A plan built by one function in isolation will lack the operational and treasury input needed to make its actions real, and insulation from challenge is not a design objective.

trap.explanation: Option A is the role misassignment and it is well constructed, because independence genuinely is internal audit's defining characteristic and the option uses that fact to argue for exactly the wrong conclusion. Independence is a reason to stay out of the decision, not a qualification to make it. Option C fails a practical test that recurs throughout this material: a contingent action that cannot be operationally executed does not exist.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Assess the key components of a contingency funding plan.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 11: Contingency Funding Planning
questions.question: A bank's contingency funding plan defines a series of escalation levels aligned to scenarios, contingent actions and liquidity measures. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: The first escalation level represents elevated monitoring of market conditions and their effect on business performance, before any material idiosyncratic deterioration has occurred.
The first escalation level is the survival level, at which the institution focuses on meeting obligations day to day and all discretionary activity ceases.
The number of escalation levels is prescribed by regulation, so that positions are comparable between institutions.
The ratio of used borrowing capacity to total borrowing capacity measures the cushion that liquid assets provide over obligatory funding needs.

questions.solution:
The graduated structure of CFP escalation levels and the liquidity health ratios that support the escalation decision.

Escalation levels are graduated from watchfulness to survival, and the first level is the mildest.

| Level | Condition | Character of the response |
|---|---|---|
| First | Elevated monitoring of market conditions and their effect on business performance | Watch and prepare; no material idiosyncratic deterioration yet |
| Intermediate | Noticeable market and idiosyncratic events adversely affecting the business and liquidity risk profile | Contingent actions begin to engage |
| Highest | Severe stress | Focus narrows to survival |

There are no prescribed guidelines on the number of levels an institution should adopt. The structure is calibrated to the institution's business model and funding profile, which is consistent with the principles-based character of the supervisory guidance generally.

On the liquidity health ratios that support the escalation decision, the two most confusable are:

| Ratio | What it measures |
|---|---|
| Used capacity to total borrowing capacity | How much borrowing capacity remains available to the institution, expressed as capacity used against capacity available |
| Liquid assets to obligatory funding needs | The cushion liquid assets provide over required funding, used to track assets available to offset volatile funding |

Option D swaps these two definitions, which is the most likely error on this material.

a.reason: The first level is elevated monitoring of market conditions and their business impact.

b.reason: Sibling swap across the escalation ladder. Survival is the character of the highest level, not the first.

c.reason: Factually wrong. There are no guidelines prescribing the number of escalation levels; the structure is set by the institution.

d.reason: Sibling swap between two liquidity health ratios. Used capacity to total borrowing capacity measures remaining borrowing headroom; the liquid asset cushion over obligatory funding needs is a different ratio.

trap.explanation: Option B is the escalation-ladder swap and is tempting to anyone who recalls that survival appears in the framework without recalling where. Ladders are always tested at their ends, so fix the first and last rungs. Option D is a definitional swap between two ratios whose names are similar enough that the distinction is easy to lose; read what sits in the denominator.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Assess the key components of a contingency funding plan.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 11: Contingency Funding Planning
questions.question: A contingency funding plan identifies events and indicators that would adversely affect the institution's liquidity. Each of the following would have a negative liquidity impact or serve as an early warning indicator EXCEPT:

options.text: Shifting the funding mix from short-term sources toward long-term sources.
The intraday debit cap with the central bank's payment system being exceeded.
Real or perceived negative publicity concerning the institution.
The institution cancelling loan commitments and refusing to renew maturing loans.

questions.solution:
Distinguishing developments that worsen the liquidity position from those that improve it, including actions the institution itself takes.

Three of the four items signal or cause deterioration. One is a deliberate improvement.

| Item | Effect | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Shift from short-term to long-term funding | Improvement | Reduces rollover risk and lengthens the funding profile. It costs more, through the term liquidity premium, but strengthens the position |
| Intraday debit cap exceeded | Negative | The institution has run beyond its permitted intraday overdraft, indicating that intraday liquidity is insufficient for its payment flows |
| Negative publicity, real or perceived | Negative | Counterparty and depositor confidence is the transmission channel; perception alone is enough |
| Cancelling loan commitments and refusing renewals | Negative | An observable signal that the institution is conserving liquidity, which the market reads as distress and which damages franchise value |

The fourth item is the subtle one. Cancelling commitments conserves cash in the immediate term, so it looks like a liquidity improvement on the cash flow projection. It is listed as a warning indicator because of what it signals: an institution that has begun withdrawing credit from its own customers is visibly rationing liquidity, and that visibility triggers the confidence effects that make the position worse.

An increase in asset quality would likewise be an improvement rather than an indicator, and is the corresponding trap on the early warning indicator list.

a.reason: Lengthening the funding profile reduces rollover risk and strengthens the liquidity position.

b.reason: Breaching the intraday debit cap indicates insufficient intraday liquidity for the institution's payment flows.

c.reason: Negative publicity, whether real or merely perceived, is a named early warning indicator operating through confidence.

d.reason: Cancelling commitments and refusing renewals is a named warning indicator, because it signals that the institution is rationing liquidity.

trap.explanation: Option D is the item most often misjudged, because on a pure cash flow view it conserves liquidity. It is on the list for its signalling effect rather than its cash effect, which is the recurring lesson of the dealer bank material: in a confidence-driven environment, defensive actions are read as confirmation of trouble. Ask not only what an action does to the cash, but what it tells the market.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Assess the key components of a contingency funding plan.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 11: Contingency Funding Planning
questions.question: A bank is assessing the data and reporting component of its contingency funding plan. Which of the following is most consistent with a sound design?

options.text: Reporting during a contingency should be produced at the same frequency and granularity as business-as-usual reporting, so that comparability with prior periods is preserved.

The plan should specify in advance the data required at each escalation level, the systems that will produce it and the owners responsible, and should be tested so that the reporting can actually be produced under stress conditions.
Data requirements should be determined once a contingency arises, since the information needed depends on the nature of the event and cannot be anticipated.
Reporting should be confined to consolidated group-level positions during a contingency, since entity-level detail slows decision-making at the point when speed matters most.

questions.solution:
Why the data and reporting component must be built and tested before a contingency, and at what granularity it must operate.

The data and reporting component answers a question the other four components assume: can the institution actually see its position, in the detail required, at the speed the decision demands?

| Requirement | Why |
|---|---|
| Data specified in advance for each escalation level | A contingency is not the moment to discover which fields are needed. The level determines the detail: elevated monitoring needs less than a survival scenario |
| Named systems and named owners | Escalation routes fail when nobody is accountable for producing the number |
| Frequency increases with severity | Business-as-usual monthly or daily reporting is inadequate at higher escalation levels, where intraday visibility may be required |
| Granularity below the group | Positions by entity, currency and jurisdiction, because liquidity is not freely transferable across them and a group surplus can conceal a trapped deficit |
| Tested in advance | The same break-glass logic that applies to contingent actions: a report that cannot be produced under stress does not exist |

The granularity requirement is the one most often understated. Consolidation is exactly what conceals the transfer restrictions and currency mismatches that determine whether a group-level surplus is actually available where it is needed.

a.reason: Scope error. Frequency and granularity must increase with escalation level. Comparability with prior periods is not the objective during a contingency; visibility is.

b.reason: Pre-specified data, systems and owners, tested so that reporting is deliverable under stress.

c.reason: Reverses the design principle and repeats the error that runs through this material: the framework must exist before the event, because during the event there is no capacity to build it.

d.reason: Polarity flip on granularity. Entity, currency and jurisdiction detail is essential precisely because liquidity is not fungible across them, and consolidation would conceal trapped positions.

trap.explanation: Option D is the well-argued wrong answer: speed genuinely does matter in a contingency, and aggregation genuinely is faster to read. It fails because the aggregated number can be positive while the position that matters is negative. Option C is the build-it-when-needed error, which is the same scope trap that appears in the early warning indicator material.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Assess the role of repo transactions in the collapses of Lehman Brothers and Bear Stearns during the 2007 to 2009 financial crisis.
questions.reading: LR2025: Repurchase Agreements and Financing
questions.question: A supervisor is preparing a note on the role repo funding played in the failure of Bear Stearns in March 2008. Which of the following best describes that role?

options.text: Bear Stearns financed a large securities inventory through very short-dated repo, and when cash lenders became unwilling to roll those trades, or would do so only at sharply higher haircuts, the firm could not replace the funding.
Bear Stearns had funded itself predominantly through insured retail deposits, so the failure followed a classic depositor run once its losses became public.
Bear Stearns held no collateral of sufficient quality to enter the repo market at all, which is why it was forced to rely on unsecured commercial paper.
The repo market functioned normally throughout, and the firm's failure was driven entirely by realised credit losses that exhausted its regulatory capital.

questions.solution:
How reliance on overnight secured funding converted a valuation concern into a funding failure for a dealer bank.

A dealer bank funds a large securities inventory in the repo market, overwhelmingly overnight. That structure has two properties that together make it fragile:

| Property | Consequence |
|---|---|
| The whole book must be refinanced every day | There is no time to react in an orderly way. A withdrawal of funding bites within hours |
| The haircut is set by the lender and is not fixed | The same collateral raises less cash if haircuts rise, generating a cash demand with no trade executed |

Doubts about collateral or counterparty $\rightarrow$ haircuts rise and rolls are refused $\rightarrow$ assets sold to fund the shortfall $\rightarrow$ prices fall $\rightarrow$ haircuts rise further

The reading records the aftermath directly: in March 2008, after the failure of Bear Stearns, lenders became reluctant to lend even against good collateral and charged relatively high rates of interest. That is the market-wide version of the same mechanism, and it is why the episode is treated as systemic rather than idiosyncratic.

The critical point for the exam is that this is a liquidity failure operating through secured funding. No counterparty defaulted on Bear Stearns, and collateralisation did not protect it, because the exposure that mattered was its own need to refinance rather than anyone's credit exposure to it.

a.reason: Short-dated repo funding a large inventory, withdrawn through refused rolls and wider haircuts.

b.reason: Sibling swap onto the commercial bank failure model. Dealer banks are not deposit funded, and insured retail deposits are the funding least likely to run.

c.reason: Factually reversed. Bear Stearns was a very large participant in the repo market; the problem was the terms on which that market would continue to fund it, not an inability to access it.

d.reason: Reverses the mechanism. The repo market did not function normally, and the failure ran through funding and confidence rather than through capital exhaustion.

trap.explanation: Option B is the model-transplant error: applying the deposit-run template to an institution with no deposits. Dealer banks fail through wholesale channels, which is why deposit insurance, the standard tool for arresting runs, was irrelevant here. Option D is the solvency-liquidity confusion in its most consequential form.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Assess the role of repo transactions in the collapses of Lehman Brothers and Bear Stearns during the 2007 to 2009 financial crisis.
questions.reading: LR2025: Repurchase Agreements and Financing
questions.question: A risk analyst is describing what the Lehman Brothers bankruptcy revealed about the fragility of wholesale bank funding. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Financial firms' commercial paper issuance declined precipitously after the Lehman bankruptcy because the paper could no longer be placed, illustrating how quickly funding conditions can change.
Financial firms' commercial paper issuance was largely unaffected by the Lehman bankruptcy, since the market distinguished cleanly between the failed firm and other issuers.
The Federal Reserve declined to intervene in the commercial paper market, on the ground that supporting unsecured wholesale funding would create moral hazard.
Commercial paper issuance by financial firms had been declining steadily from 2004, so the Lehman bankruptcy merely accelerated a trend already well established.

questions.solution:
The speed with which wholesale funding markets close, and the official response when they do.

The commercial paper market after the Lehman bankruptcy is the reading's illustration of how quickly funding conditions can change and of the fragility of bank funding generally.

| Period | What happened |
|---|---|
| 2004 to end 2007 | Issuance by AA-rated financial firms grew rapidly as leverage and balance sheets expanded |
| 2007 to 2008 | Borrowing became more volatile but continued to grow, as banks financed previously off-balance-sheet assets and met drawdowns on credit lines granted earlier |
| After the Lehman bankruptcy | Issuance declined precipitously, because the paper could no longer be placed at any price |

The middle row deserves attention in its own right. The growth in issuance immediately before the collapse was not healthy expansion: banks were funding assets that had returned to the balance sheet from off it, and funding drawdowns on committed lines granted in better times. Both are the contingent exposures crystallising, which is the wrong-way pattern that appears throughout this syllabus.

The official response was direct intervention in the market rather than abstention. The Federal Reserve established the Commercial Paper Funding Facility, which purchased commercial paper from issuers unable to roll it over, and the Asset-Backed Commercial Paper Money Market Mutual Fund Liquidity Facility, which lent to financial institutions, amid fears of a run on money market mutual funds.

a.reason: Issuance fell precipitously because the paper could no longer be placed, which is the reading's illustration of funding fragility.

b.reason: Reverses the outcome. The market did not discriminate cleanly; issuance by AA-rated financial firms as a class collapsed.

c.reason: Factually wrong. The Federal Reserve intervened through the Commercial Paper Funding Facility and the Asset-Backed Commercial Paper Money Market Mutual Fund Liquidity Facility.

d.reason: Reverses the trend. Issuance grew rapidly between 2004 and the end of 2007 and continued to grow, more volatilely, into 2008. The decline was abrupt rather than the continuation of an existing trend.

trap.explanation: Option D is the most plausible-sounding distractor because a long decline would make the collapse look like an orderly adjustment. The opposite is the point: issuance was growing right up to the event, which is what makes the reversal an illustration of fragility rather than of gradual repricing. Option C inverts a well-documented policy response.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Compare the use of general and special collateral in repo transactions.
questions.reading: LR2025: Repurchase Agreements and Financing
questions.question: A repo trader at Alameda Bank is looking to lend cash against bonds that are trading special. Which of the following best describes what the trader is looking for, and the consequence for the repo rate?

options.text: Bonds in particularly high demand in the securities lending market, which finance at a repo rate below the general collateral rate.
Bonds in particularly high demand in the securities lending market, which finance at a repo rate above the general collateral rate.
Any bond issued by the sovereign, since sovereign paper always finances more cheaply than corporate collateral of the same maturity.
Bonds accepted interchangeably as collateral without regard to the specific issue, which is what makes them cheap to finance.

questions.solution:
The distinction between special collateral and general collateral, and the direction in which the repo rate moves when an issue goes special.

| | General collateral (GC) | Special |
|---|---|---|
| What the cash lender wants | Any bond from an accepted class; the specific issue is irrelevant | One particular issue, usually because it is needed to cover a short or to deliver |
| Who has bargaining power | The cash lender | The collateral owner, because the issue is scarce |
| Repo rate | The GC rate | Below the GC rate, by the special spread |
| Consequence | Ordinary secured funding | The owner finances the position cheaply; the benefit is capitalised into the bond's price |

The direction is the whole point and is worth deriving rather than memorising. Cash lenders compete to obtain a scarce issue, and the only price lever they have is the interest they charge on the cash. Competition therefore pushes the repo rate down. In extreme cases a special can trade at or near zero, or even at a negative repo rate.

Note the role reversal against ordinary intuition: scarcity of the collateral benefits the borrower of cash, not the lender, because the borrower is the one supplying the scarce item.

a.reason: A special is the issue most in demand, and its repo rate sits below the general collateral rate.

b.reason: Polarity flip on the repo rate. High demand for a specific issue pushes its financing rate down, not up.

c.reason: Scope error stated as an absolute. Sovereign issuance is not automatically special; most sovereign paper trades as general collateral. Specialness attaches to a particular issue at a particular time, not to an issuer.

d.reason: Sibling swap. Interchangeable acceptance without regard to the specific issue is the definition of general collateral, which is exactly what a special is not.

trap.explanation: Option B is the polarity flip and it catches candidates who reason that high demand raises price and therefore raises the rate. The rate here is the price of cash, not of the bond, and the scarce item is the bond, so the cash side gets worse terms. Option D is a clean sibling swap between the two collateral categories.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Identify the characteristics of special spreads and explain the typical behaviour of U.S. Treasury special spreads over an auction cycle.
questions.reading: LR2025: Repurchase Agreements and Financing
questions.question: A repo trader is explaining special spreads to a group of newly hired analysts. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: The special spread is the amount by which a bond's repo rate exceeds the general collateral rate, and it widens as demand to borrow the specific issue increases.
The special spread is the general collateral rate less the bond's own repo rate, and it widens as traders' demand to short the specific issue rises relative to the supply available to borrow.
Special spreads are highly predictable at the level of the individual bond, because they are determined mechanically by the issue's coupon and remaining maturity.
A bond trading special finances more expensively than general collateral, which is why holders of special issues earn a lower total return.

questions.solution:
The definition and sign of the special spread, and the supply-and-demand mechanism that sets it.

$$\text{Special spread} = \text{general collateral (GC) rate} - \text{the bond's own repo rate}$$

A bond trades special when its own repo rate sits below the GC rate, so the spread is positive. The economic driver is competition for a scarce item:

Demand to short the issue rises relative to borrowable supply $\rightarrow$ cash lenders compete to obtain it $\rightarrow$ they accept a lower rate on the cash $\rightarrow$ the repo rate falls $\rightarrow$ the special spread widens

Note who benefits. The owner of the special bond captures the advantage, because it can finance the position at a below-market rate. That financing advantage is normally already capitalised into the bond's price, which is why special issues trade rich to otherwise comparable bonds.

On predictability, the reading is explicit: because a bond's specialness depends on the extent to which traders want to short it relative to the supply available for borrow, predicting the special spreads of individual bonds is quite difficult. There is, however, one predominant explanatory factor in the United States, which is the auction cycle.

a.reason: Polarity flip on the definition. A special bond's repo rate is below the GC rate, so the spread is GC less the bond's rate. The demand mechanism stated is right, attached to a reversed definition.

b.reason: GC rate less the bond's repo rate, widening as short demand rises relative to borrowable supply.

c.reason: Reverses the reading's position. Individual special spreads are described as quite difficult to predict, and they are driven by short interest rather than by coupon and maturity.

d.reason: Polarity flip on the financing consequence. A special bond finances more cheaply, which is an advantage to its holder rather than a drag on return.

trap.explanation: Option A is the sharpest distractor because it pairs a reversed sign convention with a correct description of the demand mechanism, so a candidate reasoning from the economics alone will find half of it familiar. Derive the sign rather than recalling it: scarcity of the bond gives the bond's owner bargaining power over the cash lender, so the rate paid on the cash falls.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Identify the characteristics of special spreads and explain the typical behaviour of U.S. Treasury special spreads over an auction cycle.
questions.reading: LR2025: Repurchase Agreements and Financing
questions.question: An analyst is examining overnight repo rates across recently issued U.S. Treasury bonds. Which of the following describes the typical behaviour of special spreads over the auction cycle?

options.text: At each maturity the on-the-run issue trades the most special, followed by the old issue, then the double-old, because the most recent issue is the most liquid and therefore the most attractive to short.
At each maturity the double-old issue trades the most special, because scarcity increases as an issue is absorbed by buy-and-hold investors over time.
Special spreads are uncorrelated with the auction cycle in the United States, since the Treasury issues on a fixed schedule that the market anticipates fully.
The on-the-run 30-year bond has consistently traded more special than the on-the-run 10-year, reflecting the longer bond's greater price sensitivity.

questions.solution:
How specialness decays across the auction cycle and the liquidity mechanism that produces the pattern.

The U.S. Treasury issues on a fixed schedule, with a new ten-year bond sold every three months. The most recently issued bond of a given maturity is the on-the-run (OTR) or current issue; the second most recent is the old issue, the third the double-old, and so on.

| Designation | Repo rate | Special spread |
|---|---|---|
| OTR 10-year | 0.09% | 0.14% |
| Old 10-year | 0.21% | 0.02% |
| Double-old 10-year | 0.21% | 0.02% |
| OTR 30-year | 0.18% | 0.05% |
| Old 30-year | 0.20% | 0.03% |
| Double-old 30-year | 0.21% | 0.02% |

Why the pattern exists. Current issues tend to be the most liquid, with the tightest bid-ask spreads and the capacity to absorb large trades quickly. The reading notes this is partly self-fulfilling: because everyone expects a recent issue to be liquid, those who need liquidity flock to it and thereby create the liquidity they anticipated. Dealers also hold a great deal of a new issue until it seasons and is distributed to buy-and-hold investors.

That liquidity makes the on-the-run issue ideal not only for long positions but for shorts. Most Treasury shorts are held briefly, by a desk hedging its current position, a corporation or underwriter hedging an upcoming issue, or an investor betting rates will rise. Short holders prefer liquid issues so they can cover quickly and cheaply. Concentrated short interest in the on-the-run issue is what drives its repo rate down and its special spread up.

A further regularity the table shows: the OTR 10-year trades more special than the OTR 30-year, and has done so for some time.

a.reason: The on-the-run issue is the most special, followed by the old and then the double-old, driven by the liquidity that attracts short interest.

b.reason: Reverses the ordering. Specialness decays as an issue seasons; the table shows old and double-old ten-year issues at a 0.02% spread against 0.14% for the on-the-run.

c.reason: Contradicts the reading directly, which names the auction cycle as the one predominant explanatory factor for special spreads in the United States.

d.reason: Polarity flip on the maturity comparison. The OTR 10-year trades more special than the OTR 30-year, and price sensitivity is not the driver in any case; short interest relative to borrowable supply is.

trap.explanation: Option B is the intuitive reversal: scarcity ordinarily rises as supply is absorbed, so a candidate reasoning from first principles will expect older issues to be scarcer. The mechanism here runs the other way, because specialness is driven by short demand rather than by float, and short interest concentrates in the most liquid issue. Option D inverts a stated empirical regularity.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Calculate the financing advantage of a bond trading special when used in a repo transaction.
questions.reading: LR2025: Repurchase Agreements and Financing
questions.question: A repo trader is valuing the financing advantage embedded in an on-the-run government bond. The bond was issued on 31 March and currently trades at a special spread of 0.30% below general collateral (GC) rates. The trader expects it to trade at GC rates from 30 September onward. Using the actual/360 convention, which of the following is closest to the financing value per USD 100 of market value?
questions.solution:
The financing value of a bond trading special, being the special spread earned over the period for which the bond is expected to remain special.

A bond is on special when demand to borrow that specific issue is high, so its owner can finance it in the repo market at a rate below the general collateral rate. That discount is the special spread, and it is a real economic benefit to whoever owns the bond.

$$\text{Financing value} = \text{market value} \times \text{special spread} \times \left(\frac{\text{days special}}{360}\right)$$

Step 1. Establish the period over which the bond stays special. It is issued 31 March and is expected to trade at GC rates from 30 September, so the special period runs from 31 March to 30 September:

$$30 + 31 + 30 + 31 + 31 + 30 = 183 \text{ days}$$

(April 30 + May 31 + June 30 + July 31 + August 31 + September 30)

Step 2. Apply the spread over that period:

$$100 \times 0.0030 \times \left(\frac{183}{360}\right) = 100 \times 0.0015250 = \text{USD } 0.1525$$

Interpretation: owning this bond is worth about 15 cents per USD 100 of market value, purely from the cheaper financing it commands, and that advantage is normally already embedded in its price. On-the-run issues therefore trade rich to otherwise comparable off-the-run bonds, and the richness decays as the issue ages toward GC.

a.reason: USD 0.075 uses roughly 90 days rather than the 183 days for which the bond is expected to remain special, halving the period.

b.reason: USD 0.150 uses a 180-day half year rather than the actual 183 days between the two dates. This is a 30/360 assumption applied where the stem specifies actual/360.

d.reason: USD 0.300 applies the full annual special spread without pro-rating it to the special period.

trap.explanation: Option B is the discriminating trap and is only 2% away from the answer: 180 days feels like a half year and 183 is the actual day count between 31 March and 30 September. The stem names the convention, so count the days. Option A is the more damaging error conceptually, since it truncates the special period rather than mis-counting it; the period runs to the date the bond is expected to go GC, not to the next quarter end.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Identify the causes of the U.S. dollar shortage during the Great Financial Crisis.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 19: The US Dollar Shortage in Global Banking
questions.question: A panel is discussing the causes of the U.S. dollar shortage experienced by banks outside the United States during the global financial crisis. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: The shortage arose from an increased appetite for U.S. dollar assets among non-U.S. banks, funded through cross-currency funding in the FX swap market, which left them with a U.S. dollar funding gap when that market became impaired.
The shortage arose because non-U.S. banks reduced their holdings of U.S. dollar assets, which eliminated their need for dollar funding and caused the FX swap market to contract.
The shortage refers to a mismatch between the maturity, currency and counterparty of a bank's assets and liabilities, and has no connection to the international expansion of bank balance sheets.
The shortage was confined to banks with no international operations, since institutions with foreign branches could fund dollar assets locally in the United States.

questions.solution:
The three linked causes of the dollar shortage and the mechanism connecting a bank's asset choice to its funding vulnerability.

The three causes named in the reading are not independent; they are stages of a single mechanism.

| Cause | What it means |
|---|---|
| Appetite for U.S. dollar assets | Non-U.S. banks expanded their holdings of dollar claims sharply. Foreign claims grew from about USD 10 trillion at the start of 2000 to USD 34 trillion by the end of 2007, with international claims rising from around 10% to nearly 30% |
| Cross-currency funding | The practice of investing in one currency and funding in another through FX swaps. Banks lacking a dollar deposit base converted domestic currency funding into dollars |
| U.S. dollar funding gap | The resulting shortfall between dollar assets held and stable dollar funding available, which had to be covered continually in the swap market |

Dollar assets acquired $\rightarrow$ funded through short-dated FX swaps $\rightarrow$ a standing funding gap $\rightarrow$ the swap market becomes impaired $\rightarrow$ the shortage crystallises

The balance sheet expansion sat alongside a period of financial innovation that included growth in the hedge fund industry, the introduction of new financial structures and the spread of universal banking. Auctioning of the U.S. dollar was a policy response to the shortage, not a feature of the innovation period that preceded it.

a.reason: Appetite for dollar assets, funded cross-currency through FX swaps, producing a dollar funding gap.

b.reason: Reverses the direction of the asset move. Non-U.S. banks increased their dollar asset holdings substantially, which is what created the funding requirement in the first place.

c.reason: Half right and then wrong. The maturity, currency and counterparty mismatch is a real characterisation of the exposure, but it is directly connected to the international expansion of bank balance sheets rather than independent of it.

d.reason: Reverses the population affected. The shortage was experienced precisely by banks with international operations and dollar asset books but no dollar deposit base.

trap.explanation: Option B is a clean polarity flip on the asset side, and it is superficially coherent because a shortage does follow from a supply problem. The supply problem here was in dollar funding, not in dollar assets, and the asset appetite is what generated the funding need. Option C is the half-truth construction: a correct description attached to a false claim of independence.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Identify the causes of the U.S. dollar shortage during the Great Financial Crisis.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 19: The US Dollar Shortage in Global Banking
questions.question: A lecturer asks a student to explain maturity transformation across banks' balance sheets in the context of the dollar shortage. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: Banks do not transfer funds from surplus agents holding short-term deposits to deficit agents with long-term financing needs, since that function belongs to capital markets.
A maturity mismatch is needed to fund long-term investment projects, and it allows banks to earn a spread when the yield curve is negatively sloped.
Banks may be motivated to increase their maturity mismatch excessively, making themselves vulnerable to the funding risk associated with rolling over short-term liabilities.
Maturity transformation eliminates the need to roll over short-term liabilities, because the long-dated assets it creates generate matching long-dated cash inflows.

questions.solution:
Maturity transformation as both the bank's economic function and its source of fragility, and why the incentive runs toward too much of it.

Maturity transformation is what a bank is for: it takes short-dated deposits from agents in surplus and funds long-dated projects for agents in deficit. The spread between long and short rates is the reward for performing that function.

$$\text{Spread earned} \approx \text{long asset yield} - \text{short funding cost}$$

which is positive when the yield curve slopes upward.

The incentive problem follows directly from that arithmetic. Because the spread widens as the mismatch is extended, a bank optimising near-term earnings has a standing reason to lengthen assets and shorten liabilities beyond the point that is prudent. The cost of doing so, rollover risk, is not felt until funding markets tighten, so it is systematically under-weighted in the decision.

That is precisely the pattern behind the dollar shortage. Non-U.S. banks accumulated long-dated dollar assets funded through short-dated FX swaps, which is maturity transformation and currency transformation simultaneously. Both legs had to be rolled, and both became difficult at the same moment.

Note the curve direction, which is the trap in option B: the spread is earned under an upward-sloping curve, since that is when long rates exceed short rates. A negatively sloped curve compresses or reverses the reward for the mismatch while leaving the risk intact.

a.reason: Reverses the bank's core function. Transferring funds from short-term surplus agents to long-term deficit agents is exactly what a bank does; that is the definition of maturity transformation.

b.reason: Polarity flip on the yield curve. The spread is earned under an upward-sloping curve. Under a negatively sloped curve short rates exceed long rates and the transformation loses money.

c.reason: The incentive runs toward excessive mismatch, which creates vulnerability to the rollover of short-term liabilities.

d.reason: Reverses the mechanism entirely. Maturity transformation is defined by the obligation to roll short-dated liabilities against long-dated assets; it creates rollover risk rather than removing it.

trap.explanation: Option B is the sharpest because it states a true necessity, that a mismatch is needed to fund long-term projects, and then attaches the wrong curve direction. That pairing of a correct premise with a flipped parameter is the standard construction here. Anchor it with the arithmetic: you earn the spread only when what you receive exceeds what you pay, which requires long rates above short.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Evaluate the importance of assessing maturity and currency mismatches across the balance sheets of consolidated entities.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 19: The US Dollar Shortage in Global Banking
questions.question: A researcher is defining the U.S. dollar funding gap for a study of non-U.S. banks during the global financial crisis. Which of the following is correct?

options.text: The amount of U.S. dollars invested in longer-term assets that is not supported by longer-term U.S. dollar liabilities, being the amount banks must roll over before those investments mature.
The amount by which a non-U.S. bank's U.S. dollar denominated liabilities exceed its U.S. dollar denominated assets.
A situation in which a country lacks a sufficient supply of U.S. dollars to manage international trade effectively.
A position in which an investor holds a high-yielding currency asset financed by a low-yielding currency liability.

questions.solution:
The definition and direction of the dollar funding gap, and its distinction from a trade-based dollar shortage and from a carry trade.

$$\text{U.S. dollar funding gap} = \text{U.S. dollars invested in longer-term assets} - \text{longer-term U.S. dollar liabilities}$$

The gap is the portion of a bank's dollar asset book that must be rolled over before the investments mature. The direction matters: banks were long dollar assets and short stable dollar funding, not the reverse.

Why the shortfall existed. Non-U.S. banks expanded their dollar asset holdings sharply between 2000 and 2007 without a corresponding dollar deposit base, so the difference was met from short-dated wholesale sources and from FX swaps. Evidence from the BIS survey indicates that 78% of FX swap turnover was in contracts maturing in under seven days, so a multi-year asset book was being refinanced weekly. European banks' dollar funding gap had reached USD 1.0 to 1.2 trillion by mid-2007.

Two neighbouring concepts the distractors draw on:

| Concept | Definition |
|---|---|
| Dollar shortage (trade sense) | A country lacking sufficient dollars to manage international trade, paying more dollars for imports than it receives from exports |
| Carry trade | Holding a high-yielding currency asset financed by a low-yielding currency liability, which is a return strategy rather than a funding structure |

a.reason: This is the source definition, and it identifies the rollover obligation that made the position fragile.

b.reason: Polarity flip. Liabilities exceeding assets would mean surplus dollar funding, the opposite of a gap.

c.reason: Sibling swap onto the trade-based meaning of a dollar shortage, which concerns a country's external accounts rather than a bank's balance sheet structure.

d.reason: Sibling swap onto the carry trade, which describes a yield-seeking position rather than a funding shortfall.

trap.explanation: Option B is a single-word polarity flip that inverts the entire mechanism. The sanity check is causal: a bank with more dollar liabilities than dollar assets has too many dollars, and would not have needed central bank swap lines to obtain more.
