questions.loText: Evaluate the importance of assessing maturity and currency mismatches across the balance sheets of consolidated entities.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 19: The US Dollar Shortage in Global Banking
questions.question: An analyst is assessing why the appropriate unit of analysis for a global bank's dollar funding position is the worldwide consolidated entity rather than the individual office. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: A mismatch measured on the balance sheet of one office may be offset or hedged by a position booked in another office, so office-level measurement can show mismatches that do not exist at the group level and conceal others that do.
Office-level measurement is preferable, since liquidity is legally trapped within each jurisdiction and consolidation would understate the group's true exposure.
Consolidation is appropriate because a global bank manages maturity and currency positions office by office, so the consolidated view is simply the arithmetic sum of independent local decisions.
The unit of analysis is immaterial to the measurement of currency mismatch, because foreign exchange swap markets allow any currency position to be converted at negligible cost.

questions.solution:
Why worldwide consolidated positions are the correct unit for measuring maturity and currency mismatch, and the limits of that principle.

Banks active internationally operate numerous offices across many countries, and they manage maturity and currency positions on a consolidated global basis rather than office by office. The analytical consequence is direct: a significant mismatch measured on one office's balance sheet may be offset or hedged by an on-balance-sheet or off-balance-sheet position booked elsewhere in the group.

Office-level view $\rightarrow$ mismatches that are hedged elsewhere appear real, and mismatches created across offices disappear

The source is explicit that taking banks' worldwide consolidated positions as the unit of analysis is one of the central points of the study, and it is what allowed the dollar funding gap to be measured at all. A gap of USD 1.0 to 1.2 trillion for European banks is a group-level quantity; no single office's balance sheet would have shown it.

The important qualification. Consolidation is the right unit for measuring the mismatch, but it is not a claim that liquidity is freely transferable. Transfer restrictions, local regulatory ring-fencing and currency conversion costs all limit whether a consolidated surplus can actually be applied where a deficit sits. Both statements are true at once: measure at the group level, then test whether the offsetting position can be mobilised.

a.reason: Positions booked in one office may hedge exposures in another, so only the consolidated view measures the group's true mismatch.

b.reason: Confuses measurement with mobility. Trapped liquidity is a real constraint on using a surplus, but it does not make office-level measurement the correct way to size a group's mismatch.

c.reason: Reverses the management model. Banks manage these positions on a consolidated global basis, not as independent local decisions later summed.

d.reason: Absolute-claim trap. Costless and available conversion is precisely the assumption that failed during the dollar shortage, when obtaining dollars through FX swaps became expensive and at times unavailable.

trap.explanation: Option B is the sophisticated wrong answer, because trapped liquidity is genuinely important and appears elsewhere in this syllabus as a reason to disaggregate. The two ideas answer different questions: consolidation is how you measure the mismatch, disaggregation is how you test whether the offset can be used. Option D is the fungibility assumption stated as an absolute.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Evaluate the importance of assessing maturity and currency mismatches across the balance sheets of consolidated entities.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 19: The US Dollar Shortage in Global Banking
questions.question: A banking group conducting a consolidated liquidity stress test operates subsidiaries subject to liquidity transfer restrictions and holds material balances in several currencies. Which of the following approaches is most appropriate?

options.text: Assess the effect of the transfer restrictions on enterprise-level liquidity under both normal and stressed conditions, and reflect the liquidity impact of currency conversion requirements so that offshore subsidiaries are not assumed to be free of currency mismatch.
Suspend the consolidated stress test until the transfer restrictions are lifted, since a consolidated result computed under restrictions would be misleading.
Conduct the consolidated stress test in the home currency alone, on the basis that any surplus currency can be converted as required at prevailing rates.
Net liquidity surpluses in unrestricted entities against deficits in restricted entities, since the group is a single economic unit for stress testing purposes.

questions.solution:
Why liquidity is not fungible across legal entities or currencies, and how a consolidated stress test must reflect both constraints.

A consolidated balance sheet implies that liquidity can move freely within the group. In practice two constraints prevent it, and both must be modelled rather than assumed away.

| Constraint | Source | How the stress test must treat it |
|---|---|---|
| Transfer restrictions | Local regulators require subsidiaries to retain liquidity locally; legal, regulatory and operational impediments limit upstreaming | Assess the effect on enterprise-level liquidity under both normal and stressed conditions, since restrictions typically tighten under stress |
| Currency | A surplus in one currency does not meet an obligation in another without conversion, and the swap market may be impaired precisely when conversion is needed | Reflect the liquidity impact of currency conversion requirements, avoiding an assumption that offshore subsidiaries face no mismatch |

The phrase 'both normal and stressed conditions' is doing real work. Restrictions that are loosely applied in calm markets are enforced strictly when a host regulator becomes concerned, so modelling only the normal case understates trapped liquidity exactly when it matters.

The currency constraint connects directly to the dollar shortage material. Non-US banks relying on FX swaps to convert domestic currency surpluses into dollar obligations found that route expensive and at times unavailable during the crisis, which is why an assumption of costless conversion is not tenable in a stress scenario.

a.reason: Both constraints are modelled explicitly, with the transfer restrictions assessed under normal and stressed conditions.

b.reason: Suspending the exercise removes the analysis precisely where it is most informative. Restrictions are a permanent feature of a cross-border group, not a temporary obstacle to be waited out.

c.reason: Assumes costless and available conversion, which is the assumption that failed during the dollar shortage. Currency mismatch must be modelled, not netted away.

d.reason: Assumes full fungibility across entities, which is exactly what transfer restrictions prevent. A surplus trapped in a restricted subsidiary cannot meet an obligation elsewhere in the group.

trap.explanation: Options C and D are the same fungibility error applied to the two different dimensions, currency and legal entity, and both are attractive because consolidation accounting genuinely does net these positions. Accounting consolidation and liquidity availability are different things. Ask whether the cash could actually be moved, in the timeframe required, under stressed conditions.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe the policy response by international central banks to alleviate the U.S. dollar shortage and assess its effectiveness.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 19: The US Dollar Shortage in Global Banking
questions.question: A central bank economist is describing the international policy response to the U.S. dollar shortage. Under the arrangement, the Federal Reserve extended dollars to foreign central banks against foreign currency collateral, and banks in each jurisdiction accessed those dollars through local auctions. Which of the following best characterises this arrangement, and the principal challenge it resolved?

options.text: International lending of last resort, resolving the constraint that a global institution administering a limited pool of resources could not supply dollars in the volumes required, whereas the Federal Reserve and its counterparts could create them.
International lending of last resort, resolving the constraint that foreign central banks lacked the legal authority to lend to banks in their own jurisdictions.
Cross-currency funding, resolving the constraint that the FX swap market had ceased to price contracts of any maturity.
Balance sheet expansion, resolving the constraint that non-U.S. banks held insufficient high-quality collateral to borrow in the private repo market.

questions.solution:
The structure of the central bank swap network and the specific limitation of a pooled-resource alternative that it overcame.

The arrangement is international lending of last resort. Its mechanics were:

| Step | What happened |
|---|---|
| 1 | The Federal Reserve extended dollars to a foreign central bank against collateral in that central bank's own currency, at a notional exchange rate fixed for the term |
| 2 | The foreign central bank auctioned those dollars to banks in its own jurisdiction |
| 3 | The transaction reversed at the same fixed rate, so neither central bank took currency risk |

The first challenge resolved. A dollar shortage of this scale could not be met from a pooled fund. A global institution administering finite resources is capped by the size of the pool; the Federal Reserve and its counterparts, by contrast, can create money in whatever amounts they choose. Only an arrangement built on issuing central banks could scale to the requirement.

The second challenge resolved concerns information. Each central bank lends into its own jurisdiction, to banks it already supervises and whose collateral it can assess. The Federal Reserve did not have to evaluate the creditworthiness of individual foreign banks, and it took credit exposure only to the foreign central bank. That structure limits the moral hazard and information problems that direct cross-border lending would have created.

a.reason: The swap network is international lending of last resort, and the unlimited creation capacity of issuing central banks is what a finite pooled resource could not match.

b.reason: Misidentifies the constraint. Foreign central banks could lend domestically; what they lacked was dollars to lend, which is what the swap lines supplied.

c.reason: Sibling swap. Cross-currency funding is the practice that created the exposure, not the policy response to it.

d.reason: Sibling swap onto a different concept, and the diagnosis is wrong: the binding constraint was access to dollars rather than a shortage of collateral.

trap.explanation: Option B is the plausible institutional misreading, since a lender of last resort framing invites the thought that someone lacked authority. The missing item was the currency itself. Option C is the cause-for-cure swap, naming the mechanism that generated the problem as though it were the solution, which is a construction worth watching for on any policy-response question.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe the policy response by international central banks to alleviate the U.S. dollar shortage and assess its effectiveness.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 19: The US Dollar Shortage in Global Banking
questions.question: A supervisor is assessing whether the international policy response to the U.S. dollar shortage was effective. Which of the following best describes its principal achievement?

options.text: It increased the appetite of non-U.S. investors for foreign currency assets, restoring the cross-border flows that had been interrupted.
It eliminated the U.S. dollar funding gap at European banks, which returned to a matched dollar position by the end of 2008.
It mitigated upward pressure on U.S. dollar interbank rates and reduced their volatility, relieving the funding stress on banks outside the United States.
It contributed to the reversal of carry trades, which was the primary channel through which dollar funding conditions normalised.

questions.solution:
What the swap network actually achieved, and the difference between relieving a funding stress and removing the underlying structural gap.

The response is assessed against the problem it was designed to address. Banks outside the United States could not obtain dollars at reasonable cost, which showed up as upward pressure on dollar interbank rates and in sharply elevated volatility of those rates.

Dollars supplied through the swap network $\rightarrow$ the marginal borrower no longer bids up the interbank market $\rightarrow$ upward pressure and volatility subside

That is the stated success: mitigation of upward pressure and interbank rate volatility on the U.S. dollar.

What it did not do, and why that matters for an assessment question. The swap lines addressed the symptom, being the inability to obtain dollars at a reasonable price, not the structure that produced it. The underlying dollar funding gap was a consequence of non-U.S. banks holding long-dated dollar assets without a stable dollar funding base, and that mismatch was reduced only gradually, through balance sheet contraction and asset disposal, over the years that followed. A policy response can be effective and still be a bridge rather than a cure, and an 'assess' objective expects both halves of that judgement.

a.reason: Reverses the direction of the problem. Appetite for foreign currency assets was among the causes of the shortage; increasing it further would have widened the gap rather than relieved it.

b.reason: Overstates the achievement. The swap network relieved the funding stress; it did not eliminate the structural mismatch, which unwound gradually through balance sheet adjustment.

c.reason: Mitigating upward pressure and volatility in dollar interbank rates is the stated success of the international policy response.

d.reason: Misidentifies the channel. The reversal of carry trades was part of the crisis dynamic rather than a mechanism through which the policy response worked.

trap.explanation: Option B is the overstatement trap and is the one an 'assess' objective is built to catch: it names the right beneficiary and the right direction, then claims a structural cure the measure never delivered. Distinguish relieving a funding stress from closing a balance sheet mismatch. Option A is a cause presented as a cure, the same construction as the preceding question.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Identify examples of liquidity funding risk, funding sources, and lessons learned from real cases: Northern Rock, Ashanti Goldfields, and Metallgesellschaft.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 1: Liquidity Risk
questions.question: A chief risk officer is presenting the Northern Rock failure of 2007 to a newly formed board risk committee. Which of the following best describes what happened?

options.text: Northern Rock became insolvent when the credit quality of its mortgage book deteriorated, and the resulting capital shortfall triggered the depositor run.

Northern Rock was solvent and exceeded its regulatory capital requirement, but could not replace maturing short-term funding; public disclosure of its emergency borrowing from the Bank of England then precipitated a retail run.
The run on Northern Rock began before the bank approached the Bank of England, and the subsequent government guarantee of deposits failed to halt the withdrawals.
The Northern Rock case shows that banks should never borrow from a central bank, because such borrowing must be publicly disclosed under Basel III liquidity rules.

questions.solution:
Northern Rock as the canonical demonstration that solvency does not prevent failure, and that central bank borrowing carries stigma risk.

The sequence matters and is testable in detail.

| Date, 2007 | Event |
|---|---|
| August | After the subprime crisis, institutional investors become unwilling to lend to banks heavily involved in mortgages. Northern Rock, which relied on selling short-term debt instruments for much of its funding, cannot replace maturing paper. |
| September | The FSA states that Northern Rock is solvent, exceeds its regulatory capital requirement, and has a good quality loan book. |
| 12 September | Northern Rock approaches the Bank of England and borrows about GBP 3 billion from the Tripartite Authority. |
| 13 September | The BBC business editor breaks the news of the emergency support. |
| 14 September | A run begins, the first on a British bank in 150 years. About GBP 2 billion is withdrawn between 12 and 17 September. |
| 17 September | The Chancellor guarantees all deposits at Northern Rock. The queues disappear and the share price rises 16%. |
| February 2008 | Emergency borrowing reaches GBP 25 billion; the bank is nationalised. |

Two lessons follow. First, solvency is not liquidity: the bank's assets covered its liabilities throughout, and it still failed. Second, central bank borrowing carries stigma. Banks try to keep it secret precisely because the market reads it as a distress signal, which causes other funding sources to dry up, exactly the feedback loop that destroyed Northern Rock.

a.reason: Northern Rock was not insolvent. The FSA confirmed it exceeded its regulatory capital requirement and had a good quality loan book.

b.reason: Solvent, unable to roll over short-term wholesale funding, run triggered by disclosure of emergency borrowing.

c.reason: The sequence is reversed on both counts. The approach to the Bank of England came first and the run followed the news of it; and the deposit guarantee did stop the withdrawals.

d.reason: An absolute claim resting on a fabricated rule. Basel III does not require public disclosure of central bank borrowing, and the lesson is about managing funding conservatively enough to avoid needing it, not about never using the facility.

trap.explanation: Option A is the standard misremembering, and it is attractive because bank failures are usually credit stories. Option C is the sequence trap: candidates recall that a guarantee and a run both happened but not their order or effect. If you can place the three events (borrowing, disclosure, run) in order, this question and its close cousins become free marks.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Identify examples of liquidity funding risk, funding sources, and lessons learned from real cases: Northern Rock, Ashanti Goldfields, and Metallgesellschaft.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 1: Liquidity Risk
questions.question: A risk consultant is reviewing the case of Ashanti Goldfields in 1999. Which of the following best explains the funding liquidity problem the company experienced?

options.text: Ashanti was long gold forward when the gold price collapsed, and the mark-to-market losses on those forwards exhausted its cash reserves.

Ashanti's hedge was economically sound, but a sharp rise in the gold price generated margin calls it could not fund, because the offsetting gain was an increase in the value of gold still in the ground, which is illiquid.
Ashanti rolled short-dated futures forward to hedge long-dated fixed-price supply contracts sold to customers, creating a cash flow mismatch between the two legs.
Ashanti suffered a loss of counterparty and depositor confidence after news emerged that it had sought emergency support, which caused its funding sources to disappear.

questions.solution:
Ashanti as an illustration that hedging an illiquid asset with margin-bearing contracts converts market risk into funding liquidity risk, plus discrimination against the neighbouring cases.

The facts. Ashanti Goldfields, a West African gold miner based in Ghana, sought to protect shareholders from a fall in the gold price by selling gold forward. On 26 September 1999, fifteen European central banks unexpectedly announced that they would limit their gold sales over the following five years. The gold price jumped more than 25%.

The mechanism. A short forward position loses money when the underlying rises. Ashanti was required to post margin, recalculated daily against the value of its forward agreements, and it could not meet the calls. The restructuring that followed included the sale of a mine, dilution of existing equity shareholders, and a restructuring of the hedge positions.

Why this is a liquidity story and not a hedging failure. Economically the hedge worked: the loss on the forwards was offset by the increased value of the gold still in the ground. But that offsetting gain sits in an illiquid asset that cannot be converted to cash to meet a margin call tomorrow morning. The general principle the reading draws is:

Liquidity problems arise when illiquid assets are hedged with contracts subject to margin requirements

The lesson from Ashanti and Metallgesellschaft together is not that firms should avoid forwards and futures, but that they must ensure access to funding sufficient to handle the cash flow mismatches that can arise in extreme circumstances.

a.reason: Both legs are reversed. Ashanti was short forward (it sold gold forward), and the gold price rose by over 25%. A long forward position would have gained on that move.

b.reason: Unfundable margin calls on a short forward position, with the offsetting gain locked in an illiquid asset.

c.reason: This is Metallgesellschaft: stacked short-dated futures rolled forward against long-dated fixed-price supply contracts.

d.reason: This is Northern Rock: loss of confidence following disclosure of emergency borrowing.

trap.explanation: Option A is a double polarity flip (direction of the hedge and direction of the price move) and it is tempting because 'gold miner protects against price declines' primes the reader for a falling price. Options C and D are cross-case distractors, which is GARP's standard construction for case-study items: the wrong answers are the true lessons of the neighbouring cases. Rehearse the three cases as a matched set rather than individually.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Identify examples of liquidity funding risk, funding sources, and lessons learned from real cases: Northern Rock, Ashanti Goldfields, and Metallgesellschaft.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 1: Liquidity Risk
questions.question: While delivering a training session on liquidity risk, Jane Doe, a risk manager at a national regulator, discusses the collapse of Metallgesellschaft in 1993. Which of the following lessons is most effectively exemplified by that case?

options.text: Cash flow mismatches can arise when long-dated fixed-price obligations are hedged with short-dated futures that must be rolled forward and are subject to daily margining.
A forward-sale hedging programme can generate margin calls that cannot be funded when the price of the hedged commodity rises sharply.
Disclosure of emergency central bank borrowing can trigger a retail deposit run at an institution that remains solvent.
Highly leveraged relative-value positions can force a fund to unwind into a flight to quality, widening the very spreads on which it had bet convergence.

questions.solution:
Metallgesellschaft as the canonical maturity-mismatch-in-a-hedge case, discriminated against Ashanti, Northern Rock, and LTCM.

The facts. In the early 1990s Metallgesellschaft (MG) sold a large volume of five to ten year fixed-price heating oil and gasoline supply contracts to customers at six to eight cents above market prices. It hedged that exposure with long positions in short-dated futures contracts that were rolled forward.

The mechanism. The price of oil fell. The long futures positions lost money and generated margin calls immediately, in cash. The offsetting gain sat in the long-dated fixed-price supply contracts, which would only be realised over five to ten years and generated no cash today. The trading was made worse by the fact that MG's positions were very large and were anticipated by others, which is predatory trading.

Short-dated hedge: cash out today | Long-dated exposure: cash in over a decade

The outcome. Senior management and MG's bankers became alarmed at the cash drain. The company closed out all the hedge positions and agreed with customers that the fixed-price contracts would be abandoned. The realised loss was USD 1.33 billion.

Note the sharpest distinction from Ashanti: in both cases margin calls on a hedge could not be funded, but the source of the mismatch differs. Ashanti's mismatch was between a liquid derivative and an illiquid physical asset; MG's mismatch was between a short-dated derivative and a long-dated contractual obligation. That is a maturity mismatch inside the hedge itself.

a.reason: The rolling short-dated futures hedge against long-dated fixed-price contracts is exactly the MG structure, and the cash flow mismatch it created is the stated lesson.

b.reason: This is Ashanti Goldfields: a forward-sale programme hit by a 25% rise in the gold price.

c.reason: This is Northern Rock: solvent, but destroyed by a run following disclosure of Bank of England support.

d.reason: This is LTCM: leveraged relative-value fixed income positions forced to unwind after the 1998 Russian default, reinforcing the flight to quality.

trap.explanation: Every wrong option is a true statement about a different case, which is GARP's preferred construction for case-study items and means no option can be eliminated on plausibility. The only defence is a case-to-lesson grid held in memory. Note also the near-miss between A and B: both involve unfundable margin calls on a hedge, and the discriminator is a single word, whether the mismatch is against a physical asset (Ashanti) or against a long-dated contract (MG).

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Discuss the governance structure of intraday liquidity risk management.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 6: Intraday Liquidity Risk Management
questions.question: A bank is establishing a governance structure for intraday liquidity risk. Which of the following best describes a sound structure?

options.text: Intraday liquidity risk should be governed within the operations function alone, since it arises from payment processing rather than from balance sheet decisions.
The structure should combine active risk management of the intraday position, formal risk assessment of intraday exposures, and integration with the institution's broader risk governance framework.
Because intraday exposures are extinguished by the end of each day, they need not be reflected in the institution's risk appetite statement or limit framework.
Governance should rest on end-of-day reporting, since a position measured at the close is the only figure that can be reconciled and audited reliably.

questions.solution:
The three elements of a sound intraday liquidity risk governance structure and why intraday exposure belongs inside the wider risk framework.

A sound structure has three elements, and the third is the one most often missing in practice.

| Element | What it requires |
|---|---|
| Active risk management | Real-time monitoring of the intraday position, with the ability to intervene during the day rather than observe after the fact |
| Risk assessment | Formal identification and measurement of intraday exposures across payment, clearing and settlement systems, correspondent accounts and client credit lines |
| Integration with risk governance | Intraday liquidity sits inside the institution's overall risk appetite, limit framework and committee structure, rather than being run as a standalone operational matter |

Why integration matters. The tempting view is that an exposure extinguished by the close is not a real exposure. It is: a bank that cannot meet a settlement obligation at two in the afternoon has failed, regardless of what its end-of-day balance sheet would have shown. Intraday liquidity is also the channel through which a clearing bank's withdrawal of credit can halt a dealer's activity within a single day, which is one of the named failure mechanisms.

The operations-only framing fails for the same reason. Intraday exposure is created by business decisions, such as which clients receive intraday credit lines and how large the securities settlement book is, so governance has to reach the functions that make those decisions.

a.reason: Role misassignment. Intraday exposure is generated by business and treasury decisions as much as by payment processing, so governance confined to operations cannot reach the drivers.

b.reason: Active risk management, risk assessment and integration with the broader risk governance framework are the three elements of a sound structure.

c.reason: Scope error. An obligation that cannot be met during the day is a failure whatever the closing position shows, so intraday exposure belongs in the risk appetite and limit framework.

d.reason: Reverses the requirement. End-of-day reporting is inherently lagging for an exposure that arises and must be managed within the day.

trap.explanation: Option C encodes the most common misconception on this material, that a position which nets to zero by the close carries no risk. Settlement obligations are time-specific, and failing one at midday is not cured by a healthy closing balance. Option A is a role misassignment that confines governance to the function where the exposure is observed rather than where it is created.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Discuss the governance structure of intraday liquidity risk management.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 6: Intraday Liquidity Risk Management
questions.question: A bank's risk committee is allocating responsibilities for intraday liquidity risk. Which of the following allocations is most appropriate?

options.text: The business lines that extend intraday credit lines to clients should set the limits governing those lines, since they best understand the client relationships concerned.

Limits on intraday credit extended to clients and on the bank's own use of clearing bank lines should be set independently of the business lines, monitored in real time, and escalated through the same committee structure as other liquidity limits.
Because the bank both receives intraday credit from clearing banks and extends it to clients, the two exposures should be netted and governed as a single limit.
Intraday liquidity limits should be reviewed annually alongside the balance sheet plan, since more frequent recalibration would create instability in client relationships.

questions.solution:
Independence of limit setting, the separation of the two directions of intraday credit exposure, and the frequency at which intraday limits must be reviewed.

Three principles decide this, and each of the wrong options reverses one.

| Principle | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Independence | A business line that sets the limit on the credit it extends will set it generously. Limits are set independently, which is the same principle that governs liquidity transfer pricing and the ownership of the internal price |
| Separation of the two directions | Credit lines the bank receives from its clearing banks and credit lines it extends to clients are monitored separately, because they fail in opposite ways: withdrawal of the former is a funding problem, drawdown of the latter is a credit and liquidity problem |
| Real-time monitoring | An intraday limit checked once a day is not a limit. Measures such as daily maximum intraday liquidity usage and client intraday credit usage exist to be watched during the day |

The netting error in option C is worth dwelling on. The two exposures are not offsetting even though both are labelled intraday credit. In a stress the bank's own lines may be cut at the same moment its clients draw theirs, so the two move against the bank simultaneously. That is the same wrong-way pattern seen in committed credit lines under the LCR stress scenario and in repo haircuts.

a.reason: Role misassignment. Independence of the limit setter from the business line is the point; the relationship knowledge argument is precisely the argument a business line would make for a larger limit.

b.reason: Independent limit setting, real-time monitoring and a common escalation route.

c.reason: Correlation misuse. The two exposures are not offsetting; in stress they move against the bank at the same time, so netting them conceals the combined exposure.

d.reason: Scope error on frequency. An intraday exposure cannot be governed by an annual limit review, and relationship stability is not a reason to leave a risk limit uncalibrated.

trap.explanation: Option C is the subtlest, because netting two exposures with the same name feels like sound aggregation. Ask whether they are correlated in the direction that matters: lines received and lines granted both turn against the bank in a stress, so netting them understates rather than measures the exposure. Option A is the independence failure that recurs wherever a business line is allowed to price or limit its own risk.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Differentiate between methods for tracking intraday flows and monitoring risk levels.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 6: Intraday Liquidity Risk Management
questions.question: A bank's intraday liquidity dashboard is organised into two families of measures. One family records what moved through the bank during the day; the other quantifies how much exposure that activity created. Which of the following correctly names the second family and gives an example?

options.text: Measures for understanding intraday flows, exemplified by total payments.
Measures for quantifying and monitoring risk levels, exemplified by daily maximum intraday liquidity usage and client intraday credit usage.
Measures for understanding income flows, exemplified by intraday interest earned on settlement balances.
Measures of credit level, exemplified by settlement positions at each financial market utility.

questions.solution:
The distinction between measures that describe intraday activity and measures that size the resulting exposure.

The two families answer different questions, and every question on this material turns on keeping them apart.

| | Understanding intraday flows | Quantifying and monitoring risk levels |
|---|---|---|
| Question answered | What moved through the bank today | How much exposure did that activity create |
| Members | Total payments; other cash transactions; settlement positions | Daily maximum intraday liquidity usage; client intraday credit usage; total bank intraday credit lines available and usage; total intraday credit lines to clients and counterparties; payment throughput |
| Character | Descriptive; organised by payment or by venue | Evaluative; each measure compares a position against a limit or a capacity |

The structural tell is the comparison. A risk measure sets something against something else: peak overdraft against the established line, credit lines used against lines available, outgoing payments against total payments or against a deadline. A flow measure simply records. If the measure has a denominator, it belongs to the second family.

Settlement positions is the member most often misfiled, because a net settlement obligation feels like an exposure. It is a flow measure: it records the position at each financial market utility rather than comparing it against a limit.

a.reason: Names the first family, which is the one the stem did not ask about. Total payments is a correct example of it.

b.reason: Measures for quantifying and monitoring risk levels, with daily maximum intraday liquidity usage and client intraday credit usage as members.

c.reason: Not a family in the framework. Intraday measurement concerns liquidity and credit exposure, not income.

d.reason: Not a family in the framework, and settlement positions belongs to the flow family rather than to any risk-level family.

trap.explanation: Option A is the trap created by the stem's ordering: the first family is described first, and a candidate reading quickly will answer for it. The stem asks for the second. Beyond the mechanical risk, use the denominator test, since a risk measure always compares a position against a limit or a capacity while a flow measure merely records.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Differentiate between methods for tracking intraday flows and monitoring risk levels.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 6: Intraday Liquidity Risk Management
questions.question: A bank's intraday liquidity dashboard includes a measure derived by comparing a client's peak daily intraday overdraft against the credit line established for that client. Which measure is this?

options.text: Client intraday credit usage.
Daily maximum intraday liquidity usage.
Payment throughput.
Total bank intraday credit lines available and usage.

questions.solution:
Distinguishing the measures used to quantify and monitor intraday risk by whose position each one measures.

The measures are separated by whose exposure they capture and against what the figure is compared. Getting the actor right decides most questions on this material.

| Measure | Whose position | Construction |
|---|---|---|
| Client intraday credit usage | The bank's client | The client's peak daily intraday overdraft compared with the credit line established for that client |
| Daily maximum intraday liquidity usage | The bank's own | The largest net negative position the bank itself reaches during the day |
| Total bank intraday credit lines available and usage | The bank as borrower | Lines extended to the bank by its clearing banks, and how much is drawn |
| Total intraday credit lines to clients and counterparties | The bank as lender | Lines extended by the bank, in aggregate |
| Payment throughput | Operational | Outgoing payments as a proportion of total payments, or against time markers through the day |

Note the pairing of the third and fourth rows. The bank sits on both sides of the intraday credit market, receiving lines from its clearing banks and extending them to its clients, and the two exposures are monitored separately because they fail in opposite directions. A withdrawal of lines to the bank is a funding problem; a drawdown of lines by clients is a credit and liquidity problem.

Payment throughput is measured for three stated reasons: to track volume patterns and ensure the day's payments are processed on time, to meet financial market utility requirements to submit a target percentage of payments by a deadline, and to identify peak periods and their correlation with intraday liquidity on hand and credit usage.

a.reason: Peak client overdraft against the established client line is client intraday credit usage.

b.reason: Role misassignment. Daily maximum intraday liquidity usage measures the bank's own peak position, not a client's.

c.reason: Payment throughput measures the pace at which outgoing payments are released through the day, not any overdraft against a line.

d.reason: Direction reversed. This measures lines extended to the bank and the bank's use of them, whereas the stem describes a line the bank extended to a client.

trap.explanation: Options B and D are both role misassignments and between them cover the two ways to get this wrong: measuring the bank's own position instead of the client's, and measuring lines received instead of lines granted. On any intraday measure, identify the subject first: whose overdraft, and whose line?

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Differentiate between methods for tracking intraday flows and monitoring risk levels.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 6: Intraday Liquidity Risk Management
questions.question: XYZ Bank monitors its intraday and end-of-day settlement positions at every financial market utility in which it participates, capturing transaction-level detail wherever possible and storing it for later analysis. Which measure for understanding intraday flows is the bank employing?

options.text: Total payments.
Other cash transactions.
Settlement positions.
Total bank intraday credit lines available and usage.

questions.solution:
Matching a described monitoring practice to the correct measure for understanding intraday flows.

The measures for understanding intraday flows are distinguished by what is being counted:

| Measure | What it captures |
|---|---|
| Total payments | Payer and payee information, the payment system used, the time received or originated, routing information, any suspensions, and the credit status of the payment |
| Other cash transactions | Cash movements outside the main payment flows, such as internal book transfers and non-payment cash activity |
| Settlement positions | Intraday and end-of-day settlement positions at each financial market utility in which the bank participates, maximising transaction-level detail for analysis |

The stem matches the third row word for word: settlement positions, at every financial market utility, at transaction level. The identifying feature is that the measure is organised by venue, meaning the FMU, rather than by individual payment.

Why it is monitored separately: a bank's net settlement obligation at a given utility is the single largest intraday exposure it faces at that venue, and it can flip between a receipt and an obligation from day to day. Aggregating it into total payments would conceal the concentration.

a.reason: Total payments captures payer and payee detail, the system used, timing, routing and suspensions for individual payments. It is organised by payment, not by settlement venue.

b.reason: Other cash transactions covers cash movements outside the main payment flows and does not match the stem's description.

c.reason: Monitoring intraday and end-of-day settlement positions at each financial market utility, at transaction level, is the settlement positions measure.

d.reason: Sibling swap onto the risk-monitoring measures. Credit lines available and used is a measure for quantifying risk levels, not for understanding flows.

trap.explanation: Option D is the trap for a candidate reading carefully but confusing the two families of measures: those for understanding intraday flows against those for quantifying and monitoring risk levels. Hold them apart by purpose, since the first describes what moved and the second describes how much exposure was created.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Compare the various approaches to liquidity transfer pricing (zero cost, average cost, and matched-maturity marginal cost).
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 17: Liquidity Transfer Pricing
questions.question: A risk analyst is discussing with her supervisor the alternative approaches to liquidity transfer pricing and the consequences each produces for the bank's balance sheet. Which of the following statements is most likely correct?

options.text: Under a matched-maturity marginal cost of funds approach, the bank's fixed-rate borrowing cost is converted into a floating-rate borrowing cost for the purpose of the internal charge.

Where management remuneration is based on net income, both an average cost-of-funds approach and a zero cost-of-funds approach correctly align the maturity of the bank's lending and borrowing activities.
Under a zero cost-of-funds approach, a bank typically ends up holding long-dated illiquid assets financed by stable long-term liabilities.
The largest maturity transformation on a bank's balance sheet typically arises under an average cost-of-funds approach.

questions.solution:
The mechanics of the matched-maturity marginal cost of funds approach and the distortions produced by the average-cost and zero-cost alternatives.

The three approaches differ in what the business line is charged, and the differences drive predictable balance sheet distortions.

| Approach | What is charged | Distortion produced |
|---|---|---|
| Matched-maturity marginal cost of funds | The marginal cost of funding of the same tenor as the asset, which converts the bank's fixed-rate borrowing cost into a floating-rate internal charge | None by design; this is best practice |
| Average cost of funds | A single blended rate regardless of tenor | Long-dated assets are undercharged and short-dated assets overcharged, so the bank writes too many long assets against short funding |
| Zero cost of funds | Nothing at all | The most extreme case: liquidity appears free, so business lines accumulate long-dated illiquid assets funded by whatever is cheapest, which is short-term wholesale money. This produces the largest maturity transformation |

The ranking matters and is the substance of the question. Zero cost of funds produces the greatest maturity transformation, because the internal price signal is entirely absent. The average cost approach sits between the two: it charges something, but the same something regardless of tenor, so it still systematically favours long assets.

The remuneration point is a governance amplifier rather than a correction. Where managers are paid on net income, an approach that undercharges long-dated assets makes those assets look unusually profitable, so the incentive reinforces the distortion instead of offsetting it.

a.reason: The matched-maturity marginal cost of funds approach converts the fixed-rate borrowing cost into a floating-rate internal charge matched to the asset's tenor.

b.reason: Reverses the effect. Neither approach aligns maturities; both understate the cost of long-dated assets, and remuneration based on net income amplifies the resulting misallocation rather than correcting it.

c.reason: Polarity flip on the funding side. Under a zero cost-of-funds approach the bank accumulates long-dated illiquid assets financed by short-term funding, which is precisely why the approach is dangerous.

d.reason: Sibling swap between the two flawed approaches. The largest maturity transformation arises under the zero cost-of-funds approach, not the average cost approach.

trap.explanation: Option D is the sibling swap and is the most likely miss, because a candidate who knows that flawed LTP causes maturity transformation still has to rank the two flawed methods. Order them by how much price signal survives: zero cost sends none, average cost sends a distorted one, matched-maturity sends the right one. Option C flips the funding leg while keeping the asset leg correct, which makes it read as half-familiar.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe the contingent liquidity risk pricing process and calculate the cost of contingent liquidity risk.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 17: Liquidity Transfer Pricing
questions.question: A treasury analyst is documenting the process by which the bank prices contingent liquidity risk on its committed but undrawn facilities. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Because an undrawn facility consumes no funding until it is drawn, no charge is applied until the first drawdown occurs, at which point the facility is priced as an ordinary loan.

The charge reflects the cost of holding liquid assets against the possibility of drawdown, scaled by the undrawn proportion of the facility and by the estimated probability that the balance is drawn, and it is levied on the business line that granted the facility.
The charge is set equal to the bank's average cost of funds applied to the full facility limit, since the bank must be able to fund the entire commitment.
The charge is levied centrally on the treasury function, which holds the liquidity buffer, rather than on the business line, so that commercial pricing decisions are not distorted.

questions.solution:
The contingent liquidity risk pricing process: what is being priced, how it is scaled, and who bears the charge.

What is being priced is not the loan but the readiness to make it. A committed facility obliges the bank to fund a drawdown on the customer's demand, so the bank must hold liquid assets against that possibility from the moment the commitment is granted. Those assets earn less than the alternatives, and that forgone return is the cost.

$$\text{Contingent liquidity charge} = \left(\frac{\text{undrawn}}{\text{limit}}\right) \times \text{probability of drawdown} \times \text{cost of term funding the cushion}$$

Each term has a purpose:

| Term | Why it is there |
|---|---|
| Undrawn divided by limit | Only the undrawn portion represents a contingent claim; the drawn portion is already an on-balance-sheet loan priced through the ordinary funding charge |
| Probability of drawdown | Charging as though drawdown were certain would overprice the commitment; the probability is a behavioural estimate |
| Cost of funding the cushion | The economic cost being recovered, being the return forgone on the liquid assets held in readiness |

Who pays. The charge falls on the business line that granted the facility. That is the entire point: a line able to grant commitments without being charged for the liquidity they consume will grant too many, which is the incentive problem liquidity transfer pricing exists to correct and which BIS Principle 4 requires banks to address for off-balance-sheet as well as on-balance-sheet activities.

a.reason: Scope error resting on a true observation. An undrawn facility consumes no funding until drawn but consumes contingent liquidity throughout, because the bank must stand ready. Waiting until drawdown means the commitment was free when it was granted.

b.reason: The cushion cost, scaled by the undrawn proportion and the draw probability, charged to the originating business line.

c.reason: Two errors. The relevant cost is that of carrying the liquidity cushion rather than the average cost of funds, and applying it to the full limit ignores both the drawn portion and the drawdown probability.

d.reason: Role misassignment that inverts the purpose. Charging treasury leaves the business line facing no price signal, which is precisely the distortion the mechanism is designed to remove.

trap.explanation: Option A is the most instructive miss, because its premise is correct and widely believed: an undrawn line really does absorb no cash. It absorbs liquidity capacity, which is what is being priced. Option D fails the incentive test that decides most liquidity transfer pricing questions: ask who changes behaviour in response to the charge, and route it there.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe the contingent liquidity risk pricing process and calculate the cost of contingent liquidity risk.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 17: Liquidity Transfer Pricing
questions.question: A line of credit granted to a corporate customer has a limit of USD 80 million, of which USD 24 million has already been drawn. The bank assumes a 45% probability that the customer will draw the remaining balance, and the cost of term funding the assets held in the liquidity cushion is 24 basis points. Which of the following is closest to the rate the bank should charge for the contingent liquidity risk of this facility?

options.text: 7.56 bps

questions.solution:
Pricing the contingent liquidity risk of an undrawn commitment, as the undrawn proportion of the facility weighted by the draw probability and the cost of carrying the cushion.

$$\text{Contingent liquidity charge} = \left(\frac{\text{undrawn amount}}{\text{total limit}}\right) \times \text{probability of drawdown} \times \text{cost of term funding the cushion}$$

Step 1. Undrawn amount:

$$80 - 24 = \text{USD } 56 \text{ million}$$

Step 2. Undrawn proportion of the facility. The charge is expressed as a rate on the whole facility, so the undrawn amount is scaled by the limit:

$$56 \div 80 = 0.700$$

Step 3. Weight by the probability that the balance is drawn, and by the cost of holding the cushion that must stand behind it:

$$0.700 \times 0.45 \times 24 = 7.56 \text{ basis points}$$

Interpretation: the bank must hold liquid assets against the possibility of the customer drawing the remaining USD 56 million, and those assets earn less than the alternatives. The 7.56 basis point charge passes that carrying cost to the business line that granted the facility, so the commitment is priced rather than given away. Without the charge, undrawn lines look free to the originating line and are granted too freely, which is exactly the exposure that crystallised through drawdowns on lines of credit in the LCR stress scenario.

a.reason: 0.756 bps is the correct figure divided by ten, a decimal slip.

b.reason: $0.70 \times 0.45 \times 24 = 7.56$ basis points.

c.reason: 10.80 bps = $0.45 \times 24$, omitting the undrawn proportion. This charges as though the entire facility were undrawn.

d.reason: 16.80 bps = $0.70 \times 24$, omitting the draw probability. This charges as though drawdown were certain.

trap.explanation: Options C and D are each a dropped term, and the two together define the calculation: the charge scales by both how much of the facility is still available and how likely it is to be taken. Dropping either one overstates the charge, so any answer above the correct figure should prompt a check that both weights were applied.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Identify key factors that affect the cross-currency swap basis.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 20: Covered Interest Rate Parity Lost
questions.question: John Paul, chief investment officer at Herald Advisors, is concerned about the cross-currency basis that has persisted since the global financial crisis. Which of the following is the most suitable explanation for the continued presence of a non-zero basis between two currencies?

options.text: Regulatory change has expanded the scope for speculative proprietary trading by US banks, increasing the capital devoted to closing the basis.
Given the general decline in global interest rates, the inclusion of a liquidity risk cost in swap pricing is no longer necessary.
The basis increasingly incorporates the financing and balance sheet costs incurred by arbitrageurs in maintaining the positions that would otherwise close it.
Because arbitrage positions largely eliminate counterparty exposure, the associated credit valuation adjustment costs have risen.

questions.solution:
Why covered interest parity ceased to hold after 2008: the arbitrage that enforces it is no longer free, so the basis reflects the cost of executing it.

Covered interest parity is an arbitrage relationship, not a law of nature. It holds only for as long as someone stands ready to trade any deviation away at negligible cost.

CIP holds $\Leftrightarrow$ the arbitrage is costless and unconstrained

Before 2008, dealer balance sheets were cheap and lightly constrained, so even a small deviation attracted enough capital to close it. Afterwards, several changes made carrying the position expensive:

| Change | Effect on the arbitrage |
|---|---|
| Leverage ratio and risk-based capital requirements | The position consumes balance sheet regardless of how low its market risk is, so it must earn a return on that capital |
| Higher and more differentiated bank funding costs | The arbitrageur must fund the position, and that funding is no longer available at a uniform risk-free rate |
| Counterparty credit charges | Credit valuation adjustment and margin requirements add a further carrying cost |
| Reduced proprietary risk taking | Less capital is available to be deployed against deviations in the first place |

The result is a persistent equilibrium rather than a persistent mispricing. The basis settles at roughly the cost of holding the position, so it is not an unexploited profit: it is the price of the balance sheet required to exploit it. Structural demand for dollar funding by non-US banks, the dollar funding gap, then determines the sign and size of that basis.

a.reason: Reversed. Post-crisis regulation, including the Volcker rule and higher capital requirements, reduced the capital available for speculative proprietary trading. Less arbitrage capital is part of why the basis persists.

b.reason: Reversed. Liquidity and funding risk costs became more significant in swap pricing after the crisis, not less, and the level of interest rates does not determine whether such a cost is warranted.

c.reason: The basis has come to reflect the financing and balance sheet costs of carrying the arbitrage position, which is why it no longer converges to zero.

d.reason: Internally contradictory. If arbitrage positions largely eliminated counterparty exposure, credit valuation adjustment costs would fall rather than rise. The premise and the conclusion point in opposite directions.

trap.explanation: Options A and B are polarity flips on post-crisis regulatory and pricing developments, and each would, if true, argue for the basis closing rather than persisting, which is a useful internal check. Option D is self-contradicting: read the causal chain in a distractor and confirm the premise actually supports the conclusion.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Identify key factors that affect the cross-currency swap basis.
questions.reading: LR2025, Ch. 20: Covered Interest Rate Parity Lost
questions.question: A macro strategist is briefing clients on why covered interest rate parity has failed to hold since 2008. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Deviations from covered interest parity are largest at quarter and year ends, because banks reduce balance sheet usage for regulatory reporting dates, which withdraws precisely the capacity the arbitrage requires.
Deviations are largest in the most liquid currency pairs, since high turnover makes the basis more volatile and therefore wider on average.
The persistence of the basis indicates a straightforward unexploited arbitrage, and its size measures the risk-free profit available to any institution willing to take the trade.
Because covered interest parity is a no-arbitrage identity derived from spot and forward rates alone, a non-zero basis can only reflect an error in the quoted forward rate.

questions.solution:
The empirical signature of post-crisis CIP violations, and why the basis is a price for balance sheet rather than an unexploited arbitrage.

The reporting-date pattern is the strongest single piece of evidence that the basis is a balance sheet phenomenon rather than a pricing error.

Quarter end approaches $\rightarrow$ banks shrink balance sheet for reporting $\rightarrow$ arbitrage capacity withdrawn $\rightarrow$ basis widens sharply $\rightarrow$ normalises after the date passes

If the deviation were a genuine free profit, it would not appear and disappear on a calendar schedule tied to when banks report their leverage ratios. That it does is direct evidence that the binding constraint is the availability of balance sheet, not the absence of anyone who has noticed the trade.

The other empirical regularities point the same way. The basis is generally wider for currencies whose banking systems have the largest structural dollar funding needs, because demand for dollars through the swap market is greatest there, and it widens in periods of market stress when balance sheet is scarcest and dollar demand highest. Both are demand-and-capacity effects, not information effects.

The conceptual point to carry into the exam: covered interest parity is enforced by arbitrage, and arbitrage requires a balance sheet. Once the balance sheet has a price, so does the parity relationship.

a.reason: The reporting-date pattern is the characteristic signature, and it identifies balance sheet capacity as the binding constraint.

b.reason: Reverses the relationship. Deviations are widest where structural dollar funding demand is greatest and where balance sheet is scarcest, not where turnover is highest. Liquidity narrows a basis rather than widening it.

c.reason: Misreads the persistence. The basis approximates the cost of carrying the position, so it is not a risk-free profit. If it were, the reporting-date pattern would not exist.

d.reason: Scope error. Covered interest parity involves spot rates, forward rates and the two interest rates, and it is a no-arbitrage relationship only under the assumption of costless, unconstrained arbitrage. Relaxing that assumption, rather than any quotation error, explains the basis.

trap.explanation: Option C is the trap that catches strong candidates, because the textbook framing of covered interest parity really does present a deviation as an arbitrage. The post-crisis lesson is that the arbitrage has a cost, so the deviation is a price rather than a profit. Option D is a scope error that treats a conditional no-arbitrage result as an unconditional identity.
